The effect of those tweaks likely won’t make a difference in day-to-day wear, but stare at the Apple Watch Series 12 long enough and it does seem to have larger bezels than its predecessor. Watch Series 12 vs. Watch Series 11: Sensors and chips A heavy area of focus during Apple’s presentation on the Apple Watch Series 12 was its updated sensors, and for a good reason: They’re a key reason the company is offering the majority of the watch’s new software features. Apple calls the new sensor package a “Health Sensing System,” and while it’s technically composed of the same types of sensors available on the Apple Watch Series 11 (electrical heart sensor, optical heart sensor, blood oxygen sensor, and temperature sensor), the company has implemented them in a different way. The new watch features a denser collection of LEDs for always-on heart rate sensing and 32 distinct electrodes in the electrical heart sensor for more accurate ECG readings. Apple claims its updated sensors capture heart rate readings every five seconds and heart rate variability (HRV) readings every five minutes, about 60 times and 24 times more frequently than the Series 11, respectively. The Apple Watch Series 12 is also the company’s first smartwatch with a new chip in two years. The Series 12 has an S11 chip, which is more powerful than the S10 on the Series 11 and Series 10, offers more accurate step tracking, and is capable of running Apple Intelligence and the new health features enabled by the watch’s sensors. Added efficiency from the new processor also enables 10 hours of battery life for outdoor workouts, 25% more than the Series 11. What other features the S11 unlocks down the road remains to be seen, but at the very least it should offer more longevity than the long-in-the-tooth S10. Watch Series 12 vs. Watch Series 11: Health and fitness features The boost in heart monitoring makes new software features possible on the Series 12 that aren’t available on the Series 11. That includes Readiness, a new metric that uses sleep, training load, vitals, and recent activity to determine your physical capacity for the day. All that extra heart monitoring data is also sprinkled throughout watchOS 27, adding things like HRV readings to the Vitals and Heart Rate apps and all-day heart rate data to watch faces and complications. Interestingly, while Apple introduced a redesigned version of the Health app alongside the Series 12, most of its new features aren’t exclusive to Series 12 owners. Outside of the Readiness score, all the app’s other new features should be available if you have a Series 11. Watch Series 12 vs. Watch Series 11: Apple Intelligence Both the Series 12 and Series 11 support Apple Intelligence, and, with watchOS 27, Apple’s revamped AI assistant, Siri AI. That means a dedicated Siri app and suggestions in the Smart Stack, among other AI-enabled features. Apple is also adding a collection of new “Audio Intelligence” features that aren’t coming to the Series 11. Audio Intelligence covers things like Shazam song identification, which can now happen in the background on the Series 12, and accessibility features like Sound Recognition, which can alert you to important sounds like doorbells or a baby crying if you’re deaf or hard of hearing. The more controversial features involve AI transcription. Using the S11 chip and its built-in microphone, the Series 12’s Live Rewind feature can be prompted to listen to your conversation and quickly turn around a 15-second transcript of what was said if you think you missed something. Siri Recap is more expansive, listening throughout the day or during select parts of the day and creating an overall summary of the key things you heard or talked about. Watch Series 12 vs. Watch Series 11: Price Unlike most other Apple products, the Apple Watch Series 12 isn’t dramatically more expensive than the Apple Watch Series 11. The new watch starts at $399 for an aluminum case, $699 for a titanium case, or $899 for a ceramic case. Jumping up to the larger 46mm size raises those prices by $100 for aluminum or $50 for titanium and ceramic. If you add cellular connectivity to the aluminum model, you can add another $100 on top of that. That’s the same starting price as the Apple Watch Series 11, though bumping up to the larger 46mm Series 11 only cost $429 last year, as opposed to the $499 you’ll pay for the 46mm Series 12. Not terrible in the grand scheme of things. If you’re interested in the all-day heart monitoring and Readiness scores of something like the Whoop 5.0 or the Fitbit Air, the Apple Watch Series 12 now matches those competitors while offering more accurate readings overall. If you’re not worried about those features, the Series 11 is still a good alternative, especially because it supports the majority of Apple’s upcoming wearable software features.

item.title: Our Sun Might Actually Be a Planet Killer
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.00
Stellar evolution can be really chaotic, so it’s no surprise that a planet or two—or more—gets sucked into the abyss at some point in cosmic history. According to new research published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, billions of years ago, our young Sun may have gobbled up a planet around 5 to 10 times Earth’s mass. Importantly, the latest analysis strongly suggests that it’s possible to find detectable “fingerprints” of this lost planet inside the Sun. What’s more, this particular model also matches independent measurements of the Sun’s interior, bringing astronomers closer to solving this galactic murder (?) case. “Our new study suggests that a planet several times more massive than Earth may have fallen into the young Sun and left a lasting chemical imprint deep inside it,” Mutlu Yildiz, the study’s sole author and an astronomer at Ege University in Turkey, said in a statement. Powering a star The latest work stems from two separate mysteries. First, conventional solar models generally had trouble replicating actual observations of the solar convection zone, or the star’s outermost layer. Second, compared to other stars, the Sun’s surface had a notable deficiency of lithium compared to similarly sized stars. The reason the latter was an issue was because lithium—composed of three protons—should be among the earliest elements to emerge from stellar evolution. To this peculiar observation, Yildiz had a peculiar proposition: What if an old planet’s consumption altered our star’s chemical composition? “We were interested [in] whether these problems might have a common origin in the early chemical history of the Sun,” Yildiz explained. “Since planets are made of material that is chemically different from the gas in the disc, we wondered whether the early engulfment of a planet could have left a chemical signature inside the young Sun.” Finding the best fit For the study, Yildiz used an open-source module to map stellar evolution across a wide range of theories, exploring different scenarios of accretion that would result in the Sun as we know and see it today. The model that fit best was, indeed, a hypothetical that included the Sun’s consumption of a “super-Earth-mass” planet billions of years ago. The numbers are also consistent with known measurements of the Sun’s interior and lithium content. It also may explain why, compared to similar stellar systems, our solar system doesn’t have as many super-Earth-sized planets. “We thought planetary engulfment might affect the solar structure but did not expect the calculations to converge on such a specific super-Earth mass range,” Yildiz added. “That was one of the most interesting outcomes of the study.” A cold case? In concluding the paper, Yildiz stressed that his calculations “strengthen the physical plausibility” that our Sun swallowed a super-Earth planet. It is not confirmation that this actually happened. Still, the results are a tantalizing candidate for the “key missing ingredient” in our solar and stellar models, according to the paper. So, future theoretical and observational work might want to keep this scenario in mind. “Our paper asks whether the Sun itself could still carry observable evidence that such an engulfment actually happened, and we believe it could,” Yildiz said. “The next step is to see if these fingerprints can be independently detected.”

item.title: AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: ANC Isn’t the Only Upgrade
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.64
Apple’s annual hardware event had a lot to offer this year. Easily the biggest splash came from the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first-ever foldable phone, with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also giving its $2,000 foldable a run for its money. While a new generation of AirPods, the AirPods 5, might not achieve the same highs as a first-of-its-category iPhone, there are quite a few things you should know if you’re in the market for new AirPods without the “Pro” name. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: ANC Non-Pro AirPods aren’t known for their prowess in active noise cancellation (ANC). It’s not that Apple doesn’t have the chops; it’s that they’re only semi-in-ear, meaning they don’t have silicone ear tips. Because of that, they don’t have the same tight seal as the AirPods Pro, which helps block out sound. That being said, they do have ANC, and it’s not all created equal among generations. According to Apple, the AirPods 5 have 50% better noise cancelling than the AirPods 4, which is a pretty drastic increase. It’s hard to really relay how that feels without hearing them myself, but on paper, it’s hard to argue. If you want better ANC, the AirPods 5 are the way to go, even if AirPods Pro 3 blow both of those pairs out of the water. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Sound Good ANC doesn’t mean much if the sound isn’t just as good, and in this generation, Apple improved in that department, too. Apple says the AirPods 5 have a new “multiport architecture” that’s based on the AirPods 3 Pro. The result, according to Apple, is “richer, more detailed sound across an even wider range of ear geometries.” Sound, again, is one of those things you have to hear to believe, but clearly Apple paid attention to improving the sound quality in this generation, so you should expect a step up over the last generation. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Battery life Battery life is where things get a little more complicated. While the base model of AirPods 5 has the same battery life as its predecessor—a pretty pedestrian four hours on a single charge when ANC is activated—you can actually shell out a bit more money for a different tier with some extra juice. The $149 AirPods 5 (that’s $20 more than the base) will get you an extra hour of battery life with ANC on. That’s still not great in the scheme of most wireless earbuds (about six hours is pretty standard), but if you’re strictly comparing between generations of non-Pro AirPods, then the more expensive model of AirPods 5 definitely take the cake. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Features While both generations share a lot of the same features, there are some subtle differences to note outside of ANC. In addition to better ANC, the AirPods 5 also have next-gen Adaptive EQ, according to Apple. Thanks to this upgraded Adaptive EQ, the AirPods 5 can tune sound to the specific shape of your ears across a larger range of frequencies. The result, Apple says, is a “more immersive and accurate sound.” AirPods 4 do have Adaptive EQ, for the record, but Apple claims that the new generation just does it better. The differences continue to pile up when you consider the more expensive tier of AirPods 5. By shelling out $149, you get two things that neither the base tier of AirPods 5 nor the AirPods 4 have: wireless charging and stem controls. For the first time, the more expensive tier now lets you swipe on the wireless earbuds to control volume. Not groundbreaking, but it can be better than reaching for your phone every time. Similarly, wireless charging in the charging case isn’t mind-blowing, but it’s nice to have. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Fit This is one area where not much has changed. In its announcement, Apple didn’t say much about any kind of physical redesign, so the AirPods 5 likely look and feel pretty similar to the AirPods 4. These are still semi-open-ear, meaning they nest in your outer ear instead of being inserted like AirPods Pro.

item.title: A Metal Detectorist Just Discovered Finland’s Largest Hoard of Viking Age Silver—But Was It Plunder?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.08
The municipality of Sysmä and the surrounding Päijät-Häme region of south-central Finland seem to have been a hot spot for people looking to bury their treasure roughly one millennium ago. Multiple stashes of precious items have been uncovered in the area over the past decade, according to local archaeologist Esko Tikkala of the Lahti Historical Museum. But for the first time in well over a century, the Sysmä dirt has given up a truly record-breaking hoard: a massive trove of ancient silver coins dating back to the era of the Vikings and collectively weighing in at nearly 10 pounds (4.5 kilograms). Metal detectorist Kalle Lappinen made the discovery a little over a week ago on September 3rd, in a forest just outside the Sysmä “church village” (kirkonkylä). This mass of silver, divided between two containers made of bark, is now the largest known cache of Iron Age treasure ever unearthed in the country—beating a roughly 4.9-pound (2.2-kg) cache of coins and other precious objects found in Nousiainen, to Sysmä’s west, back in 1895. Lappinen dutifully alerted authorities to his discovery, leading to a full excavation of the treasure led by Tikkala the following day, according to a press release from the Lahti Historical Museum, translated via Google. “There are quite a lot of coins in this hoard,” Tikkala told the site Live Science. But, he admitted, “I have not had time to go through them.” Currency exchange According to Tikkala, this as-yet-uncatalogued hoard of coins and other precious items appears to be twice as large as the cache of 1,700 coins and other valuables uncovered in Nousiainen over 130 years ago. Just the weight of the silver in Lappinen’s new metal detector find alone—unappraised for its antique value—would fetch nearly $10,000 today on the open market. (It is so important to have hobbies.) Tikkala noted that the provenance of these ancient coins, which likely date back to somewhere between 1000 and 1050 CE, implied extensive trade and maybe some high-seas travel. Several of the coins appear to have been minted elsewhere in Scandinavia as well as in what is now Germany during the reign of the Holy Roman Empire. Some of these coins originated from Britain in the years just before the Norman Conquest of England in the 11th century. And still others appear to be a kind of silver coin made in the Islamic world, known as a dirham, which could indicate an origin anywhere from Al-Andalus in what is now Spain to the most eastern reaches of the former Byzantine Empire. Hoard senseless Although this once hidden treasure dates back closely to the era when Vikings used to terrorize the North Sea, Tikkala and his research partners have reported no evidence tying the find directly to any Norseman’s plunder just yet. That said, there has been evidence that Vikings did fairly routinely use the dirham as currency. The presence of so-called “payment silver” or hacksilver—scrap intended to be cut into smaller units for payments by weight—may also yield more clues as to the identity of whoever buried this stash in the first place. Both Vikings and Scotland’s old Pictish tribes are known to have used this method, sometimes while trading with the Romans. According to the museum’s press release, the hoard also includes a silver bracelet, a silver clasp, and one silver bead, which may offer further clues. “The coins have not yet been cleaned, separated or counted, so their exact weight, quantity and more precise timing will only be determined in further research,” the museum noted in its press statement, translated via Google. “In any case, there are thousands of coins.”

item.title: FCC Grants First Robotics Ban Exemption to a Robomower Company
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.57
The FCC this week released a public notice stating that the U.S. Department of War (DoW, formerly the Department of Defense) has “granted Conditional Aprovals for certain routers and advanced robotics devices.” That includes four robotics platforms from Swedish robot mower company Husqvarna. Asus was also granted approval to sell many of its Wi-Fi routers in the U.S. The exemption comes just over a month after the FCC announced a broad ban on new robotic devices not made in the U.S., including robot vacuums and robot mowers. That followed the agency’s similarly broad Wi-Fi router ban in March. Both bans effectively choked off the flow of new products for their respective industries, as virtually no routers nor robots satisfied the bans’ strict requirements. While the companies on the FCC’s “covered list” could continue to import and sell existing devices that had already been approved for sale in the U.S., they would not be able to bring new ones over without a special exemption from the DoW. Asus has only been granted a temporary reprieve; the notice states that its exemption, which covers Asus’ “RT Router Series, ROG GT Series, ROG Strix GS Series, TUF Gaming Series, ExpertWiFi Series, ZenWiFi Mesh Series, 5G MiFi Series, repeaters, and wireless access points,” will terminate on March 6, 2028. The same goes for several wireless routers from Comtrend, another Taiwanese firm given conditional approval in the FCC’s notice. Husqvarna, which produces both residential and commercial automowers, will be able to sell products that use its “305v IQ, 310v IQ, 420v IQ, and 440v IQ robotic platforms” indefinitely. In a statement on its website, Husqvarna says the approval means those platforms, “which are expected to be launched in the U.S. in 2027, as well as the already approved models currently available on the market, are exempt from the FCC Covered List.” “This validates that Husqvarna Group is setting the standard for trusted robotic mowing,” Husqvarna Group CEO Glen Instone says, “and reflects our rigorous standards for quality, security, and how we manage customer data following strict EU consumer privacy rules.” Husqvarna has not made much of a dent in the residential market so far. Instone acknowledges that “limited residential penetration” and says the company sees “significant growth potential in the years ahead.” This is the first exemption that’s been granted to a robotics company since the ban went into place. Last week, I wrote that the U.S. robotics ban was screwing us out of good new robomower features shown off at IFA in Berlin, such as devices with dedicated edge-trimming arms. None of Husqvarna’s mowers have such features, but perhaps they will soon. That alone isn’t incredibly encouraging, given the company’s current stable of automowers all cost well into the thousands of dollars, but perhaps it’s a sign we’ll get to see some of the others, like the intriguing Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max, relatively sooner than later.

item.title: Report: Roughly Half the World’s Governments Underestimated Covid Deaths by the Millions
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.80
Aside from maybe a few blinkered members from some of society’s more fortunate demographics (e.g., white-collar remote workers, monied introverts, etc.), most people don’t particularly recall the covid-19 pandemic fondly. But new research from social scientists in London and Jerusalem is now providing strong indications that the scope of this tragedy was far worse than many governments let on. Moses Shayo and Ariel Karlinsky, two researchers who specialize in political and health economics, compiled an unusually comprehensive dataset from “all-cause mortality” reports, taken across 134 countries and territories both before and during the covid-19 pandemic. They then compared this more concrete data, some of it obtained by local journalists via freedom of information laws, to contemporaneous official government pronouncements during the heights of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021. As many as 45% to 55% of these nations, Shayo and Karlinsky found, misreported covid’s death toll—in most cases underplaying the severity of the crisis. Compared to the 5.08 million deaths attributed to covid-19 by state officials during this two-year period, the researchers determined that the actual number of covid-related deaths (based on these governments’ own hard numbers) was more than twice that: about 12.47 million. “Our evidence shows that manipulation was remarkably widespread and large in magnitude,” Shayo and Karlinsky said in a press statement. In the 62 countries where they found covid deaths were underreported, aspiring and successful “informational autocrats” managed to avoid counting 14.5% of the expected covid deaths on average, they found. Means, motive, and opportunity Shayo and Karlinsky devoted considerable effort in their study, published in the Journal of Economic Growth, to dissecting and delineating between possible explanations for why a given country might have underreported its covid-19 deaths. Plenty of nations, they noted, simply did not have the resources to adequately keep up with the punishing deluge of deaths, whether in terms of medical diagnostics, hospital access, or sheer personnel. But, as they adjusted for these factors, the researchers found a troubling correlation indicative of multiple premeditated efforts to minimize the scope of the pandemic’s impact. Shayo and Karlinsky used state-level data on the share of adults with either a college education and/or internet access, alongside information collected by the United Nations’ Human Development Education Index, to craft a metric for each nation’s relative “audience sophistication.” The measure—when viewed alongside the structural checks and balances reining in each government’s executive power—tended to mirror the scale of underreported covid deaths. “In countries where formal and informal checks and balances are weak, executives tend to act as ‘informational autocrats,’” Shayo and Karlinsky said. “The most important set of constraints appear to be institutional constraints on the executive. Additionally, the severity of underreporting drops significantly the more sophisticated the domestic audience is,” the pair wrote in their study. “We find less evidence relating it to cultural factors and to macroeconomic incentives to underreport.” A tyranny of small decisions Shayo and Karlinsky stopped short of claiming causality, however, merely framing it as “probably noteworthy” that states with the most accurate covid-19 reporting were “strongly associated with constraints on the government’s ability to effectively manipulate information.” More benign institutional policies might lead certain state bureaucracies to repeatedly err on ambiguous deaths, leading edge cases to either be always or never logged as covid-related, they noted. “[Some] countries may be reluctant to report a given death as Covid unless they are absolutely certain the death was due to Covid, even though this violates [U.N. World Health Organization] WHO guidelines, [independent] of capacity or intention to obfuscate,” according to the pair, who are currently based at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel. (Shayo is also a professor at King’s College London). In perhaps the duo’s most unsurprising finding, Shayo and Karlinsky uncovered signs that incumbent politicians somehow succumbed to the temptation to skew government data in their favor: “There is also evidence that misreporting is higher in countries holding elections during the pandemic,” they wrote.

item.title: Showrunner Confirms Harrison Ford Will Not Appear in ‘Blade Runner 2099’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.78
We had a feeling Harrison Ford wasn’t going to be part of Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099 series. Though Rick Deckard, his “replicant-or-human?” character from Ridley Scott’s 1982 classic, did play a major role in Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner 2049, and Ford clearly has no problem playing aging versions of his classic heroes (see also: Indiana Jones, Han Solo), you can imagine he was satisfied with where Deckard’s story ended. But there was always a chance Deckard could pop back up in Blade Runner 2099. Last we saw, Deckard was alive and reuniting with his daughter, and Ford is still constantly working at 84 years old. However, Blade Runner 2099 creator and showrunner, Silka Luisa, has outright confirmed that won’t happen. In an interview with Polygon, Luisa set the record straight. “Harrison Ford is not in the show. I feel like as a Blade Runner fan, I would want to know that, so I’m just gonna be a full disclosure: I wish, but no,” she said. “It was important to [Alcon Entertainment, which controls the Blade Runner rights] that we separated ourselves from both films in terms of characters. From a mythological and canon point of view, we do reference back into the films. I can’t give that away without spoilers, but that was why having Ridley [Scott] a part of the show was such an important piece.” Luisa called working with Scott “awesome” and credits him with being “the visual author of Blade Runner.” She also noted that Blade Runner 2099 could continue after its first season—but even if it doesn’t, it’s designed to stand on its own, a refreshing consideration in an era when so many series lay the groundwork for sequels that aren’t yet announced. “We originally sold the show as a limited series,” she said. “This is a cinematic property. We have to retain some sense of filmic storytelling. Obviously, there’s always hope that audiences love the world and the characters and that it could continue. But in terms of this first series, it is a complete story within itself. That was really important.” Blade Runner 2099 stars Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh (but not Harrison Ford). It premieres November 25 on Prime Video. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Anthropic Claims It Stopped Suspected Bioweapons Research Conducted With Claude
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.74
A new report from Anthropic, the AI firm that’s perhaps most positioned itself as the industry’s conscience, claims that the company had to thwart multiple potential schemes over the past year by scientists intending to use its Claude AI to engage in biological weapons research. The company’s Threat Intelligence team detailed five case studies on “biological misuse” of Claude in the report—including gain-of-function research that would make the mosquito-borne illness chikungunya more dangerous and a scheme to catalogue animal venom compounds”. Anthropic’s team noted that many of these cases were ambiguous, plagued (as so much biowarfare policy has been) by “dual use” problems in which projects meant to safeguard the public against biological weapons can often easily be inverted into making biological weapons themselves. The company said it hopes its report will “spark a conversation within the AI industry, and with governments, about emerging biological risks and how best to counter them.” Former Pentagon official Andrew Weber—who served for over five years as the assistant secretary of defense for nuclear, chemical, and biological defense programs—reviewed the report ahead of its publication on Thursday for The New York Times. Weber, now with the Council on Strategic Risks, told the Times that the company’s findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of the AI sector’s most state-of-the-art models. A cautionary fable Anthropic’s team noted that the risks posed by biowarfare research conducted with Claude have mostly emerged with recent releases, “most notably Claude Fable 5.” To that end, the company has worked to strengthen Fable 5’s ability to recognize when bad-faith actors are attempting to copy its capabilities via “distillation,” a similarly thorny “dual-use” technique whereby the work product of a more capable “teacher” AI is extracted to train a smaller “student” AI. Anthropic said in the report that it has foiled illicit distillation attacks targeting Claude from seven labs based in China since first making the issue public this February. It’s unclear if any of these distillation attacks overlapped with the bioweapons case studies, because the firm chose not to name the parties responsible. And, in some cases, many of these biological researchers were working hard to evade identification. Anthropic’s report noted that the parties attempting to create a more powerful and deadly strain of the chikungunya virus had “tunneled traffic through U.S. infrastructure to evade our regional blocks, and used a zero data retention (ZDR) service to hide content.” But what most alarmed the firm about this chikungunya case was that the queries asked of Claude were ostensibly seeking help in drafting a grant application for research the user evidently intended to perform at a military institute. The “combination of content and institutional association” was so troubling that Anthropic said it conducted another internal investigation, even after finding that Claude had rejected the user or users’ requests. Venomous schemes Anthropic’s case study involving the venom peptides came from a user who was apparently attempting to construct an atlas of these signaling molecules as they appear in venom toxins produced by animals in nature. The Threat Intelligence team noted that plenty of venom research has benign applications—including treatments for migraines and cancer pain relief. What alarmed them about this Claude user’s research, however, was that despite its supposed purpose of identifying potentially new painkillers and antidepressants, the researcher had asked for help building an atlas that also catalogued venom peptides capable of inducing paralysis. “[It] could, therefore, be used to generate both novel therapeutic or harmful compounds,” the team noted. Anthropic’s head of threat intelligence Jacob Klein told the Times that the subtlety of these risky queries was one of the challenges inherent to ensuring that the company’s AI tools are used responsibly: “You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” he said.

item.title: Apple’s Biggest AI Advantage: It’s Not Trying to Build God
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.49
Apple had a lot to talk about during its “Surprise and Shine” product launch event on Wednesday: a new CEO, revamped AirPods, an Apple Watch that can record your conversations, and of course, a much-anticipated foldable iPhone. The only thing missing was grandiose proclamations about how AI is going to revolutionize everything in the world, and maybe even kill us all. Not so long ago, believing such a thing would’ve been considered at the very least fringe, even within the sci-fi-indoctrinated ranks of Silicon Valley. It wasn’t until the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022 that people started accepting the idea that AI—long an intellectual taboo in tech circles—could in fact become a mainstream tool, and perhaps have as big a cultural impact as the iPhone or the internet. And while people have been warning about the danger of runaway AI for decades, those fears escalated sharply earlier this year, following a series of autonomous hacks which showed how frail our existing cybersecurity infrastructure can be in the face of swarms of self-coordinating agents that tech companies seem unable (or unwilling) to control. Anxiety about the future reached a new height this week after an AI safety researcher at Anthropic named Evan Hubinger wrote in a social media post that the very technology his company is racing to build has a greater than ten percent chance of wiping out humanity. It got the world’s attention. In a sign that AGI fears had breached the mainstream, Sheryl Crow, of all people, wrote on Instagram that she was “begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent [unconstrained AI development] from going forward.” U.S. lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle called on Congress this week to rein in the race to build artificial “superintelligence”—a term that started as a warning but has since, in a strange trick of rhetorical alchemy, been embraced as a marketing buzzword by the biggest American AI labs. Hubinger’s views on the apocalyptic potential of AI can seem confounding: Why would he help to build something he thinks could exterminate every one of us? But that idea is hardly unusual in his industry. Many of the most powerful players in the AI race have long said, quite plainly and in public, that the technology could go terribly wrong and be the agent of our extinction, whether that’d be through some engineered doomsday virus, a cybersecurity takeover, an AI-triggered nuclear exchange, or some other machine-made catastrophe our mortal minds can’t even hope to fathom. (The whole idea behind superintelligence, after all, is that it’ll be playing hyperdimensional chess while we humans are still struggling to play checkers.) Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and CEO, has said there’s as high as a 25% chance that AI goes “really, really badly.” (Read: that humanity is toast.) Elon Musk believes there’s about a 10%-20% chance that things could go terribly wrong. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been reluctant to assign a specific probability to that outcome, but he doesn’t believe it’s zero. In a perverse but very real way, the world-killing power of superintelligent AI is, for tech leaders, a feature, not a bug. You can’t have an all-powerful machine God capable of curing cancer and freeing us from drudgework without some risk that it’ll turn on us. That will seem deeply inhuman to most sane people who don’t have any prospect of becoming uber-wealthy from the AI boom. But make no mistake, it is a fundamental presupposition these companies are operating from, and they don’t even try to keep it a secret. The language they use is typically more dialed-down, but the bottom line, they’ll say, is that humanity should accept some chance of annihilation for a shot at the golden age they believe AI can lead us into. All of which makes Apple’s rather muted approach to AI stand out. The company has been widely regarded as a slowpoke since the debut of ChatGPT, focusing on its hardware business while just about every other tech giant did an about-face to make AI a top priority. Its launch of “Apple Intelligence” in 2024 was more of a whimper than a bang, and to this day its AI muscle is largely dependent upon models from Google, its erstwhile competitor. AI wasn’t completely absent from its Wednesday product launch event, but it was more of a background theme than the shiny center of attention. No doubt freshly minted Apple CEO John Ternus has been keeping a watchful eye on the public backlash to AI data centers and fears over an AI-pocalypse, and thinking that perhaps the best way to win over people’s hearts and minds is not to talk about AI as if it were some omnipotent God we’re summoning into being, but just another tool to help you do the things you already do, like touching up photos and getting walking directions from Siri. And for millions of people who are increasingly fearful of the future, that’s likely to be a sales pitch they can actually get behind. READ MORE:

item.title: Google May Finally Release Laptops You Can’t Just Ignore
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.44
The first wave of Google’s touted Googlebooks seems ever more impending, with leak after leak telling us these are more than mere next-gen Chromebooks. Yet another deluge of data from a previously exposed “Lenovo Googlebook 15” shows us Google is really trying to make Googlebook an actual MacBook competitor in more ways than one. This Lenovo Googlebook 15 leak stems from MacObserver, which published full, detailed renders of this upcoming device as well as a full specs sheet. To summarize, it’s a moderately powerful laptop made for daily use thanks to its Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip and up to 32GB of LPDDR5x. You read that right; this Chromebook sequel can now support twice as much memory than any Chromebook ever could. The Googlebook would also have options between 256GB and 512GB of SSD storage, which seems to indicate Google still wants you to rely on cloud storage. And if you were wondering if Lenovo and Google wanted this device to seem premium, it’s touting a 2,880 x 1,800 resolution OLED display that maxes out at 120Hz. It even comes with a haptic touchpad. With all that together, we don’t expect this laptop to cost closer to $1,500. This Lenovo ThinkPad T16 Gen 5 has the same kind of screen—though at 16 inches—and the same chip. It costs more than $1,700. Pricing will naturally be Googlebooks’ Achilles heel. Just knowing how RAM prices are going, more buyers are looking toward cheaper MacBook Neo-level laptops. Lenovo now has its own IdeaPad Vibe models that will likely cost far less and should run all the usual PC software you’re used to. Google has yet to describe how its upcoming operating system will work and whether it can truly make more Android apps work better natively on a larger display. If that were it, then Googlebooks would just be another run-of-the-mill laptop being slowly squeezed by the RAM shortage. But MacObserver has shared a few more details about “Googlebook OS,” which seems to be the modern name for what was previously codenamed Aluminum OS. If you already guessed it has something to do with AI, congratulations. Documentation suggests you’ll be able to access Gemini for “personal proactive help,” likely in the form of cross-app actions like writing your emails or adding calendar events for you. Google is certainly going to fill these laptops to the brim with AI. An APK teardown by Android Authority earlier this month suggested that the laptops could use AI to automatically create “Collections” of your loose files sitting in your downloads folder and desktop. It could prove an actually useful feature if you have never learned any skills at file management. Surprisingly, the Lenovo leaks also mention a “Google facial authentication” that could be face unlock functionality, almost like Windows Hello’s facial unlock. There’s also a fingerprint reader for further biometric access. These Googlebooks also sport a special “G” key in place of the Windows button you find on most PCs’ keyboards. This key is likely how Google expects you to access these AI functions. And if you wanted to know what that “Glowbar” was for on these upcoming laptops, it’s supposed to indicate your laptop’s battery and charging levels. Most surprising of all, Google and its partner OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) seem like they will launch dedicated accessories for Googlebooks, including a “Lenovo AI Mouse” with an RGB light strip around the back. We expect the mouse may sync with the laptop’s Glowbar, but for how it will actually incorporate AI, we can expect it may interact with Google’s AI-ified mouse cursor. We’ll have to wait to see how many of these AI features actually run fully on-device and whether any of them prove useful. At the very least, the number of leaks indicates we won’t have to wait long.

item.title: Live Updates From Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ iPhone Event 🔴
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.14
A new era at Apple is upon us. Newly appointed CEO John Ternus is now at the helm of the $4.75 trillion-dollar company, and the first foldable iPhone is reportedly going to be announced this Wednesday, Sept. 9, at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event at Apple Park. While the foldable iPhone will likely steal the show, we’re also expecting to see the rumored iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Raymond Wong, Gizmodo’s Senior Editor of Consumer Tech, and Adriano Contreras, Gizmodo’s Social Media Editor, will be reporting live from the Steve Jobs Theater before, during, and after the keynote, which kicks off at 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT. In an internal memo sent to staff on his first day as CEO, Ternus said the launch “is going to be phenomenal.” Let’s see if Apple can change the world again. Be sure to bookmark this page and check back often as we live blog it all. Don’t get too upset by any headlines you read that say the new Apple Watch Series 12 screen is smaller than previous models. However, MacRumors pointed out that the Series 12 specs page lists the screen surface area as 1,196 sq mm. The Apple Watch Series 11 watch face was 1,220 sq mm on the 46mm version. The 42mm version has dropped from 989 sq mm to 970 sq mm. That’s about a 2% difference for both versions of the Series 12. The casing is now also slightly larger, resulting in an almost imperceptible growth in the screen borders. I don’t imagine most users would be able to spot the difference, though I may be more intrigued to see screen size shrinking instead of growing, for a change. —Kyle Barr the Apple tiktok team is once again killing it (last one is insane tho 😭) pic.twitter.com/HFAGJnzWiG — Dylan (@DylanMcD8) September 10, 2026 Apple’s new Instagram and TikTok scrolling promos for the iPhone Duo are tongue-in-cheek in the way I find surprising for the Cupertino tech giant. One of the ads shows somebody at a coffee shop with their laptop and a large cup of joe, while somebody with a Duo sits next to them and receives a proportional, Alice in Wonderland-sized coffee. Another ad shows an iPhone having a nice dinner date with an iPad mini. As one of the shrinking number of tiny tablet fans, I feel almost like the crochety father who does not want my precious child mingling with the likes of iPhone. —Kyle Barr If you were wondering what the difference is between this generation of AirPods and the last generation, I got you. Spoiler alert: AirPods 5 are improved in pretty much every way. —James Pero The iPhone 18 Pro is a very similar phone to the iPhone 17 Pro, from the screen to the shape and everything in between. However, the biggest differences are more than skin deep, with some promising improvements to the iPhone’s cooling and chip design. It’s also the first iPhone with a mechanical aperture, something that will only get a few people excited. Luckily for Apple, I’m one of those people. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra and their new audio recording features have people talking, and let’s just say people keep bringing up always-recording smart glasses in the same sentence. Siri Recap is supposed to listen to you throughout the day and offer a summary of what you did and who you talked to. Live Rewind is a user-activated feature that can summarize conversations you just had. Apple’s support document detailing Siri Recap and Live Rewind mentions that they’re exclusive to the S11 processor inside the new watches. That’s partly because they have a “secure exclave” that processes this audio on-device. The document reads, “Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by watchOS, apps, the user, or Apple.” The data in the exclave is not stored or transcribed, but the encrypted file is processed for transcription on your iPhone’s own secure exclave. Users can choose to save these summaries on their iCloud accounts. You can read the full explanation for yourself here. Apple seems to know this is a sore spot for privacy-centric users, so we’ll see how well they take to it when the Series 12 watches hit the scene later this month. —Kyle Barr Both the exterior and interior displays of the iPhone Duo rely on a 1:4 aspect ratio. That’s very different than what you’re used to with most candy bar-style phones, but it also means these devices are much, much better for watching content you don’t get on TikTok. Apple showed the device playing games at its full-screen height without any black bars around the content. For movies, it’s going to get interesting. Despite some dubious X post you may have seen, IMAX films use either a 1.90:1 or 1.43:1 aspect ratio. Sure, that fits the Duo’s screen better than you would on a regular mobile phone, but it would still require some black bars to make it fit. Did Christopher Nolan ever want you to watch The Odyssey on your phone? I imagine the very idea would give him a migraine. —Kyle Barr BREAKING: Apple's Polishing Cloth is compatible with the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4/Series 12 pic.twitter.com/0yxMME2qur — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 9, 2026 Okay, everybody calm down. It’s official, your Apple polishing cloth (which recently had its price slashed to $9) is indeed compatible with both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Go ahead and feel free to smooth that folding phone until it’s as smooth as glass. Oh wait, it’s already made of metal and glass. Whatever, just keep scrubbing. Apple commands it. —Kyle Barr How much are you willing to pay for the return of the Ceramic Apple Watch? A Series 12 ceramic model starts at $809 at the 42mm size in either pearl white or night blue colorways. The watches come with both GPS and cellular connectivity, but they’re easily the most expensive version of the Series 12. Meanwhile, an Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $719. —Kyle Barr Burgundy happens to be my favorite color, which means, of course, I’m very smitten with the iPhone 18 Pro. Burgundy is also a modern region in France that’s today known for its wine-making. During the Medieval period, it was a duchy that proved to be one of the most important regions for the late Medieval political field. In the 15th century, Duke Charles the Bold tried his damndest to create an independent kingdom of Burgundy through diplomacy and war. He was a known patron of the arts, and his nascent kingdom also became a center of chivalric etiquette. Unfortunately, Chrales’ dream of a revived Burgundian kingdom died at the Battle of Nancy against the Swiss Confederation. Still, Burgundy lives on thanks to Charles’s epic motto, “Je L’ay Emprins,” which translates to “I have dared it.” —Kyle Barr It’s THIN. It’s VERSATILE It’s DURABLE. It fits in your pocket. And it FOLDS. Meet iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/lVpBmC36hx — Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) September 9, 2026 All the videos showcasing the iPhone Duo include this slick-looking animation where it seems the exterior screen bleeds over into the interior display. I want to believe this is how it will look in-person, but there’s another side of me that wonders if the look of this animation will depend on whether you’re staring at the device straight-on. Also, I want to know if it works on other apps, not just the home screen. —Kyle Barr Netflix made a special version of its app for the iPhone Duo that makes use of both the exterior and interior displays. On the outside, you’ll scroll through clips from some of the streamer’s shows, and then opening it up, you’ll be greeted with a larger screen-filling video. Apple does want you to use its device for watching shows and content, though it’s also partnered with Zoom and Slack for making use of the larger 7.58-inch interior display. —Kyle Barr Apple imagines you’ll treat your iPhone Duo like a miniature, pocketable tablet. That makes sense, given the Apple Pencil compatibility and the consistent bezels. To that end, Apple’s also making a Folio case for the Duo with a built-in gumstick kickstand. It also covers up the exterior screen in this mode, but you weren’t looking at it anyway. The Folio case is only available in a tan taupe color and navy blue. —Kyle Barr iPhone Duo prices. $3200 for 2TB model. pic.twitter.com/aopePNw1nx — Mark Gurman (@markgurman) September 9, 2026 Foldable phones are expensive—there’s no doubt about that—but if you want the top-of-the-line iPhone Duo, you’re going to have to really shell out. The iPhone Duo with 2TB of storage costs $3,200 before tax, which is a ton of money (but somehow less than a Vision Pro). Still, I think I speak for most wallets when I say… ouch. —James Pero Apple says that, starting Sept. 14, you’ll be able to download the next OS update to all your Apple devices, including iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, watchOS 27, and so on. Just know that all the new Siri AI capabilities are still listed as a “beta,” which is how Apple plans to wash its hands when the chatbot inevitably makes a mistake. Additionally, some anticipated features, like the Apple Watch “Audio Intelligence” features, won’t be available until later. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch doesn’t seem all that different from the Series 11, at least on the surface. Beyond a whole slew of new health metric tracking, the big additions are all in how these watches now include extra AI features that use audio capture. The most important ones you’ll get to know are “Siri Recap” and “Live Rewind.” Siri can use your data and combine that with your audio to give you a rundown of what you did that day. Live Rewind can enable users to see a summary of what somebody just said to you when you weren’t listening. Those specific features won’t be available until a beta comes out this October. —Kyle Barr That foldable iPhone won’t be available until Oct. 23, more than a month after the iPhone 18 Pro hits the scene. Preorders start Oct. 16. Here’s the big news: the iPhone Duo will start at $1,999. At the very least, $2,000 is a lot less than the $2,500 rumors originally suggested. —Kyle Barr Apple’s new C2 modem supports 5G mmWave. For reference, previous modems, the C1 and C1X, both in-house products, didn’t have that. Apple says the C2 also allows for 50% faster uploads, which is nothing to scoff at. —James Pero The iPhone Duo is using a special screen layer that Apple promises is doing a few things, but the most important aspect is how it may reduce the chance you’ll see the crease. We’ll have to see that for ourselves, considering the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts life with minimal crease, but it becomes more apparent the more you open it up. —Kyle Barr Naturally, multitasking on the iPhone Duo looks very iPad-esque. You can stack apps vertically or horizontally, and it looks like there’s some intuitive dragging and dropping. In a way, Apple has been making foldable phone software for years, just not on a foldable phone. —James Pero Apple says using the iPhone Duo won’t be restricted to your digits. You’ll be able to use an Apple Pencil with USB-c on the interior or exterior screen. However, Apple makes no mention of the more versatile Apple Pencil Pro, which may remain only usable on an iPad. —Kyle Barr Apple’s first foldable phone also has a FaceTime camera built into the screen on the right side when it’s opened up. This means you can have your phone open and have multiple people take up different parts of the screen. What we really want is to take video calls while—hopefully—being able to keep using your device. —Kyle Barr There’s a whole lot of new features coming to Apple Watch Series 12, but at least it doesn’t cost any more than before. It starts at $399 and now—finally—comes with ceramic options. —Kyle Barr Apple has two new versions of AirPods 5. Both have better ANC, but only the more expensive model has swipe controls and wireless charging. You’ll also have to shell out more money for one more hour of battery life. The base model gets four hours with ANC on, and the more expensive model gets five hours with ANC on. —James Pero Look at those specs. As you might’ve expected, the Watch Series 12 is better in basically every way imaginable, with better sensors, of course. —Matt Wille Apple’s updated AI will now synthesize all your health information, like sleep data, exercise, and heart rate, and give you a “Health Age” score. What if I don’t actually want to know that much about myself? —Matt Wille The new Apple Watch will take your heart rate up to 24x more than its predecessor. Apple says it’s now the “most accurate heart rate sensing” available in a wearable. —Matt Wille The AirPods 5 now feature better ANC, which promises around five hours of battery life thanks to a reengineered power cell. And despite everything getting more expensive, they still cost the same $129 as the AirPods 4. The AirPods 5 with a wireless charging case will now cost $149. —Kyle Barr That’s right, RAMageddon has come for the iPhone. The new iPhone 18 Pro will start at $1,200, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max will ask for $1,300. That’s both $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, respectively. Let’s just admit that—considering today’s memory prices—it could have been way worse. —Kyle Barr Apple’s planning to support Google’s SynthID watermarks for AI-generated images, but it’s now also trying to beat deepfakes with a reference photo future. Essentially, Apple will host an original image in its Private Cloud Compute servers that doesn’t have any modifications. —Kyle Barr The iPhone Pro’s camera is getting more professional with additional controls. Now, with Pro Camera controls, you can adjust things like aperture, white balance, shutter speed, and more. The Pro controls also work with video, allowing you to adjust shutter speed for more motion blur. You can also maintain focus on moving subjects with AI. For anyone who takes iPhone photography seriously, I assume these will be pretty rad. —James Pero But it’s still pretty damn cool. Apple has added a mechanical aperture to its 48-megapixel main “fusion” camera lens, which means that you’ll have much more control over depth of field for your shots. It’s going to be a very pro-centric feature, but at least it’s one of those features that will potentially make amateur photogs more willing to reach for their phone instead of their camera in a pinch. —Kyle Barr The iPhone 18 Pro is supposed to offer much better performance, and a big reason for that is because the iPhone should be much better at keeping cool. Apple said the phone now has a 3X larger vapor chamber, which is important because the redesigned A20 chip now has its silicon die placed next to its memory, which means the 2nm chip can seat closer to the thermal system. All this means that, maybe—finally—the iPhone 18 won’t be as toasty as usual. —Kyle Barr The A20 Pro is Apple’s newest high-end iPhone chip and comes with two “neural engines.” That equates to quite a few improvements, according to Apple, including “2x more compute.” There’s also a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. Whether you really feel the results will depend on what you’re doing, of course, but it looks impressive on paper. —James Pero Apple mentioned that some of Siri’s capabilities may be rate limited but didn’t offer more details during its event. We’ll just have to find out for ourselves if Apple wants us to buy into an iCloud subscription to get the most use out of AI. —Kyle Barr Siri’s AI enhancements are finally here. They were in the latest betas, but if you’ve been waiting for the full release, know that Siri has more “personal context” that allows it to understand what you’ve been posting in your emails or messages, and it can take some actions on your behalf. Siri also has several “expressive” options for voice, but only on the more recent iPhone models. This has all been well-established since WWDC, but we’ll see how well it performs on the millions of iPhones that can use it. —Kyle Barr There it is: Burgundy is the new color for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Other colors for the iPhone 18 Pro: Deep Black, Glacier (light blue), and a new silver. The glass panel on the backside is also color-matched to the aluminum frame. —Raymond Wong iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Check out the new color with color matched back. Burgundy is the new color#appleevent pic.twitter.com/1maaD28lsw — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 John Ternus really had us going there for a second. “Intelligent Personal Hub?” I mean, come on, we were all thinking smart home hub, right? —James Pero While the folks in Cupertino, California are greeting John Ternus, the rest of us plebs watching the livestream are greeted with a very Apple-ish opening trailer, or perhaps multiple trailers. And suddenly, Tim Cook’s voice, then Tim Cook, who reveals he’s no longer the head honcho. It’s John Ternus, y’all. They’re really making a big deal out of this. —Kyle Barr Ternus didn’t say the signature “Good Morning,” like Tim Cook always did. Guess he’s doing things his own way. He said Apple has been doing a lot of imagining and we’ll see some of those things today. —Raymond Wong John Ternus is out on stage and attendees gave him a loud ovation. So much love for the new guy. —Raymond Wong Standing ovation for John Ternus! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/kXPDk3NLNt — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 New Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! Where is John Ternus? Probably behind the stage getting ready to hop on and “Good Morning” us all. —Raymond Wong New Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/KMQXtQWqMs — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Thanks to the iPhone 17 Pro’s 8x zoom, I was able to scope on Apple’s head of marketing Greg Joswiak and chief of software engineering, Craig Federighi. Dude’s hair still still looks incredible. Gotta find out what conditioner he uses to get that kinda volume. —Raymond Wong I spy Craig Federighi and Greg Jozwiak at the #appleevent pic.twitter.com/QAW9wUSz64 — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 I’m seated inside of the Steve Jobs Theater. If you’ve never been here, know this: the theater has plush leather (?!) seats, outlets for each one, and the speaker system is one of the very best I’ve ever experienced. —Raymond Wong 15 minutes until the #appleevent keynote! pic.twitter.com/Cpjopg4iIT — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Apple’s new leader woke up super early and shared this teaser to his X account. But what is it? The variable aperture for the iPhone 18 Pro Max? Some glimpse of a close-up of the foldable iPhone? Make your guesses in the comments. —Raymond Wong — John Ternus (@johnternus) September 9, 2026 Here’s my food review of the breakfast for invited media: B. I’m wolfing down this mini chocolate croissant and an apple tart. I’m going to need the sugar to power me through the long day. The coffee is mid, too. Edible, but nothing special. I’m old enough to remember when the food and drinks situation was amazing. Of course, this was in the early days when the Steve Jobs Theater had just opened. —Raymond Wong We just picked up our badges and have arrived at the Steve Jobs Theater. The current temperature is 72 degrees Fahrenheit in Cupertino, and it’s supposed to reach a high of 96 degrees by the late afternoon. I’m definitely feeling a bit antsy, but I can’t wait to see the so-called iPhone Duo. Is this the foldable that will make foldable phones mainstream? We shall see. —Raymond Wong Got my #AppleEvent badge! Ready to see the foldable iPhone pic.twitter.com/vhcDNwJoVH — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Maybe I should have stuck to my prediction that Apple will call the foldable iPhone the “iPhone Duo.” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said on X last night that he believes Apple has decided to call it the iPhone Duo, with the device starting at $2,000 and shipping in September. A storage option with 2TB could cost around $3,000 he said. The Apple sleuth also said that the iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil and launch in dark blue and white colorways. John Ternus could do the funniest thing ever and not call it the iPhone Duo just to screw with Gurman, though. That would be pretty funny. —Raymond Wong Well, no regular iPhones, that is. Rumor has it Apple will only be announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max today, with no iPhone 18 in the mix. It’s an interesting choice from Apple, a company that usually hopes to offer something lower-end for users who aren’t ready to shell out $1,000+ on a new phone. But hey, we are expecting to see the foldable iPhone today. That’s basically two phones in one, right? —Matt Wille Apple has just released a firmware update for a product that does not exist yet Beats 360 Firmware 4A203 is out. It confirms the Beats 360 name and the 4 colors: Black, Pink, White, Cloud It also includes HD images of the upcoming products pic.twitter.com/a24FDZcu1m — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 8, 2026 AirPods aren’t the only audio product that should be on your Apple radar right now. According to leaks, Beats has a new pair of wireless headphones in the works called the Beats 360. There are even some HD images leaked along with them, and they look… very Beats-y. Whether these are announced at today’s event is another story, but the timing of the leak is certainly interesting. —James Pero Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are likely going to cost at least $100 more, according to Bloomberg’s ever-consistent Apple leaker Mark Gurman. So what kinds of hardware upgrades will Apple try to suggest are worth the ballooning cost of memory? Gurman says there should be some big camera upgrades this year that will include a mechanical aperture on at least one of the new lenses. This grants more fine-tuned control over your photos, and it may be my main reason for personally opting for the bar-style phone instead of the upcoming foldable. The other big upgrade may be Apple’s downsizing of the Dynamic Island. It could appear smaller on your phone without any content on it, but Gurman suggested users will be able to toggle between up to three live activities at one time. Compared to something like the relatively pointless Camera Control switch, the Dynamic Island has proved itself a worthwhile feature over time, and it’s nice to see it with more usability. —Kyle Barr It’s looking like AirPods with cameras in them are a long shot on today’s laundry list of releases, but AirPods 5 might make an appearance. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, AirPods 5 will bring a few perks over the last generation, including better active noise cancellation (ANC). There will be two models, according to Gurman, and one of them will have wireless charging in the case while the other won’t. Sure, it’s not as mind-blowing as wireless earbuds that can remember where you left your keys, but it’s something. —James Pero You shouldn’t expect any massive hardware update from Apple’s wearables this year. Instead, the main reason Apple wants you to be excited may be for new software updates—and of course that means AI. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman suggested The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will have a feature that summarizes your day, and that may include conversations. This AI Siri-enabled feature may be called “Recaps,” according to Gurman. The big question is whether Apple will have it run all the live-long day or if you can set it to only start recording at certain times or in certain locations. Apple will, of course, try to emphasize how it will keep your data secure, but I don’t imagine many users are still that enticed by more self-surveillance features. Also, don’t expect this feature to come to any past Apple Watches, which is especially annoying considering how many recent Apple Watch models can’t even get watchOS 27. —Kyle Barr One of the less-anticipated product reveals for the “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday may be a new version of the Apple TV 4K set-top box. It’s a good thing too, since the old one was looking a little long in the tooth. A new box necessitates a new processor upgrade, and MacRumors claims—based on some pre-release code—that we may see an A19 or A19 Pro chip. This six-core SoC was first built for the iPhone 17 generation, but that means Apple may also be upgrading the RAM spec from 4GB to 8GB or more. We’d hate to see what that does to the price. A current-gen Apple TV 4K went from $130 to $200 in Apple’s big across-the-board price hike back in June. —Kyle Barr We’ve been reading purported details about the foldable iPhone, iPhone 18 Pros, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5 for months now. Here are all the major rumors on what to expect from John Ternus and company tomorrow. Spoiler alert: it’s full of spoilers! —Raymond Wong Guys, I’ve been in Cupertino for 24 hours, and let me tell you, it’s dry out here. I’m very excited to see Apple’s first foldable iPhone. Can’t say the same about my skin drying up. Today is a planning day with the Consumer Tech Team. We’re gonna be working like maniacs to bring you all fast and accurate coverage of everything that Apple announces tomorrow. —Raymond Wong

item.title: This ‘Cell Tower in the Sky’ Just Completed a Record-Breaking 18,641-Mile Round Trip to Japan
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.79
An oblong silver airship recently completed a 30-day journey, flying through Earth’s stratosphere to deliver mobile broadband connectivity to cellphones. Aerospace company Sceye launched its Service Test 1 (ST1) mission on August 9 for a trans-Pacific flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. The airship operated for a week over Japan to test its capability to provide high-speed connectivity from the stratosphere for emergency and disaster response scenarios. “This mission proved not only that our technology, vehicle systems, payload, and operational infrastructure are ready for connectivity services, but also that the stratosphere is where the future non-terrestrial infrastructure lies,” Mikkel Vestergaard Frandsen, Founder and CEO of Sceye, said in a statement. “The stratosphere is what will enable the always-on future—including the promised land of 6G.” Going up Sceye’s experimental vehicles, officially called High Altitude Platform Systems, are designed to operate like cell towers in the sky. Their balloon-like design allows them to stay suspended in the stratosphere for months or years at a time. The airship relies on the buoyancy of helium to stay airborne instead of consuming fuel or electrical energy. Meanwhile, solar cells placed on top of the airship’s hull power its communications payload and help it maintain its position against stratospheric winds. During its latest test flight, Sceye’s ST1 traveled 18,641 miles (30,000 kilometers) before arriving at the airspace near Sceye’s headquarters in Moriarty, New Mexico, on September 5. The vehicle completed additional testing before a planned termination and descent. Testing, testing ST1 carried SceyeCell, an airborne cellular network antenna designed to deliver wide-area mobile broadband directly to standard devices from the stratosphere. When deployed at full scale, a single airship could cover the equivalent area of approximately 500 terrestrial towers, according to Sceye. During the flight, the airship demonstrated mobile broadband communications, including text messaging, voice calls, internet access, and video streaming. The platform also tested emergency calls using an emergency alert messaging system designed for large-scale disasters, as well as communications with drones. With SceyeCell, the company is aiming to compete with satellites delivering connectivity from low-Earth orbit without the operational cost of being in space. The stratosphere, according to Sceye, is close enough to Earth for high-capacity connectivity and observation while at a high-enough altitude to offer a wide-area reach. Sceye’s vehicles operate similar to a geostationary satellite, except 1,800 times closer to Earth, according to the company. “Together ground, stratosphere, and space – each operating at their optimal strengths, will change the course of humanity,” Frandsen said.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Upgrade for the Cameras
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.69
You’re going to end up squinting long and hard at the new iPhone 18 Pro to spot the differences between the new and previous generations. To save your eyes, I’m here to give you the breakdown of what’s actually changed. TL;DR: you’re going to care if you’ve always wanted more control over your phone’s cameras or a phone that doesn’t get as hot as quickly. Of course, the other major differentiator is the launch price. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro now start at $1,200 and $1,300, respectively. They’re both $100 more than what the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max cost in 2025. That’s a symptom of the ongoing RAM shortage, and Apple has already increased the price of its iPhone Air and iPhone 17e just after it revealed its iPhone 18 at Wednesday’s event. If we’re being honest, the biggest change this year is more what this means for the iPhone lineup. First, the new, most expensive device in Apple’s newly announced cellular lineup is the iPhone Duo, a wide foldable that takes the cake as the largest shakeup in iPhones since—well—ever. It’s a device built for media consumption, whereas the iPhone 18 Pro is relegated as the “professional” level device for people who really want the best phone pics. Also, Apple has decided to hold off launching a new regular iPhone 18 this month. It may save it for next year, when it debuts an iPhone 18e budget device and—possibly—an iPhone Air 2. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Colors Goodbye, Cosmic Orange. The new leading color for 2026 is a dark red burgundy. It’s not exactly the kind of color that creates a slew of tone-matched accessories like orange did, though it’s certainly more obvious than some past devices like the iPhone 14 Pro’s ultra-dark purple. In addition, the iPhone 18 Pro also comes in a muted “glacier” blue, a silver colorway, and—finally—an actual black, rather than some dark gray. It may be a semi-controversial take, but I never liked the look of the iPhone 17 Pro’s orange. It was too bright, too in your face, and way too trendy. Burgundy happens to be my favorite color—not the least because of the interesting history behind the area of Burgundy in France. I guess we’re setting up a war between the Prince of Orange in the Netherlands and the Duke of Burgundy, but I digress. Apple is also color-matching the back glass to the phone itself, whereas the iPhone 17 Pro’s back glass appeared a lighter shade than the rest of the device. Apple is sticking with aluminum sides for this generation—a decision that still rankles some who miss the sturdier titanium frame. Just like the previous generation, the front glass is still using Ceramic Shield 2, while the back panel is base Ceramic Shield. They’re still sturdy devices and are rated IP68 for dust resistance and survivability in water up to 6 meters for 30 minutes. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Screen If you’re comparing each generation’s screen, you’ll first notice the iPhone 18 Pro has a shrunken Dynamic Island. That’s because Apple managed to stick its infrared camera—used for FaceID—behind the screen. Now, the Dynamic Island is 25% smaller when not in use, but it can expand to include up to three live activities at once. The iPhone 18 Pro is still sporting a 6.3-inch OLED display, while the Max version boosts that size to 6.9 inches. Each model supports the usual ProMotion up to 120Hz of refresh rate, the same as the iPhone 17 Pro. You could stare at each screen for hours and find there’s essentially no difference between the past and new generations of slab phones. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Internals The phones’ internals are where things get interesting. First up, Apple’s new phone is breaking through with its first 2nm chip, the A20 Pro. Compared to the 3nm A19 Pro inside the iPhone 17 Pro, the smaller die size leads to better efficiency. The six-core CPU also integrates neural accelerators to handle all the new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI tasks in iOS 27. Apple also claims the CPU has 50% more memory bandwidth than the A19 Pro. To assist with that AI, there’s also a new dual-16-core neural engine. GPU-wise, Apple claims it’s given the new phone a big boost. It’s supposed to be 40% faster than the previous generation, so that could be a big boon if you were looking to game on your phone. Apple has also reengineered its chips so it packages the processor die close to the phone’s memory, reducing latency and allowing it to sit directly on the newly redesigned vapor chamber. The extra capabilities of this new chip would mean Apple has to do more to keep these phones running well. As to that, the company says it created a new vapor chamber that supposedly has 3X more surface area than the iPhone 17 Pro’s. Not only is that chamber supposed to aid with cooling, it may greatly enhance sustained performance by 40%. These all seem like small things, but these internal additions add up. As a final note, Apple is including its N1 Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 chip in both the Pro and Pro Max phones—same as last year. However, this year the Pro and Pro Max chips now sport different modems. The iPhone 18 Pro contains the new C2 cellular modem, which Apple says is more efficient than the C1. However, the iPhone 18 Pro Max doesn’t have a listed modem in its spec sheet. As first noted by MacRumors, the two phones have different LTE bands, which indicates they’re not running the same exact chip setup. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Battery The improvements to the iPhone 18 Pro chip are significant, though they may not play out into huge performance improvements if you’re already used to the iPhone 17 Pro. What may be more grokable is that if you jump from 17 Pro to 18 Pro, there is an increased battery life. The new eSIM-only models contain a 4,288 mAh capacity battery, slightly larger than the previous generation’s 4,252 mAh. In reality, it’s the efficiency claims that are doing the most for battery life. Apple claims you’ll be able to get iPhone 17 Pro Max battery life on a regular iPhone 18 Pro. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is supposed to have the best longevity of any iPhone ever. Apple claims you can get 36 hours on a non-Max iPhone 18 Pro during video playback tests, but those don’t matter one bit compared to real-life scenarios. Again, this is something we’ll have to test ourselves. Both phones also support ultra-fast charging, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max meant to hit 50% battery in 30 minutes. It’s essentially equivalent to what we had on the iPhone 17 Pro. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Camera Apple explicitly wants you to know the iPhone 18 Pro is its camera phone. For the first time, Apple’s adding a mechanical aperture to its main 48-megapixel wide lens, allowing up to four f-stops of f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. Those settings can drastically change your camera’s depth of field as well as how you can light and frame your subjects. Samsung previously tried this on its Galaxy S9 and S10 series, though those phones only allowed for either a wide-open or f/2.4 aperture. China-centric phones like the Xiaomi 14 Ultra include variable apertures between f/1.63 and f/4.0. Still, this is a new capability that no previous iPhone could claim. Most regular phone users will stick with automatic settings. On the flip side of things, if you were actually interested in understanding more about how photographers understand cameras, the iPhone 18 Pro could be your first taste. Google’s latest camera capabilities in devices like the Pixel 11 Pro are all focused on software for photo processing. Somehow, it’s Apple who’s trying to give its users more fine-tuned control. The iPhone 18 Pro still has three lenses: a 48-megapixel Fusion wide lens, a 48-megapixel Fusion periscope telephoto lens, and a 48-megapixel Fusion ultra-wide lens. Other than a variable aperture, not much has otherwise changed. Apple said it has upgraded its photo processing pipeline to help it produce better photos. Apple also added new “Pro” controls to the camera app to finally give all the “shot on iPhone” people more manual options for their photos and video—such as shutter speed or white balance. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Software features The iPhone 17 Pro is perfectly capable of running all the newfangled iOS 27 features, including Siri AI. However, there’s at least one other iPhone 18 Pro-exclusive feature: Apple Reference Image. The phone will essentially take your photo and process it through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers to create an unalterable reference photo. If somebody takes your shot or deepfakes it, you’ll be able to compare theirs to your original. Other than that, iPhone 17 Pro users may have very few reasons to upgrade. The main focus this year is on cameras, and if you only got your “Pro”-level phone for clout, then there’s not much here for you to care about. However, for those of us waiting for the most powerful iPhone, this one certainly fits the bill. Also, if—like me—you were dreaming of a Pro-level iPhone in red, burgundy may be the closest we’ll ever get. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are up for preorder Sept. 12, and they should start shipping Sept. 18.

item.title: Never Forget, AI Slop Is Polluting 9/11 History on the Internet as We Speak
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.55
became known as the Man in the Red Bandana after stories spread about his heroism on September 11, 2001. Now, an AI-generated image purporting to show Crowther rescuing people from the World Trade Center is going viral—the latest example of how fabricated images could distort our collective memory of 9/11 for generations. The 24-year-old Crowther was working on the 104th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center when a plane struck on that fateful day. Crowther, an equities trader, was also a volunteer firefighter and is credited with helping save the lives of at least a dozen people. He reportedly helped guide people to the lone functioning stairwell and even carried some people down the stairs himself. He died when the South Tower collapsed. President Donald Trump awarded Crowther the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday and, as always, the president had to make it about himself, insisting he doesn’t like that the man in the red bandana had become much more famous than him. Trump on a deceased 9/11 rescuer: “The Man in the Red Bandana. Have you heard of him? He’s become more famous than me. I don’t like it. Very unhappy. But he’s become much more famous than me.” — FactPost (@factpostnews.bsky.social) September 8, 2026 at 8:25 AM Crowther’s story of heroism is very real according to multiple witnesses, but the image that’s going viral of Crowther isn’t. There are no known photos of Crowther in action on September 11th. One major problem with the proliferation of AI images is that AI image detectors can be unreliable. Gizmodo ran the image above through ChatGPT and asked if it was created with AI. The response from ChatGPT: “It very likely is not AI-generated. It appears to be a genuine historical photograph rather than an AI-created image.” The explanation from ChatGPT went on to insist that the image has features “you’d expect from a real news photograph” and that it’s “consistent with photographs taken during the evacuation of the World Trade Center after the September 11 attacks.” When Gizmodo uploaded the image to Grok, the chatbot claimed that it was “a well-known photograph from the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks,” but when pressed on whether it was authentic, Grok finally admitted it might be fake. Claude said the image was a photo but likely a dramatization and not created with AI.
