When I asked Claude to do a reverse image search, the chatbot said it “confirmed” the image was from a documentary or similar that depicted the events and wasn’t made with AI: “So to directly answer your question: no, this doesn’t look AI-generated — it’s a reenactment/dramatization photo…” The definitive documentary on Crowther, Man In Red Bandana (2017), does feature an actor very briefly recreating some of his actions while saving people, but it doesn’t match up with the AI image that’s currently going viral. The actor playing Crowther in that documentary is wearing a white t-shirt, not a button-up shirt and tie. When we tried Gemini and asked if the image had the SynthID watermark, which is added to all images created with Google’s AI tools, the chatbot said that it couldn’t check that. Google opened up SynthID detection to all Gemini users last year, so that was a weird claim. After being pressed, the chatbot said we were right that this feature had been added and Gemini hadn’t found it to have SynthID. The hallucination and initial refusal to check should definitely give us pause when relying on the safeguards AI companies have supposedly created for us to fact-check our own reality. In a somewhat odd twist, Google’s AI overview insists the image is a “dramatic scene from the 1999 disaster television miniseries Aftershock: Earthquake in New York,” something that’s both untrue and would date the image to before the terror attacks of 2001. The image is not genuine and was definitely made with AI. Anyone can tell that just by looking at it, to say nothing of the fact that reverse image searches reveal it was likely never published before this week. Other AI images of Crowther have also popped up this year, like the one below from Facebook. Roughly 25% of Americans alive in 2026 weren’t born yet on September 11, 2001. The images that live on and spread online shape how we understand that day. And there are plenty of other AI images circulating online that purport to show what happened that day. Even when the underlying events are grounded in reality, fake images distort how we understand history. In some ways, this isn’t exactly a new problem. Here at Gizmodo, we spent much of the 2010s debunking fake historical images that were created with Photoshop-style tools. But there was a built-in friction with old-school Photoshop. Users were required to have some degree of talent and spend a bit of time creating fakes. These days, anyone can prompt a fake image using nothing but words and output a photo-realistic result in seconds. That low barrier to entry has created an environment where we often refuse to believe things that are real because they could be AI. People like Donald Trump even exploit this, insisting that authentic photos and videos must be AI because they’re inconvenient to his narrative. There have been a lot of those instances, believe it or not. And we’re all much dumber for it. READ MORE:

item.title: Android's private DNS feature solves a problem most people don't know they have
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.69
If you care about protecting your privacy online, you've probably seen an ad for VPNs. You likely also know to seek out private messaging apps like Signal and Proton Mail. But there's another change you need to make in order to protect your phone's web traffic from prying eyes, and it's a relatively simple fix. Your DNS isn't private by default It's time to change this DNS stands for Domain Name System. It's what enables you to get somewhere by typing a website name rather than having to enter an exact numerical IP address. Without DNS, typing howtogeek.com would only yield an error message. Out of the box, your phone's DNS activity is quite likely neither encrypted nor private. Your internet service provider (such as Comcast or Verizon) or carrier (Verizon, T-Mobile, or AT&T) can see every site you visit. If you’re on a public Wi-Fi network, you run the risk of a snoop taking a peek at your activities as well. Third-party DNS providers like Cloudflare, NextDNS, and Mullvad offer a way to browse the web while hiding your domain name requests from your ISP. It does so by encrypting your DNS activity, just as encrypted email masks the content of your messages and HTTPS hides what data a website is transmitting to your device. How to enable Private DNS on Android It only takes a couple taps To keep your phone from leaking your domain name requests, you'll need to dive into your network settings. You can do so by swiping down from the top of the screen and tapping on the gear icon that opens your phone's Settings app. Then navigate to "Network & internet." Towards the bottom, you'll see an option for "Private DNS." Tapping here provides you with three options: Off, Automatic, and Private DNS provider hostname. You’ll likely see “Automatic” enabled by default, which means your phone will use DNS encryption when it detects the option available. This leaves you at the whim of your ISP or carrier, who may prefer to track and monetize your browsing activity rather than protect it. “Off” disables DNS encryption entirely. For a continuous private connection, you'll want to select a private DNS provider hostname, and you will then need to enter an address in order for the changes to take effect. If you don't yet know one to put here, you can find several options in our list of the best DNS servers for secure browsing. Just keep in mind that you will need to enter a hostname into this field, not an IP address. In other words, you’ll need to enter the private web address your provider offers, rather than a series of numbers and periods. Once you've entered your selection, you can confirm whether things are working using the Safer.com Browser Privacy Test. That said, there are circumstances where this fix may not be the one you’re looking for, and you’d actually be better off leaving the default setting in place. Private DNS does not fully mask your web activity There is still a lot your ISP can learn about you DNS encryption, whether via DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT), doesn’t fully prevent your ISP from seeing what you do online. While you’re shielding your DNS lookups, all the traffic that follows still happens over their connection. This means the ISP can see the destination IP address you connected to and how much data was transmitted. The company can also see how much time you spend on the site before switching to another. You’ll need to take other steps if you sincerely wish to prevent others from gaining insights into what you do online. The more technically minded who are interested in self-hosting can rent a cheap VPS, install Wireguard, and tell all of their devices to use this VPS as a full-tunnel VPN endpoint. Those of us who aren’t interested in that whole song and dance can look into commercial VPN options. They often provide mobile apps that make encrypting a connection as simple as possible, often requiring only a single tap and granting some permissions. Just know that if you opt to use a commercial VPN, such as Private Internet Access or ProtonVPN, they tend to offer their own encrypted DNS. In that situation, you’ll want to leave the private DNS setting on your phone set to “Automatic” and trust the VPN connection to shield your DNS lookups instead. There’s no way to go online without leaking at least a little Private DNS encrypts your DNS lookups, but it doesn’t mask the resulting web traffic. VPNs may go a step further, but your ISP can tell you’re using one, and you must trust your VPN provider not to abuse your trust. It’s even possible to tell someone is using TOR, even if that may be all you’re able to tell. In other words, don’t start browsing the web with the false assumption that everything you do is private, but by reducing your online footprint as best you can, you reduce how much information can be monetized or used for online attacks.

item.title: 5 3D-printed clock projects you should make time for this weekend (Sep 11 - 13)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.51
I don’t currently have any visible clocks on display in my house. I’m never without my watch or phone, and I decided that if I were to sacrifice some space for a dedicated timepiece, it would need to be something special, different, or interesting. That’s exactly what these 3D-printed clocks are. Fully functional mechanical 3D-printed clock Complete with pendulum You can buy a simple clock mechanism for relatively cheap; they’re even available for sale on the MakerWorld shop. Most of the clock designs featured today don’t actually make use of a simple mechanism, instead opting for more interesting ways to keep time. This mechanical clock is fully 3D printed except for one part: the pendulum rod. The designer recommends an “M6 threaded rod with a minimum length of 1.1 m" in order to keep the mechanism moving and the clock accurate. This design “costs” around 700g in filament and presents you with a detailed yet satisfying build project. Take a peek at the detailed instructions before you print it to see what’s entailed—it looks a lot like putting LEGO kits together to me. Once built, the clock should keep itself running and will almost certainly start a conversation with anyone who is visiting. This is the revised second version, but the original is still available (which requires more non-3D-printed parts). Word Clock Bring it to life with an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Zero W A word clock is, unsurprisingly, a clock that tells the time with words. Rather than seeing the numbers 10:20, you’ll see the words “twenty past ten” instead. This is a fun spin on the simple act of telling the time, bound to brighten up any kitchen, office, or anywhere else you want to stick it. This 3D-printed word clock uses an addressable LED strip, a printer with a multi-material system (like Bambu Lab’s AMS), and a Raspberry Pi Zero W or ESP32 microcontroller. Some soldering is required, and you’ll need a few extra bits like screws and wires (on top of 2m of LED strip). Flip clock With an RTC module to track the time when it’s off An oldie but a goody, this flip clock design has been sitting on Thingiverse since 2020, with a GitHub repo dedicated to the build that includes a bill of materials, plus instructions for printing, assembling, and calibrating the clock. At the end of it, you’ll have a physical moving flip clock made from 3D-printed parts. Powered by a small Arduino-compatible microcontroller, the clock uses stepper motors and drivers to move the flaps. In addition to tracking time even when the power is off, the clock will automatically adhere to US daylight saving time. Wandering hour clock Once you figure out how it works, it’s great I spent a few minutes staring at this clock, trying to figure out how exactly one is supposed to read the time. It turns out that it’s incredibly easy: the current hour always points at a minute counter at the bottom of the screen. So as 9 o’clock approaches the 60-minute mark, 10 o’clock will reach the 0-minute mark and start again. A rework of an existing project, the wandering clock depends on an upcycled IKEA Bondis wall clock (though you could probably adapt other mechanisms to suit), a few screws, and some bearings. The Printables project has detailed instructions for assembling everything, and of course you can customize the colors to suit whatever room you’re putting it in. Cube clock Two cubes move to tell the time This minimalist cube clock works with Bambu Lab’s clock component kit or cheap IKEA (and other) clock mechanisms. It’s incredibly simple: the background is a static cube, while two more cubes sit on top. One is connected to the minute hand, the other to the hour hand. As the time changes, so does the shape of the clock, making for an interesting and ever-changing timepiece. There’s nothing particularly complex about this one, but it’s the perfect example of a fast project that you can make yourself using old clock mechanisms that might just be lying around. Go even further by customizing the clock face, changing the colors, or adding a light to the back of the design. Many of these projects depend on an ESP32 or similar microcontroller. Check out some more 3D printing projects you can only make with an ESP32.

item.title: My Android notifications kept arriving late—these settings were the problem
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.23
I've had problems with Android notifications arriving late for years. Usually, it's not a huge deal—if someone needs me urgently, they'll just call instead of texting me. But not all notifications are equal. An Instagram Reel shared by my friend can wait an hour for a reaction, but an important work email about a meeting that's been canceled or moved up a few hours can't. Since I can't afford to miss notifications like those anymore, I finally decided to figure out what was causing the delays and fix the problem. Battery Saver is delaying your notifications Battery life comes at a cost Some people like to keep Battery Saver (aka Power Saving Mode on some devices) permanently enabled on their devices for a few good reasons. Modern phones are plenty fast, so sacrificing a fraction of a second for apps to load to extend the battery life of your phone by up to a few hours is a worthwhile tradeoff. However, on top of throttling the CPU's maximum clock speed and disabling various other performance optimizations to reduce power draw, Battery Saver actually does a number of other things to your phone. The most important thing for us today is that it heavily restricts or outright stops background sync for non-essential apps. Some apps might work just fine, but others might fail to sync for hours. Fortunately, the fix is super easy. Head over to Settings > Battery and disable Battery Saver or switch to Balanced mode, depending on what brand your phone is. Battery optimization is stopping apps from syncing in the background Give specific apps more freedom Android has a pretty clever feature that optimizes battery use on a per-app basis. It allows your phone to throttle apps you don't use and prioritize background activity for your most-used ones. It's a pretty clever system for the most part, but it's also one of the most common sources of delayed notifications because apps are optimized by default. This includes your email app of choice, Slack, Asana, and other important work-related apps that you might only use for a few minutes a day but can't afford to miss notifications from. At the same time, social media apps will probably get more priority if that's what you use the most on your phone. Fortunately, you can adjust this default behavior fairly easily. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps. Find an app on this list that's experiencing delayed notifications and tap on Battery usage, then switch it from Optimized to Unrestricted. The exact wording varies from brand to brand, but since it's built directly into Android, the setting is there—and it's most likely what's causing your delayed notifications. Your app is being cut off from the internet in the background Let your important apps use data Data Saver is another core Android feature that optimizes cellular data usage. It's disabled by default, but if you enabled it at some point and forgot to turn it back off, you might not even be aware of it. Some phones display a persistent notification at the top, but not all (or the option to do so might be disabled by default). In any case, it only takes a few seconds to check. Go to Settings > Network and Internet (or equivalent) > Data usage > Data Saver and disable the feature. If you must keep it on because you're on a limited plan, there's an option to leave data unrestricted for some apps, which is the perfect compromise. Again, the wording differs between brands, so just poke around until you find it. Android is restricting an app you haven't opened lately Even unused apps deserve notification access Pause app activity if unused is another semi-problematic core Android feature that was introduced with Android 12. It's surprisingly aggressive at what it does: it puts an app into complete hibernation, kills notifications, revokes permissions, and wipes cache data if it hasn't been used in 3 months. This can be problematic if the app in question is something you access very infrequently but still need to keep up with, like a specific smart home app, security alert app, travel app, or similar. Unfortunately, there's no global setting to switch off app hibernation, but what you can do is disable it on an app-by-app basis. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps, find the app you suspect got disabled, and disable Pause app activity if unused. On my phone, it's the Manage unused apps toggle that needs to be turned off. Like with the settings I discussed previously, the exact wording might differ between brands, but if your phone runs Android 12 or newer, it's there. A manufacturer-specific setting is restricting apps on its own Your phone might have a hidden battery saver Everything I've discussed so far has been general fixes that you can use on every Android phone. However, some brands have their own additional battery management features and optimizations on top of those built into Android. Unfortunately, since there are so many brands and things are constantly changing with updates, going over all of them here could quickly turn into its own article. So, if you're still experiencing delayed notifications after trying all of the fixes above, I recommend doing a little research on your specific device to see if there's a hidden toggle or feature that you can change to force background sync for problematic apps. Most notification delays have a simple explanation I'm sure that most Android owners can relate to the frustration of delayed notifications that happen here and there. The majority of the time, the cause is some data- or battery-saving feature that's built into Android, and luckily, the fix is often as simple as changing a single option.

item.title: I got DOOM running on Android Auto, and it's exactly as impractical as it sounds
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.96
“Can it run DOOM?” It’s the question people love to half-jokingly ask about every gadget with a screen. Android, of course, can run DOOM — but what about Android Auto? That’s an entirely different beast. At first thought, you might think it would be an easy and resounding, “Yes! Of course, Android Auto can run DOOM.” That is the correct answer, but it’s far from easy. Android Auto exists in a weird place between full-blown Android and a glorified monitor. Android Auto is Android, but also not It’s complicated The thing that makes Android Auto so useful is the fact that it’s literally the same Android that’s on your phone. Even if you didn’t already know this, you’re well aware of the benefits. It’s the reason why your phone apps are present, signed in, and ready to be picked up where you left off on the car screen. That being said, not all of your phone apps are available in the Android Auto interface. Developers need to build in-car compatibility into their apps, ensure they meet Google’s car app quality guidelines, and they must fit into a Google-approved driving category. Android Auto apps generally fall into five categories: navigation, media, communication, utilities, and “parked.” Apps in the first four categories can be used in some capacity while driving, but the “parked” category is for apps that can’t be used while the vehicle is in motion. This includes video players, browsers, and games. So, it’s obviously not as easy as toggling a switch to make an app suddenly work on an Android Auto screen. That’s why only a small fraction of the apps on your phone are available, and an even smaller selection of games. Plus, most games are simply too complicated to be worth playing on a small screen in your car while parked. But when did practicality stop anyone from putting DOOM on a strange device? DOOM can run on Android Auto If you’re willing to do the work As I said at the top, DOOM can indeed run on Android Auto. However, it’s not as simple as downloading the official mobile version of DOOM from the Play Store. Instead, we’ll need to take advantage of a clever GitHub project. DOOM Mobile is a cross-platform implementation of the classic 1993 game that works on Android, iPhone, Windows, and MacCatalyst. Unlike many other projects that utilize emulators and wrappers, this is a full C# port of the original engine. It runs fully natively on your phone, and that’s evidence of the fact that you need to own a real copy of DOOM to play. The game needs a DOOM data .wad file in order to play past a short demo. I’ll be the first to admit that most of the technical explanation is out of my wheelhouse. For those who are interested in the nitty-gritty, I’ll spit out some details. Game frames are rendered using hardware-accelerated SkiaSharp v3 integrated with DrawnUI for .NET MAUI. The wall and level calculations are computed in C#, but the final rendered game texture is passed through a shader to allow GPU-side visual processing. Controlling the game works with touch or keyboard controls, depending on your device. On a phone, you can swipe around to move and turn, tap to shoot, and simply select items from the HUD and on-screen menus. That’s how the game is controlled on an Android Auto screen. Now, here’s the big catch. You can’t download an APK from the project’s “Releases” tab. Instead, you’ll need to compile it yourself in Microsoft Visual Studio with the .NET Multi-platform App UI workload installed or JetBrains Rider. I have no experience with either of these, so I enlisted the help of a good friend. After I installed the APK on my phone, it appeared in the Android Auto launcher with all of the other apps. No hacks or developer options required. It opened and was playable with touch controls just like on my phone. Next time you’re stuck in traffic, you can pick off some monsters with your BFG. That’s one more for the list of devices that can play DOOM.

item.title: These 5 underrated smart home upgrades keep your lights working when the internet goes down
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.72
Smart bulbs are one of the most common entries into the world of smart home devices, but they're not without their problems. If your internet goes down, you may find that you lose features or simply can't control your bulbs at all. There are several ways to stop this from happening. Use Matter devices with local control Alexa doesn't always need the cloud Popular smart home ecosystems such as Alexa and Google Home have made many smart homes heavily reliant on the cloud. With a Works with Google Home light bulb, for example, when you ask your smart speaker to turn on the light, the spoken command is sent from your speaker to Google's cloud, which interprets the command and sends a message to the smart bulb manufacturer's cloud, which sends the appropriate command to the bulb to turn on. If the internet goes down, the whole thing falls apart. Matter changes this, because commands are designed to travel locally over Wi-Fi or Thread. Google states that when you're at home, commands to Matter devices are carried out locally without an internet connection. The same is true of Alexa. Alexa can communicate with Matter devices locally, allowing supported Alexa-enabled devices to control them even when the internet is down. With supported Echo devices, Alexa voice commands can also continue to work during an internet outage. Move lighting automations to Home Assistant Run your smart home completely locally If features. There is an alternative that can be set up to work completely locally. Home Assistant is free and open-source smart home software that you run on your own hardware. You can run it on anything from a Raspberry Pi or old laptop to a mini PC or NAS. Home Assistant is designed with local control and privacy as the focus. The beauty of Home Assistant is that it doesn't care what ecosystem your smart home products are designed to work with. You can add Alexa-compatible devices, Apple Home devices, and Google devices, and control them all just the same. You can even set up a local voice assistant that allows you to control your smart home with your voice, without the need for an internet connection. Switch from Wi-Fi to Zigbee bulbs Your lights don't need an internet connection Just because you're using Home Assistant, it doesn't automatically make your smart home entirely local. If you're using Wi-Fi smart bulbs that are controlled by a cloud service, then your smart home is still not fully local. Commands from Home Assistant still need to reach the cloud to control your lights. You can make your lighting fully local by using Zigbee smart bulbs so your bulbs can talk directly to your smart home over your local Zigbee network without needing to use the cloud. Even proprietary systems such as Philips Hue can be controlled locally by Home Assistant using Local Push. Some optional Hue features still rely on the cloud, but all the core features can work locally. You can also cut Philips Hue out of the loop completely and connect your Philips Hue bulbs directly to Home Assistant using an option such as Zigbee2MQTT. With a suitable Zigbee coordinator, Home Assistant can then control your smart bulbs directly, without the need for a Hue Bridge. Another benefit of Zigbee is that even if your router goes down, Home Assistant can continue to talk to your smart bulbs over the Zigbee network. Automations that control your lights can continue to run as long as they're not reliant on your local Wi-Fi network. Add Zigbee binding Keep your lights working even when your smart hub is unreachable Even though Zigbee smart bulbs can be controlled from Home Assistant without an internet connection or even a local Wi-Fi network, they still need something to send them commands. If your Home Assistant server is out of action, you won't be able to control your bulbs from your phone, from dashboards, or using smart buttons that send commands via Home Assistant. That's where Zigbee binding can help. It's possible to bind a Zigbee controller such as a remote or smart button directly to a specific Zigbee bulb. With the binding in place, the command is sent directly from the controller to the bulb over your Zigbee network, without needing to go through a smart home hub or Zigbee coordinator at all. With supported devices, even if your smart home hub has shut down or your Zigbee coordinator has come unplugged, the Zigbee button can talk directly to the Zigbee bulb and turn your lights on and off. Use smart switches with local control Dumb bulbs don't care if the internet is down With smart bulbs, the hardware required to communicate with other devices is inside the bulb itself. You can take this out of the bulbs' hands by installing smart switches and using them with standard dumb bulbs. Smart switches solve many of the problems with smart bulbs, including the fact that if you turn off the power to a smart bulb at the switch, you can't control it at all. With a smart switch, you can manually turn the power on and off at the switch while still controlling the switch itself through your smart home. If your internet goes down, or your smart home server stops working, you can continue to use a smart switch manually, although you may lose remote control. It's one of the best options for setting up lighting that continues to work how the rest of your household would expect. Your lights don't have to rely on the internet Cloud-based smart devices are very convenient, but convenience comes at a price. Not only can these devices stop working properly when the internet goes down, but smart home companies can even stop supporting cloud-based smart home devices altogether. That's why a fully local smart home can often be the better choice.

item.title: There's a tiny computer hiding in most USB-C cables (and it isn't always used for good)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.43
Two USB-C cables can look identical, cost wildly different amounts, and behave nothing alike. The reason sits inside the connector housing: a chip that talks to your devices before any power moves. It's genuinely useful engineering. It's also a convenient place to hide something nasty. What is that tiny computer about? The e-marker chip that negotiates power and speed The component is called an e-marker, short for electronically marked cable, and it lives inside the connector shell rather than the cable itself. It communicates with chargers and devices over the Configuration Channel (CC) pin, telling connected hardware what the cable can actually do. It draws its own power from the VCONN pin—up to about a watt—which is what lets a passive-looking cable participate actively in a negotiation without any external supply. That negotiation happens before anything else. Power Delivery transactions begin by addressing the cable itself in a stage known as SOP prime, and only once the cable's capabilities are established does the rest of the process continue between source and sink. The chip publishes its specification as a set of 32-bit values called Vendor Defined Objects, or VDOs, covering things like the manufacturer and model, the signalling protocol and maximum transfer speed, whether the cable's controller can communicate independently with the charger or device, and the hardware and firmware version. Not every cable has one. Cables rated at or below 3A aren't required to carry an e-marker chip; anything expected to handle more current needs one. In practice, a cable carries an e-marker if it is rated above USB 2.0 speeds or above 60W. Either one, not necessarily both. Given that USB Power Delivery now reaches 240W, and that pushing that much energy down an unrated cable risks overheating or fire, the chip functions as a safety mechanism as much as a feature flag. Plug in a cable with no chip and both ends assume the worst case, capping you at 60W and 480Mbps regardless of what your laptop and charger are capable of. What are its downsides? Opaque specifications and a perfect hiding place The first problem is honesty. Charging capability and data capability are separate fields in the e-marker, and manufacturers set them independently: a genuine, spec-compliant 240W cable can declare its data capability as 480Mbps, the same speed as a cable from 2001. Buyers reasonably assume that an expensive, high-wattage cable is also a fast one. The chip cheerfully says otherwise, in a format nobody without a protocol analyzer can read. The second problem is worse. If a connector housing can accommodate a microcontroller, flash storage and firmware, it can accommodate other things. Security researcher Mike Grover built the O.MG cable as a penetration-testing tool for red teams and awareness training. Hidden inside the connector is a web server, a keylogger and a keystroke-injection engine reachable over Wi-Fi, so the cable can type commands, capture what's typed back, and be driven remotely from across the room. Elite models store up to 650,000 keystrokes, support geofencing to trigger payloads by location, and can self-destruct to render the cable inert. In December 2024, industrial CT scanner manufacturer Lumafield imaged an O.MG cable and found sophisticated electronics and an antenna packed into the connector, alongside a second set of wires connecting a secondary die hidden beneath the primary microcontroller. Those bond wires are roughly the thickness of a human hair, and the arrangement would evade inspection techniques that can't assess an assembly volumetrically. Even an X-ray image can't reliably show whether a cable has been tampered with, because the additional electronics are so small and so cleverly integrated that they're nearly indistinguishable from regular components. Should you worry? Real risk, modest odds, and defenses worth knowing Proportion matters here. No real-world juice jacking attack has ever been publicly documented, though researchers keep proving it's technically possible, most notably at USENIX Security 2025, where Graz University of Technology researchers presented ChoiceJacking, the first family of USB attacks to bypass existing juice jacking mitigations by injecting input events while a data connection is being established. It let a malicious charger spoof user input and enable data transfer or code execution on eleven Android and iOS devices without consent. Apple and Google have since shipped fixes in iOS 18.4 and Android 15, and on current iPhones connecting a new USB device requires a passcode or Face ID. The standards body's answer has existed for years and gone largely unused. The USB-IF launched its Type-C Authentication Program with 128-bit cryptographic verification of chargers, devices, cables and power sources, managed through DigiCert. It remains optional, with no mandatory requirement for OEMs to adopt it. Practical defense is therefore about provenance rather than detection. Use your own cables, buy from the manufacturer or an authorized seller, and label what's yours. Keep your phone locked when charging in public and decline connection prompts you didn't initiate. A Malicious Cable Detector exists for around $40, using side-channel power analysis to flag the electrical signature of an implant, but its own documentation frames it as a first-line screen rather than a forensic instrument, and it can never prove a cable is clean. Weight and feel tell you nothing. Cables are computers now, so treat them accordingly The e-marker exists for good reasons, and it makes modern fast charging possible. But it normalized the idea of silicon inside a connector, which is exactly what makes malicious implants so hard to spot. Buy your own cables, from people you trust.

item.title: The one cheap smart home upgrade your router needs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.51
Occasionally rebooting your router and modem is pretty normal, and some routers even have a reboot schedule function that can take care of this for you. Though problematic network equipment should be replaced, adding a smart plug to your setup can save you effort and even automate the entire process. Buying the right smart plug It depends on your smart home platform Rebooting your router usually means cutting power for around 10 seconds, then firing it back up and waiting for everything to return to normal. While you can do this by physically walking to the router, being able to do so remotely is more convenient. To enable this functionality, you’ll need a smart plug. This can’t be just any smart plug, however. After all, smart plugs that depend on Wi-Fi will cease to function when the network goes down. Instead, you should pick a smart plug that uses a different type of wireless communication. Which you choose largely depends on what smart home platform you’re using. For Home Assistant users, the sky is the limit. As long as you add the necessary adapter to your setup—like a Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 for Thread or Zigbee and a ZWA-2 for Z-Wave—you’re set for as long as your server is up, and the plug has power. You can also use Bluetooth smart plugs to achieve the same outcome. Apple Home users can choose Matter over Thread devices, particularly since modern Apple hubs like the HomePod mini and Apple TV 4K operate as Thread border routers. The same is true for some models of Amazon Echo and Google Nest devices. Of course, you’ll also need to pair these devices with smart plugs that use the Thread protocol. Both Google and Amazon have been slow out of the gate to embrace local control of smart home technology, which is why I’d urge alternatives. Limitations to be aware of Another reason to pick a local solution like Home Assistant Keep in mind that when your router goes offline, so too will your primary means of communicating with your smart home dashboard. This is true of all smart home platforms, which means that although you’ll be able to turn your plug off manually, you won’t necessarily be able to switch it back on. Home Assistant users can get around this by building a script that restarts their router, tying basic on-off functionality to a Zigbee (or similar) remote, or building an automation that detects connectivity issues and restarts the router or modem. If you aren’t using Home Assistant, you’re pretty much out of luck when it comes to manual restarts, though there are some other options you can explore. Perform restarts manually No need to unplug anything If you want to reboot your router or modem manually using Home Assistant, head to Settings > Automations & scenes and click on “Scripts” at the top of the page. Now click “+ Create script” and add a Device action for the plug you want to switch off (or add two, if you have separate network equipment) to turn off. Add a delay, then turn your network equipment back on again. You can now add your script to a dashboard of your choosing, or run it using the Scripts menu any time you need it. Alternatively, you can use a remote and create an automation so that the remote either runs the script you’ve created (perhaps with a long press) or bind buttons accordingly so that they control your smart plugs. This bypasses the need to switch your plug on manually using your Home Assistant dashboard (which is inaccessible whenever your network goes down). Some brands of smart devices can be bound so that they do not need a hub. For example, IKEA's Tretakt plug can be bound to a Rodret remote by holding the pairing button down while within range until the light flashes. Schedule regular reboots It certainly can't hurt My TP-Link Archer AX72 modem includes a “Reboot schedule” that restarts the modem at a time of my choosing. I don’t use this, mostly because I’ve got a smart home to do the heavy lifting. My router is only around a year old, so I’m hoping to get a bit more life out of it before it starts routinely giving up the ghost. That said, there are some good arguments to be made for routinely restarting your router. If you find that your router routinely crashes, a weekly restart might be the remedy you need until you get around to replacing it. You can schedule this basic functionality with most smart home platforms. Home Assistant makes it easy with its advanced automations, but you can get around the limited automation possibilities in a platform like Apple Home by creating two automations (one to turn the plug off, another to turn it on, a minute apart) provided you’re using Thread and not Wi-Fi. Go one better and reboot automatically Automate it! By far the best solution is to only restart your router when you need to. You can use Home Assistant to monitor your home internet connection and only initiate a restart after a set period of no connectivity. Check out our full guide on how to do this. Amazon, Google, and Apple’s smart home platforms lack the ability to create these kinds of complex automations. Some smart plugs may connect to an ecosystem-dependent app that allows them to be programmed, but that’ll depend on exactly what you’ve got. If you’re looking for another solution, why not give the Keep Connect network equipment smart plug a whirl. It’s a purpose-built device that only cuts power to your network equipment when the internet connection goes down. Keep Connect Automatic Router Rebooter - Brand - Keep - Schedules - Yes This is not your typical smart plug. The Keep Connect Automatic Router Rebooter triggers a power cycle when it detects a connection loss to automatically reboot your devices without you having to lift a finger. Take the time to improve your home network Rebooting your router can solve all manner of network problems, but you should really look at replacing network equipment that is constantly letting you down. Check out our top picks for routers.

item.title: Loaded dice, card cheaters, and other unethical board game parts you can 3D print
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.08
The great thing about 3D printers is that they can make almost anything these days. The bad thing about 3D printers is that you can make almost anything with them. There are some obvious, actually illegal things that will get you in trouble if you print them. Though I won't mention them here, you can get on a watchlist on your own without my help! Then there are things that are legal, but they're a bad idea to 3D print. But what about things that aren't necessarily illegal, and are technically fine to print, but are also really unethical? Loaded dice If you've seen the movie "Casino", you know to leave these at home In case you somehow don't know, "loaded" dice are designed to fall on a specific number almost every time. In a fair die, there's an equal chance of landing on any given number, but if you change the weight distribution of the die to favor a specific number on the bottom, then you can control which number shows at the top. Traditionally, this is done using metal weights inside the dice, but with a 3D printer, where you can design the interior structure precisely, all you have to do is determine where the weight of the infill is. Indeed, with RevK's Loaded Dice, you need to set the infill density to 95% for it to work, and there are six models in total, each favoring a different potential number. Given how light PLA is, it's not really obvious that these dice don't have a uniform weight distribution. But a much larger issue would be that the dice were 3D-printed in the first place. So it's not like you're going to surreptitiously switch these out for store-bought fair dice. That said, people are getting really good at processing 3D prints so that you can't even tell they were made with a 3D printer. ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 - Build Volume - 256 × 256 × 256 mm - Connectivity - Wi-Fi The ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 builds on the solid foundation of its predecessor and adds an affordable, effective multicolor system to the mix. - Heated Build Plate - Yes - Top Print Speed - ≤500 mm/s - Max Plate Temperature - 110°C - Max Print Temperature - 350°C - MULTICOLOR PRINTING - Yes A card shuffler that deliberately deals winning hands Though, to be fair, you need more than just a 3D printer for this one! You may have heard (as reported by the BBC) of those rigged high-stakes underground poker games involving NBA players and lots of high-tech cheating equipment. Well, if you look into it, you'll see that part of the scam involved a modified casino-grade card shuffler. This device is supposed to ensure a fair deal in games like Texas Hold'em, but by hacking and modifying the device, you can precisely determine where any given card is at any time. Now, that machine costs a fortune, and I guess those illegal modifications aren't cheap either, but as you can see above, a Reddit user used a 3D printer, a Raspberry Pi, and some other miscellaneous electronics and parts to make their own. It's an incredibly cool project, and it would make you the god-king of your local poker game, but I suspect it's going to be hard to convince your friends that they should use your homemade card shuffler when the next game night rolls around. Printing extra Scrabble pieces If you really need to get the last word in Some people take Scrabble far too seriously, and although this wonderful 3D model set of Scrabble tiles by jjpowelly are meant to let you replace lost tiles without buying a whole new box, clearly unscrupulous players could print out extra tiles and secrete them up a sleeve to gain an advantage. If you look closely at any of these tiles, it should be apparent that they are 3D-printed, but if you only slip in one or two letters, I bet you could get away with it. If you're playing with all 3D-printed tiles anyway, well, all bets are off, I guess. Printing your own tabletop miniatures is a gray area What would the emperor do? In the world of tabletop gaming, 3D printing has been rather controversial. This isn't about gaining an unfair advantage in the actual gameplay (which isn't how something like Warhammer works anyway) but more about copyright and intellectual property. With resin 3D printers and even modern FDM printers, you can create high-quality miniatures and then paint them. The tabletop community and the companies who sell official models to sustain themselves have had to reckon with this, and official games now have rules on what pieces may be 3D-printed, or how much of a given model is allowed to be 3D-printed. In the end, if you're using 3D printing as a way to avoid paying for (admittedly expensive) official models, there's certainly an ethical dimension to that. For no other reason than the hobby itself might disappear if this technology puts its custodians out of business. Follow your own conscience I can't stop you from printing whatever you want, and if you're just making stuff for your own personal amusement, there's no harm in it. However, with great power comes great responsibility. And owning a 3D printer gives you more than enough power to act in a fair and just manner.

item.title: 5 open-source desktop apps that I always recommend instead of their paid rivals
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.83
Any time I recommend software to a friend, there is always an inevitable question: How much does it cost? The quality isn't necessarily the discerning factor—no one wants to pay for something if it isn't necessary. That makes free, open-source tools very easy to recommend to most people without a moment's hesitation. Beyond simple costs, open-source programs also aren't going to change their licensing terms and suddenly lock you out like a paid service could. Open-source software doesn't usually require an account either, though there are a few notable exceptions. Bitwarden The password manager I can always recommend Bitwarden is an open-source password manager with clients for every major desktop operating system and browser. It is capable, easy to use, and free. When you compare it to paid products, you'll find it has most of the same features without worrying about monthly fees and Bitwarden's free tier covers unlimited passwords and devices. Additionally, the code is public and audited, and if you're particularly privacy-conscious, you can self-host a Bitwarden compatible server on your own. The only real trade-off is a simpler UI when compared to programs like 1Password, and a few "quality of life" features like password monitoring (to keep an eye on leaks and breaches) do require an inexpensive subscription. LibreOffice A full office suite for free LibreOffice offers Writer, Calc, and Impress in one convenient package as an alternative to Microsoft's Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Of course, LibreOffice is free and open-source. It has no subscription, requires no accounts, and you don't have to worry about Copilot randomly being inserted during an update you don't want. If you're doing the most common document or spreadsheet tasks, you'll find that LibreOffice is completely up to the job. It even handles DOCX and XLSX files well most of the time. I've only occasionally run into issues with important Excel workbooks, and then only when there were complex automations attached to the spreadsheet. You can download LibreOffice from the official LibreOffice. Make sure to double-check which file format you use—if someone is expecting a DOCX file, you should make sure to send them a DOCX. If you want something that looks a bit more like Microsoft Office, you could try ONLYOFFICE instead. KDE's Kdenlive Great video editing without a subscription or the weird cancellation terms Video editing is a common need these days, but the most powerful tools are locked behind a subscription fee. If you need something basic, Kdenlive is a great option. It offers a timeline-based workflow—much like Adobe Premiere—without any cost. It is a great option for anyone doing light to moderate video editing, including YouTubers, teachers, small business owners, or hobbyists. If you need more advanced color grading tools, I'd recommend checking out DaVInci Resolve rather than jumping straight into a subscription model—DaVinci Resolve is not open-source, but it is free, and its tools are second to none. Make sure to enable hardware encoding the render settings if it isn't already. You'll save yourself a ton of time. GIMP The 3.x update makes GIMP easier to recommend GIMP has had a slightly rocky history. Fortunately, recent releases have significantly improved the program's usability and added new important features, like non-destructive layer effects, that it previously lacked. If you can't justify paying for a Photoshop subscription, but you need to retouch or edit photos, GIMP is a solid option. The big thing you don't get are features like generative fill, which you can replace with local AI models if you really want. GIMP also has a pretty healthy plugin ecosystem, so if it can't do something natively, there is a very good chance you can find a plugin to fill the gap. Audacity Simple, reliable, and it runs on anything Trimming clips, normalizing audio, or removing background noise are all common audio editing tasks, and you don't need a full DAW or Adobe Audition subscription to do it—Audacity will get you 90% of the way there for free. Audacity covers all the basics you'll need for audio editing and is extremely simple to use. The user interface isn't super minimalist either, which means there are fewer functions hidden behind sleek user interfaces. I normally prefer that, since it makes figuring out what an app can actually do a little bit easier. You can't go wrong with recommending a free, open-source tool Recommending paid software always comes with a lot of caveats. If your recommendation falls flat, someone is out of money, and they may be stuck in an agreement with weird cancelation terms. Open-source tools have no such drawbacks. In a worst-case scenario, the open-source tool isn't quite what someone needs, and they move on—no harm done. Most of the time, the free option is perfectly adequate. Always download these apps from their official sites, trusted package managers, or their official GitHub repos. Because these tools are so popular, they are frequently repackaged with adware by third-party sites looking to make a quick buck.

item.title: 5 new PowerToys features that are useful even if you're not a Windows power user
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.48
Microsoft's PowerToys suite of Windows utilities, which you can download from GitHub or install through the Microsoft Store, has earned a reputation as a tool designed for — and used exclusively by — Windows power users. But the reality is more nuanced. Yes, PowerToys includes a number of features you'll probably never need if you're a regular person who uses your Windows PC for entertainment, web browsing, and some light work. But the suite also packs a fair number of utilities that virtually every Windows user will find handy, no matter how "basic" their use of a Windows PC may be. With some of them, I genuinely don't understand why Microsoft hasn't already made them part of vanilla Windows. Since PowerToys recently received a cool new update, I'm going to share five PowerToys features, both old and new, that you should be using even if you don't consider yourself a Windows power user. Power Display Every Windows user with an external display will find this feature handy Ever since I upgraded to an OLED monitor, Power Display has become my favorite PowerToys feature. I recommend it to everyone who uses Windows with an external display, whether it's a desktop PC or a laptop connected to a monitor. through your monitor's menus. Better still, you can also adjust volume, color temperature, input source, and other options by enabling them in the Power Display options menu. These controls work across all the monitors connected to your PC, as well as in both SDR and HDR modes. Personally, I only use the brightness and contrast sliders because that's enough for my needs. Since my monitor is simply too bright for my taste at maximum brightness, I tweak its brightness all the time. When I'm working, I keep it well below 50% (usually at 30% or lower), set it between 60% and 70% when gaming in SDR or watching videos, and crank it up to 100% when playing games in HDR. Without Power Display, I would've had to constantly open the monitor's menu or keep it in HDR mode and constantly reach for the SDR content brightness slider, something I actually did for the first week or so before enabling Power Display. Find My Mouse I'm baffled Microsoft hasn't made this feature available in stock Windows Back when I started using macOS, I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Apple's desktop OS lets you locate your mouse pointer simply by shaking it. It's a very handy feature to have when you're using a 34-inch ultrawide monitor as I do. I eventually found a Windows alternative after installing PowerToys called Find My Mouse, and honestly, I really don't know why Microsoft hasn't added it to vanilla Windows yet. This is something virtually every Windows user could benefit from. If you don't want to mess with extra options, you can simply enable Find My Mouse in the Mouse Utilities menu and choose your preferred activation method. But if you want to go the extra mile, you can adjust the appearance of the mouse spotlight, create a custom activation method, and add excluded apps where the feature won't work while they're in the foreground. Always On Top Pin any window on top of others with a keyboard shortcut Always On Top is another PowerToys module I reckon many regular Windows users will benefit from. It does exactly what it says: it pins a specific app window on top of other windows with a single keyboard shortcut. The pinned window also gets a noticeable border around it, clearly showing that the feature is active. A sound notification also plays when you pin or unpin a window, so you'll always know when a window gets pinned. I usually use it when I need to calculate something with the Calculator app or when I'm writing about an app, such as PowerToys, and want to keep its window visible at all times. I reckon there are countless other scenarios where a feature like this can come in handy, and I'm sure virtually every Windows user will need it sooner or later. So, why don't you download PowerToys and enable it today? Window Hopper Switch between open windows of a single app Window Hopper is a recent addition to PowerToys, and since I’m always juggling multiple browser windows while working, I’ve been using it nonstop ever since Microsoft added it to the suite. It allows you to cycle between windows of a single app, much like the Alt + Tab shortcut lets you switch between all the open windows on your Windows desktop. It's simple and effective, and something I reckon most Windows users will find handy. Peek Preview any file in File Explorer by pressing Space Peek is another simple yet effective PowerToys module that virtually every Windows user can benefit from. Like Quick Look on macOS, which lets you preview files in Finder, Peek allows you to preview files in File Explorer with the press of a button. You can think of it as a minimal photo-viewing app, but Peek is much more powerful. It can open multimedia files, PDFs, HTML, and INI files, show you a summary of folders and files it can't open, and more. It's one of my favorite PowerToys features and yet another PowerToys feature I don't understand why isn't already part of the stock Windows experience. PowerToys is actually really simple to use Don't be daunted by PowerToys and the suite's massive number of modules. Navigating the app is super simple: all you have to do is click a tab, and it will immediately expand to show you all the features inside, which you can then peruse. What I recommend for newcomers is clicking the Welcome to PowerToys button in the lower-left corner, which lists every available feature and explains exactly what it does. After learning about them, you can enable only the ones you want and ignore the ones you don't need. I'm fairly certain you'll discover a few features I didn't mention here that will become indispensable to your daily workflow.

item.title: My favorite kitchen upgrade proves that a real smart home is more than plugs and bulbs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.27
Putting sensors all over the home and connecting them to Home Assistant is fun, I know, but it isn't for everyone — not yet. Thankfully, there are smart home upgrades that don't require any apps. I may have replaced every light switch in my home with a smart one, but my favorite smart home upgrade doesn't connect to my Homey Pro at all, and it's an improvement my entire family likes as much as I do. It's time to buy an instant hot water dispenser Our electric kettle has now entered the donate pile I didn't grow up with an electric kettle. Instead, my family boiled water in a saucepan on the stove whenever we wanted to make tea. Discovering an electric kettle as an adult felt like black magic. As a tea lover, this was a giant leap forward. When Waterdrop reached out to me about their M6CG instant hot and cold countertop water dispenser, it felt like a similar leap forward. After just one use, I knew I wasn't going back. My wife and two kids all had the same reaction. We haven't reached for our electric kettle since. In fact, we're giving it away. A countertop instant hot water dispenser doesn't take any time to boil, so I can stop taking shade from my European colleagues whose 240V kettles boil water much faster than is possible in America. A countertop hot water dispenser instead functions more like a tankless water heater, heating water as it comes out to get it to the right temperature. Since we're talking about a small stream of water, they can function off a regular 120V wall outlet with no extra electrical work required. Just place your cup under the dispenser, press the button, and watch hot water instantly dispense. Set water to the temperature you need Some units also turn off automatically after pouring the right amount I'm an avid tea drinker, but that doesn't mean I've taken the time to do it right. Before now, I turned my kettle on, waited for it to come to a full boil, and then poured water into my mug. It didn't matter whether I was drinking black tea, green tea, or herbal tea — I steeped them all at over 200 degrees. If you're cringing at this, I get it. It's no wonder I never liked green tea before. Waterdrop's dispenser has a control panel on the front that lets me set the temperature I need. I can't set exact temperatures and must instead settle for increments of around 20 degrees, but that's a huge step up from what I had before. The Waterdrop M6CG also wants to know how much water to dispense. With an 8oz mug, this is awesome. We can place a mug under the dispenser, tap a few buttons, and walk away to set a timer. When we return, the tea has already steeped in the time that it would take an electric kettle to come to a boil. This process may not be automated, but you can add it to the list of ways a smarter home can help you get up in the morning. An under-sink model greatly helps with washing dishes If you're a homeowner, I can't recommend this upgrade highly enough While I like the M6CH enough that I wouldn't go back to an electric kettle, it is far from a perfect product. This particular model is huge — too tall to fit under most of my kitchen cabinets. It's also very heavy, being about as unwieldy to move as a Ninja Slushi XL. This is particularly frustrating if you have to move it in order to lift the water tank in the back, which you'll need to do every other day as you dump out the old water and add in the new. This dispenser is also limited to dispensing 4oz, 8oz, 16oz, or 20oz of water, but not the 12oz that many of my family's mugs hold. Thankfully, I was also sent the Waterdrop K6 under-sink model, which places an instant hot water dispenser next to your kitchen faucet. I was able to install it myself with a couple of hours of work. The resulting dispenser doesn't take up space on my counter and never has to be manually refilled or emptied. While it can't automatically stop dispensing the way the countertop model can, it dispenses water much faster, so there is hardly any need. While I still use this model for tea, it's just as useful for washing dishes. It can't fill an entire sink with water, but the K6 can instantly pour hot water directly into a bowl or pan. I've found this to make easy work of even the most soiled of dishes, and this upgrade has drastically reduced how much scrubbing is required. As a parent who spends hours of my day at the kitchen sink, I love this upgrade dearly. It's not the only smart home upgrade I've made in my kitchen, but it's easily my favorite. Don't limit your smart home imagination to IoT devices Neither of these hot water dispensers is internet-connected, and there is no Matter logo on the side of the box. Yet being able to get hot water instantly, and at a precise temperature, is exactly the sort of awesomeness I envision a smart home being able to deliver. While homeowners have the most flexibility to install the best models, with countertop options available, renters don't have to miss out. That's good, because purified drinking water is the perfect upgrade to pair with that water tracker you 3D printed.

item.title: 4 UniFi mistakes that turn a simple setup into an overcomplicated nightmare
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.14
So, you're wanting to get started with Ubiquiti's UniFi networking gear, huh? I love my UniFi setup, but I definitely made some mistakes. Here are the four biggest mistakes I see people make all the time in the UniFi community, and how you can avoid them. Forgetting to budget for PoE You'll pay for PoE one way or another I love my UniFi setup, but it relies heavily on PoE. At my church, we also run UniFi, and all of the access points there also rely on PoE for power. The problem is, PoE switches are more expensive than non-PoE switches. So, often, a beginner might opt for the cheaper, non-PoE switches to save some cash. However, once you start plugging things in, you'll realize real quick that almost every UniFi accessory needs some form of PoE to run. Access points, doorbells, cameras, and more all require power over ethernet to function. If you don't buy a PoE-capable switch, then you can buy a PoE injector for each area you need power over Ethernet. While this does work, it can quickly add up to be far more expensive than just getting that PoE switch from the start. I personally went used for my PoE switch, and found a 48-port 500W PoE UniFi switch second-hand for $250 shipped and it is more than what I need for my setup, but it gets the job done. Cranking up Wi-Fi power to fix every dead zone More power does not always mean better coverage More power equals better coverage, right? Well, in a sense, yes, but practically, no. You see, with a mesh network like UniFi, more power means that your phone will stay connected to a specific node for longer—often too long. The way mesh networks work is your phone holds onto a node until it reaches a specific connection strength to a node, and then it releases and grabs the next most powerful node that it can. When you crank the power on all your nodes up to high, your phone will stay connected to a node for too long. Just because you have a radio connection to a node doesn't mean you have usable Wi-Fi. So, if your phone reports that it has a high signal strength to a node, it'll stay connected to it, even if you can't actually use the internet. The ideal setup is where your phone releases from a node at right around the furthest distance you can be from it while still using the internet, and then having another node to pick up the slack as soon as you release from the first node. This can take some trial and error. Some nodes might need to be on high power, while others are on low, and others could be somewhere in-between. So, don't default to high power thinking you'll get the best coverage from that—it might actually do the opposite of what you're thinking it will. Copying someone else’s UniFi settings without understanding them Just because it works for someone else's setup doesn't mean it'll work for yours The great part about buying UniFi is there's a robust community surrounding the company's products. However, that isn't always a great thing. Often, people will ask for help with some specific problem, and people will chime in with what fixed it for them. That's great, but those tips shouldn't be taken as the answer. What works for other people should be used as a starting point for finding out what your specific setup needs. This is especially true if you're just getting your information from a YouTube video. Don't get me wrong, I love YouTube tutorials—I make them myself for the maker space. However, tips from a YouTube video should, again, be seen as tips and not instructions on how to fix your exact problem in most instances. So, before you start applying changes from a YouTube video or Facebook group, do some research to understand what those changes are actually changing. Knowing what a setting does will help you better understand how it applies to your own setup, and how to modify it for your needs if it doesn't work first try. Buying for your dream homelab instead of your actual needs Overbuying equipment often leads to an overcomplicated setup I'll admit, I have definitely fallen prey to watching YouTube and building a UniFi cart of all the equipment that I would love to have in my homelab. Then, I quietly empty the cart and walk away, realizing that spending $10,000 on networking equipment isn't the best financial decision. The thing is, finances aren't the only reason it's not best to buy and build your dream homelab before just covering what your needs are. Overbuying equipment often leads to an overcomplicated setup. For instance, your homelab might only need two Wi-Fi nodes and an 8-port switch. However, that 48-port switch looks nice. And the aggregation switch would be good too, right? Don't forget the NVR and NAS, even though you only have one camera and use Dropbox for everything. It all sounds great at first, and sometimes overbuying a little can be helpful, like buying a 16- or 24-port switch instead of 8 so you have room to grow. However, more equipment just adds more maintenance. For instance, at home, I have my Dream Router 7, a 5-port 2.5G switch, my 48-port PoE switch, two Wi-Fi nodes, and one camera. That's it. At my church where I'm about to do a full buildout, I'll have around 8 switches, a Dream Machine Pro Max, an NVR, a NAS, and dozens of both Wi-Fi access points and cameras. Having a big complicated setup makes sense for a 20,000-square-foot church and school, where it doesn't make sense in my 1,300-square-foot home. UniFi is prosumer for a reason The great thing about UniFi is that the equipment is designed for both professional and consumer use cases—hence the term prosumer. There are so many great pieces of UniFi gear to buy, but not everything belongs in a home environment. So, before you spend that big money on that huge cart you've built, step back and think about what your needs actually are. Then, once you've got the equipment you need, make sure to apply the tips I've laid out above for the smoothest experience possible.

item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.50
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Honor's Magic 9 Pro Max debuts at Venice Film Festival: ARRI partnership will continue
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.12
What you need to know - Honor was featured at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, and it brought the Robot Phone with it to highlight its cinematic capabilities with ARRI. - What truly captivated users was another appearance: the Magic 9 Pro Max in moss green, which consumers saw for the first time. - Honor announced that it will continue its huge ARRI partnership with the Magic 9 Pro Max, bringing many features you'd find on the Robot Phone. - The Magic 9 Pro Max will debut in China on September 28. Honor paraded at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival with its cinematic devices. However, the Robot Phone's presence at the festival wasn't the only big thing Honor had in store. Earlier this morning (Sept 9), Honor revealed that it brought the Robot Phone's cinematic videography capabilities to the 83rd Venice International Film Festival. The company recognizes the attention the phone has received for its "innovative mechanical gimbal design and professional-grade cinematic imaging capabilities." The Robot Phone was crafted in collaboration with ARRI for professional camera-grade features. While this has captivated consumers, Honor says it plans to extend its partnership with ARRI for its next flagships. At the festival, Honor revealed its upcoming Magic 9 Pro Max in moss green—the first time consumers have witnessed it. Another exciting tidbit is that the phone features ARRI's logo on the back by its cameras. Honor states the device even features "the lens layout follows the design language of one of the most iconic ARRI cinema cameras." Creators will find ARRI's LogC3 to help preserve highlights and shadows for post-production. Additionally, ARRI Wide Gamut 3 delivers a broader, more distinct color space, with ARRI Looks handling controlled cinematic color styles. The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max will debut on September 28 in China. Honor and ARRI continue I'm a big fan of photography and, more recently, recording better videos. Bringing that sort of "professional-grade" software and tech into a phone is huge. To have the ability right in your pocket makes it easier for people who care about that kind of thing. For creators, I'm sure it's a major win. They can streamline their devices and purchases a little more—if they prefer, of course. I still love photography on a traditional, more powerful camera, but a phone is up there. Cinematic styles and vibes played a key role in Honor's Robot Phone debut in August. The phone features an automatic gimbal that is just as curious as a little robot. Honor states it combined its technology with ARRI Image Science and professional cinema workflows. The Robot Phone is equipped with two 200MP lenses. The gimbal hosts one of these 200MP cameras with an f/1.6 aperture on a 1/1.28-inch sensor. The periscope telephoto lens arrives at 200MP with 2.7x optical zoom. Several features such as ARRI LogC3, ARRI Wide Gamut 3, and ARRI Looks with its in-house H1 Image Chip help solidify Honor's "cinematography" position with the Robot Phone. AI is woven in to help reduce strenuous noises and to optimize your video's high dynamic range. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max launch is a few weeks away. It'll be interesting to see if Honor takes any of these features up a notch for the traditional slab phone form factor. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.08
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: You can now test Nothing’s upcoming devices before launch
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.93
What you need to know - Nothing’s Community Review Program is back, giving selected fans early access to upcoming products before public launches. - Participants must sign an NDA, respect embargoes, share first impressions, and publish detailed reviews and additional content. - Applications close September 10, but spots aren’t guaranteed, and the program isn’t available to fans in India. Nothing is giving its community another chance to test its upcoming products before anyone else. The company has reopened its Community Review Program, allowing select fans to get hands-on time with Nothing hardware and software before public launches. The program offers select members early access to Nothing products, a direct line to the company, and an opportunity to help shape what it builds next, per the company's announcement. Nothing is particularly interested in applicants with experience in 3D animation, graphic design, music and sound production, and product reviews, but no skills are needed to apply. If you love technology, it's enough. There are some strings attached, though. Because participants may handle unreleased products, they'll need to sign an NDA, follow Nothing's embargo dates, and maintain strict information security. They are also required to give their first impressions of the Nothing Community and social media, publish a full review after launch, and create additional content such as unboxings or product use cases. It’s important to note that being chosen once does not place you on a permanent VIP list. Nothing's previous program terms made clear that participation for one product doesn't guarantee selection for future reviews, so every round is effectively another chance to get in. Review devices are issued under the terms of the current program, so applicants should verify the latest conditions before applying. Nothing will also cover the associated shipping costs. Applications are open until September 10, though selection isn't guaranteed. The program is also unavailable to fans in India. Judging by past instances of this initiative, the brand does indeed implement user feedback. Earlier in 2024, Nothing had a public campaign called “The Community Edition Project” for the Nothing Phone 2a. Over several months, the company asked its community to submit designs for the phone's hardware, wallpapers, packaging, and marketing. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The winning hardware design had phosphorescent (glow-in-the-dark) elements on the back of the phone.
