item.title: Healthcare AI’s next test is integration
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 4.43
Sponsored Provided byEnsemble The entrance of major AI companies into healthcare is a meaningful and welcome development, accelerating the technical foundation available to the industry. Their models are increasingly capable of processing long clinical records, interpreting complex terminology, comparing documentation against evidence and generating coherent summaries from large volumes of information. For clinicians, operators, and administrative teams who spend significant time searching through fragmented data, these advances are helping reduce cognitive burden and make high-value information easier to access. But healthcare leaders should not confuse model capability with operational capability. Healthcare’s administrative challenges are caused by fragmented information, fragmented workflows, and fragmented accountability, not a lack of information. The industry has spent decades investing in systems that capture activity: electronic health records, billing platforms, payer portals, scheduling systems, call center platforms, and analytics applications. Each system records something important. But few were designed to reason across the full chain of decisions that determines whether patients get timely access, clinicians have the right documentation and providers are reimbursed appropriately. This is the problem that AI must now confront. Revenue cycle is becoming one of healthcare AI’s proving grounds The revenue cycle is the process healthcare providers use to get paid for care — from scheduling and registration through coding, billing, payer follow-up, and payment collection. It is unusually suited to rigorous AI deployment because it combines high transaction volume, complex reasoning, structured and unstructured data, measurable outcomes, and significant operational variation. It also sits at the intersection of financial performance, patient access, and administrative workload. A single claim can be influenced by patient insurance information, clinical documentation, coding rules, payer-specific policies, prior authorization requirements, medical necessity criteria, and many other data sources and operational processes. A breakdown in any one of those areas can create downstream consequences weeks or months later. This is why generic automation has often fallen short. Traditional robotic process automation works well when workflows are stable and rules are predictable, but healthcare administration is neither. Payer requirements change. Documentation expectations evolve. Exceptions are common and often material. Large language models improve part of the equation, extracting meaning from narrative text, summarizing records and supporting reasoning over complex documentation. But when used alone, they inherit important limitations. They may produce plausible outputs without sufficient traceability. They may lack awareness of local workflow constraints. They may miss payer-specific history or context that determines whether an action is likely to change an outcome. Why foundation models will become necessary but insufficient The major AI firms are solving real technical problems for healthcare. Better context windows make it easier to process longitudinal records. Stronger reasoning improves the interpretation of complex clinical scenarios. Better multimodal capabilities may eventually help connect text, imaging, structured data, and clinical signals in more useful ways. Safer model behavior and healthcare-specific tuning will continue to improve adoption. These capabilities will make healthcare work faster, more consistent and easier to navigate. But they will not, on their own, solve deep-rooted administrative complexity. Much of healthcare’s operational knowledge does not live in general medical literature, coding manuals, or public payer guidance. It lives in the accumulated experience of what actually happens after decisions are made. For example: - Why does one appeal strategy outperform another? - Which documentation gaps are most likely to cause reimbursement delay? - How does a specific payer respond to a particular clinical argument? These insights are behavioral, operational, and longitudinal. They emerge from years of transactions, outcomes, exceptions, and human judgment. As foundation models become more capable, access to baseline healthcare knowledge will become less differentiating. Most leading systems will be able to interpret ICD-10 codes, recognize medical terminology, summarize payer policies, and reason over public clinical criteria. The durable advantage will come from how organizations combine that model intelligence with proprietary operational data, structured knowledge, workflow context, and governance. The technical shift: From automation to orchestration Agentic orchestration turns foundation model understanding into coordinated action — intelligence that can follow work across systems, apply the right rules, adapt when something changes, and keep learning from what happens next. A prior authorization workflow, for example, may require retrieving clinical documentation through fast healthcare interoperability resources (FHIR) APIs, mapping patient history to payer criteria, identifying missing evidence, generating a submission packet, routing exceptions to a specialist, monitoring payer response, adjusting patient care pathways, and learning from the outcome. This type of workflow requires coordination. It also requires guardrails: regulatory requirements, privacy standards, clinical policies, coding rules, payer criteria, and organizational risk thresholds. One promising approach is hybrid architecture that combines LLMs with structured knowledge bases, symbolic logic, reinforcement learning, and deterministic validation layers. At Ensemble, this is the design principle behind EIQ, our revenue cycle intelligence engine. EIQ brings together operational activity, clinical documentation, payer behavior, and reimbursement outcomes into a continuously learning intelligence layer that’s integrated with the hospital’s electronic health record (EHR). It supplements the system of record with a system of intelligence, designed to connect information and surface actions most likely to improve outcomes. EIQ uses a neuro-symbolic approach that combines LLMs and custom small language models with rules-based reasoning. That architecture is built on one of the most robust datasets in healthcare, informed by more than a decade of award-winning operational performance, transaction history, payer behavior, and operator decision-making. The language models help interpret information and generate human-readable outputs. The symbolic layer represents policies, rules, payer requirements, and workflow constraints so the system can apply guardrails, make reasoning steps more traceable and recommend actions that fit the specific operational context. What the next decade will reward The contribution of major AI firms to healthcare will be significant. Their models will become faster, safer, more capable, and more accessible. But the next decade of healthcare AI will be defined by integration, not model capability alone. The organizations that create the most value will be those that connect models to governed data, operational workflows, domain expertise, human oversight, and measurable outcomes. They will understand that healthcare intelligence cannot live in a separate interface. It has to exist inside the decisions that shape access, documentation reimbursement, and patient experience. item.title: This road map could help us decide whether to deploy solar geoengineering
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.24
A San Francisco nonprofit has published a detailed road map of the experiments, studies, and infrastructure that it says would be needed to make informed decisions about the use of solar geoengineering, MIT Technology Review can reveal. Scientists have now spent half a century exploring the possibility that we could counteract climate change by releasing reflective particles into the stratosphere, mimicking the cooling effects of volcanic eruptions. But even after at least hundreds of studies on the concept, known as stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), big gaps remain in the scientific understanding of how well it would work and what else it might do—and there has been no systematic plan for clearing up that uncertainty. Reflective, a research organization that funds studies on solar geoengineering, has today attempted to fill that gap with the release of its SAI Research Roadmap. “Our mission is to equip the world with the data and tools required for informed decision-making about sunlight reflection fast enough to matter,” says Dakota Gruener, the organization’s cofounder and chief executive. “Our sense is the world may need to make very consequential decisions on timelines far shorter than our research system is prepared for.” The hope is the exercise will guide scientific efforts and encourage philanthropies or government agencies to fund high-priority work and “responsibly accelerate research,” says Gruener. If all the work is done in a coordinated way, it would take about a decade and cost around $370 million—and if it’s not, it would require roughly 20 years and nearly $1.4 billion, the report estimates. While Gruener stresses that Reflective doesn’t advocate using this form of solar geoengineering, the report does make the case for conducting outdoor experiments, which would release successively larger amounts of sulfur dioxide (or materials that would convert into it) in the stratosphere to observe what happens. That is a controversial standpoint. Since 2002, hundreds of academics have signed an open letter calling for a ban on outdoor experiments and an "international non-use agreement," arguing that such a powerful technology could never be governed in a globally equitable way. And some signatories argue that more studies can never address one of the biggest questions about using solar geoengineering: Who gets to do it. “The first-order questions, from my perspective, are not technical,” Aarti Gupta, co-initiator of the non-use initiative and professor of global environmental governance at Wageningen University in the Netherlands, told me in a recent on-stage interview. “The core question is: Who would control a planet-altering technology like stratospheric aerosol injection? Who would develop it, and who would deploy it, and to what end? To serve what purposes, and whose purposes? Those questions are very fundamental, because this planet-altering technology will have winners and losers.” ‘Fast enough to matter’ Since Gruener incorporated Reflective in late 2023, the nonprofit has quickly become an important player in solar geoengineering research. It has now raised more than $20 million from a number of prominent charities and individuals, and it’s provided around $4 million to several dozen research groups. Reflective has also undertaken a handful of its own projects to promote research, including the development of an open-source solar geoengineering simulator and an online hub for collaborative research. Earlier this year, Reflective released its SAI Uncertainties database, which identified a long list of scientific unknowns and engineering obstacles that would need to be addressed before even a small-scale solar geoengineering effort could move ahead. (I wrote about the specific scenario and the unknowns in this earlier piece.) Some of the biggest uncertainties involve what gas or particles would make the most sense to use and what would happen once they were released in the dry stratosphere. It’s not clear, for example, whether they’d spread out in a way that maximizes the reflectivity—or clump together and quickly fall out into the troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere. The road map builds upon the database, highlighting the path to addressing most of those questions. The road map The initial phase in Reflective’s road map, labeled “foundational knowledge,” includes additional computer simulation studies and lab experiments designed to shed light on the potential impacts on different regions, ecosystems, and phenomena, including ocean circulation patterns, ice sheets, and crop yields. The report also notes the need to begin developing more observational tools during this phase to improve understanding of the baseline conditions of the stratosphere—and, in turn, our ability to assess any effects from the eventual release of materials. This first stage would last two to three years and cost $30 million to $75 million, though some of the analysis and observational work would continue into subsequent phases. The next stage would include using modified aircraft to release 10 metric tons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, four times over the course of two seasons. The full research stage could take four to eight years and cost $70 million to $150 million, the report says. The work during it may reduce uncertainty about the “cooling efficacy” of solar geoengineering, or how much the planet would cool per ton of sulfur released, by about 25%. The experiments during the next phase would step those levels up dramatically, releasing 25,000 tons of sulfur dioxide over the course of one season, at least once but possibly twice. That research stage, which includes other work as well, would last four to 11 years, run $270 million to $1.1 billion, and decrease efficacy uncertainty by around 66%, according to the road map. The final phase of research would be ongoing monitoring of full-scale solar geoengineering, if the world goes ahead with it. The goal would be to gather real-life data on the technology in action, update estimates of the effects in models, and spot any “unexpected or undesired consequences.” Gruener says that the road map is intended as a Version 1, meant to be “concrete enough for people to argue with.” But Reflective intends to update the plan as it receives additional reactions from researchers and other observers, and it will invite such feedback through a mechanism on the site. She also notes that there are firm “stage gates,” set up between the latter stages—in other words, research shouldn’t proceed to the next phase if the experiments suggest that the releases don’t have the hoped-for impact, show worrisome downsides, or fail to resolve crucial uncertainties. “Our road map has these gates precisely because there may be points where the answer is ‘You should stop,’” she says. Termination shock Most observers I spoke to about the report agree that these studies could reduce uncertainty about the effectiveness of solar geoengineering and our technical ability to carry it out. But highlighting the scientific importance of outdoor experiments won’t necessarily make them any easier to move ahead with. Several earlier proposals to carry out such experiments, including Harvard’s SCoPEx and the UK-based SPICE project, were ultimately halted amid opposition from environmentalists or policymakers. In addition, not everyone agrees that experiments at those scales will get us to the point where we’re capable of making an “informed decision.” Wil Burns, a research professor and legal scholar at American University and a signatory to the International Non-Use Agreement, fears that scientists won’t be able to understand the extent of the potential downsides, including impacts on the protective ozone layer and changes to regional precipitation patterns, until we’re carrying out full-fledged solar geoengineering. “The research would give you some answers,” he says. “I just don’t think it gives you answers that are that relevant. To get to those relevant answers, you have to deploy at scale—and I just don’t think that’s ever tenable.” That’s because, in his view, using the technology would violate principles of intergenerational equity: If the world continues emitting greenhouse gases, increased levels of solar geoengineering would merely mask the continued warming of the planet. Burns says that means future generations—people who had no say in its use—couldn’t turn it off without triggering a sudden surge of warming, known as termination shock. “What that would do, in my mind, is put a sword of Damocles over future generations,” he says. “So even if you could, quote-unquote, ‘prove it works,’ I don’t think from an intergenerational perspective it would ever be tenable.” (Some researchers, however, have argued that the risks of termination shock are less likely than often assumed—and that solar geoengineering could be slowly dialed down over time.) ‘The right approach’ Ilan Gur, the former CEO of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), the UK research department that funded 21 geoengineering research projects last year, applauds Reflective’s road map. “Whether you’re a scientist or a policymaker or just a concerned citizen, our goal should be as quickly and efficiently as possible to answer the biggest questions scientifically that would tell us [whether] this is an approach that might work or that would never work,” he says. “We should all want to spend the effort and money to buy down that uncertainty, so my view is 100% the approach that Reflective is taking is the right one.” Sebastian Eastham, an associate professor in sustainable aviation at Imperial College London who is leading an ARIA-funded research project exploring another approach to engineered cooling, agrees that the outdoor experiments described in the Reflective road map can’t resolve all the unknowns. But he says the map helps begin a conversation about how to make decisions concerning the use of a tool with potential benefits and risks, in the face of escalating climate dangers. “Every hard decision that has ever been taken has been in the context of unresolved uncertainty,” he says. “That’s just the nature of things.” Eastham adds that it’s become essential to move beyond computer simulations to address some of the key questions, arguing that appropriately designed and executed outdoor experiments can teach us so much more than millions of hours of computational processing time “that it almost becomes irresponsible to say, ‘Well, there cannot be ever any experiment.’” The risk is “that we spin our wheels running the same computational simulations over and over and over again,” he says. That could prevent researchers from learning essential things about the effectiveness or the dangers of stratospheric aerosol injection. Weighing the risks Gruener says the risks that solar geoengineering could exacerbate inequality need to be considered, but notes that unchecked warming also threatens to disproportionately harm developing regions. She also acknowledges that outdoor experiments won’t fully address the scientific unknowns but stresses that they can answer a lot—and carry little environmental risk. She notes that 10 tons of sulfur dioxide is less than 2% of the amount that the global aviation industry releases into the atmosphere each day. “Some people will be uncomfortable with any discussion of any outdoor experiment, but if we want decisions made on good science … then these are questions that an experiment will be necessary to address,” Gruener says. She fears that the rising dangers of climate change will put growing pressure on nations and other actors to move forward with solar geoengineering, even if no one has done the necessary research to reduce scientific uncertainty and sort out the technical challenges. “We don’t think the alternative is decisions not happening at all,” she says. “We think the alternative is decisions being made in a panic or on lack of evidence.” Deep Dive Climate change and energy Why heat pumps are still so hot in the US A key tax credit in the US ended, but heat pump sales are still going strong. Batteries just broke another record in the US Huge grid-scale batteries are thriving, but smaller residential systems have lagged. item.title: Powering AI is an architecture problem
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 2.12
Sponsored Provided byON.energy On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world's largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of load off the grid in seconds. And it wasn't the first time. Two years earlier, a single failed surge arrester dropped roughly 60 Virginia facilities and 1,500 megawatts at once. No one could anticipate so much uniform load responding to grid faults the same way, at the same time. The AI power debate is mostly about generation: more turbines, more solar, more transmission. The grid needs more electrons. But the outages in Virginia weren't supply failures; they were architecture failures. And a giant wave of interconnections is arriving on that same architecture, putting grid reliability at risk. It's a problem nobody wants to own. Asking more from the grid The grid was built around predictable loads: steel mills, refineries, and houses at dinnertime. Different load sizes, same process—drawing power smoothly, misbehaving occasionally, and recovering gracefully. But AI data centers don't behave that way. An AI campus can swing 70% of its load in milliseconds during a training run, then trip offline just as fast at the first sign of trouble upstream to protect billions in compute. Each is rational alone. Together, at gigawatt scale, they're a problem the grid has never solved—and the next wave of data center campuses is planned at exactly that scale. Where the old stack breaks The standard data center power stack hasn't changed in decades. Medium-voltage power arrives, transformers step it down, low-voltage uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units condition it, and it reaches the racks. Push that design to AI scale, and it cracks in three places. First, the UPS sits deep inside the building, close to the racks. But its batteries are an undersized spare tire, designed to handle an outage for a few minutes, not to absorb load swings this fast and volatile around the clock. Second, the UPS spends most of its life in bypass. Legacy converters waste enough power that operators run in eco-mode: A static switch feeds the racks directly from the grid and nothing filters in either direction. The compute's swings go out raw, and grid transients—sub-millisecond events that can damage or take down equipment—come in too fast for any switch to catch. Third, the protection logic was written when "large load" meant 50 megawatts. This protection logic can't see the grid it is now a part of, so when trouble hits upstream, it does exactly the wrong thing: it drops out. In the 2024 Virginia event, most of the lost load traced to protection schemes that count voltage dips and disconnect on the third one—as designed, at the worst moment. This isn't sloppy engineering. It's careful engineering the load has outgrown. Moving into the path The fix is three moves, made together. Move it up—from 480 volts to medium voltage (13.8 kilovolts and higher), the voltage large sites draw from the grid. Move it out—from the data hall to modular enclosures near the substation so the building holds only compute and the cooling that keeps it alive. Move it into the path—instead of a battery that watches and reacts, a system every electron runs through, all the time. There's nothing to detect and nothing to switch because nothing was ever routed around it. On paper, three straightforward upgrades. In practice, they rewrite every line item downstream. Making the change When thousands of GPUs spin up together, the system absorbs the swing and hands the grid a flat load profile. When a disturbance hits, the equipment behind it never notices. A difficult neighbor becomes a predictable one. And when the utility needs help, it becomes a useful one. Interconnection changes, too. The utility certifies one medium-voltage box instead of untangling every transformer, UPS, chiller, pump, and switchgear lineup behind it. Engineers swap chip generations without a fresh interconnection study. Months come off the permitting timeline. Inside the fence, UPS rooms become compute or cooling space. Density per construction dollar climbs. And the economics flip. Equipment that runs at medium voltage, sits outside, and stores its own energy can qualify for tax credits, and earn revenue in grid programs like peak shaving and demand response. Backup power stops being insurance and starts paying for itself. The architecture test In early 2026, we tested a full-scale system at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a U.S. Department of Energy facility and the only place in the Western Hemisphere that can replicate real grid faults and AI-scale load swings concurrently in the same loop. We hit it from both directions: real AI load profiles hit the compute side at full medium voltage. Grid faults hit the utility side, including a full zero-voltage event. The compute side didn't flinch. Neither did the grid side. It cleared the large-load voltage ride-through requirements from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the grid operator, with room to spare. Those rules exist because operators no longer take facilities this size on faith, and more are coming. Most of the industry treats them as hurdles. A medium-voltage, inline system clears them out of the box. Compliance isn't an added feature. It's what the architecture does. The new layer Much of what looks like a grid problem in the AI buildout sits inside the fence, in equipment sized for a load that no longer exists. Move the right pieces up, out, and into the path, and a grid liability becomes a grid asset. Density goes up. Permitting time comes down. Backup power earns its keep. The engineering works—and the next wave of AI factories is being built on it. The industry hasn't named this layer yet. We call it the medium-voltage AI UPS. The name matters less than the choice: those factories can arrive as a strain on the grid or as strength for it. We already know how to build the second kind. This content was produced by ON.energy. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: FCC Cuts Swedish Smart Mower Maker a Break With First Exemption to Robot Ban
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.25
It’s been just over a month since the US banned foreign-made advanced robots, which include robot vacuums and certain pool-cleaning bots. But this week, the FCC announced the first exemption to the rule, clearing several robot lawn mowers from a Swedish company. The "conditional approval" applies to robot mowers from Husqvarna: the 305v IQ, 310v IQ, 420v IQ, and 440v IQ series. The US Defense Department issued the company after determining that its robots “do not pose risks to US national security” amid concerns foreign bots could pose a spying or sabotage threat. What’s interesting is that the exemption seems to be indefinite, starting on September 9, 2026, with no apparent end date. That’s a major difference from the other conditional approvals the FCC has issued to drone and Wi-Fi router manufacturers, including Asus, which received an exemption in the same order. According to the FCC’s guidelines, exemptions for foreign-made drones can last up to 12 months. For Wi-Fi routers, the period is up to 18 months. But for advanced robots, the FCC guidelines omit any mention of a limit to a conditional approval. That said, the guidelines note: “Applicants must submit Conditional Approval applications by January 1, 2028,” indicating that the window to apply will eventually close unless the White House makes changes. The FCC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the indefinite nature of Husqvarna’s exemption. But it might be a sign that other, more mundane robotics, such as robot vacuums and swimming pool cleaners, could receive the same treatment. That said, the US has ongoing concerns about China’s influence over trade and the electronic supply chain. Another aim of the Trump administration has been to bolster US manufacturing. In the meantime, Husqvarna is touting that it's the first robotics vendor to receive the FCC’s conditional approval. "The Conditional Approval means that these specific platforms, which are expected to be launched in the US in 2027, as well as the already approved models currently available on the market, are exempt,” it said. To receive an exemption, companies need to supply a detailed list of answers, including potential plans to build robot manufacturing in the US and the “country of origin for all components in the robot,” along with the country of origin of the device’s software and firmware. Husqvarna says the conditional approval validates that it’s “setting the standard for trusted robotic mowing, and reflects our rigorous standards for quality, security, and how we manage customer data following strict EU consumer privacy rules.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Company Linked to Theft of 153M Driver's Licenses Confirms Possible Breach
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.04
IDScan.net admits it may have suffered a breach, after a hacker appeared to steal over 153 million driver’s licenses from the vendor’s ID verification system. Louisiana-based IDScan hasn’t responded to requests for comment about the situation. But cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who first reported that a mysterious site on the dark web was selling access to millions of US and Canadian driver’s licenses, also discovered that the company quietly posted a “Notification of Data Security Incident” on its website. The notice, dated Sept. 4, says IDScan is investigating a possible breach. “While the investigation is ongoing, IDScan.net has determined that an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud,” it says. “The types of information contained within the affected data may include full names and driver’s license or other government-issued identification numbers.” IDScan offers identity card and passport verification services to clients, including the rental car company Hertz, delivery provider FedEx, and video game retailer GameStop. The alleged breach suggests the company was storing IDs from numerous consumers, who were likely unaware. If confirmed, the breach could be one of the worst in recent history, exposing millions of people to identity theft. For now, IDScan says it’s providing affected users with free credit monitoring and identity protection services and is urging them to be vigilant against phishing and fraud. Interestingly, IDScan’s breach notification page doesn’t appear in major search results because the company added code to the site to prevent web crawlers from indexing it. In the meantime, some consumers are already suing IDScan. Court records appear to show that over a dozen class-action lawsuits have been filed in the US against the company, up from four a week ago. The FBI also told PCMag it’s been investigating the potential breach. The dark web site that was selling the 153 million driver’s licenses appears to have been removed, but the hackers could easily spin up a new site or sell the information to other cybercriminals through private channels. item.title: Are You Using the Wrong Phone for Your Carrier? 2 Million Speed Tests Reveal the Truth
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.92
We recently published our definitive list of the Best Mobile Networks in the US for 2026, a deep-dive, data-driven report based on more than 2 million speed tests. You can read the full story here, but we can reveal that among the country’s three major carriers, T-Mobile comes out on top not only nationwide but also in many of the states and major cities tested. We also delve into mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs), where Mint Mobile, owned by T-Mobile, triumphs. But choosing the right service provider is only half the battle. You also need to figure out which phone to use. Our Best Mobile Networks dataset doesn't just cover the carriers—it also tracks the actual phones used in all those speed tests. This companion piece breaks down which phone models perform best on each network. (In case you didn't know: Not every phone performs the same way on every network.) So how do we do this? To start, we narrow the field to 5G-capable phones that have been tested at least 1,000 times in data from our partner sites, CoverageMaps.com and BestPhonePlans. The phones must also have been available for purchase from the manufacturer as of mid-August 2026. (That excludes new phones recently announced by Google and Apple.) Using those test scores, we generate a Speed Index on a 1-10 scale. We also consult PCMag’s published reviews for each phone, which we convert to a Rating Index of 1-10, as well as customer satisfaction ratings for the phone makers from our Readers’ Choice survey earlier this year. We use all those numbers to arrive at a cumulative Mobile Phone Index to determine which manufacturers and specific devices rank highest, both overall and for each mobile network. (Our full methodology is at the bottom of this story.) The Best Phone Brand Across All Carriers You've picked your carrier. The hunt for the best phone on that network starts with the platform (iOS or Android?) and the brand. Apple has the top Speed Index and Review Index and comes in a close second to Google for Satisfaction. All of which means that Apple handily comes out on top as the Best Phone Brand across the three major US carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon). (Note: Click the arrows in our interactive charts to view various elements of our survey results.) When we narrow things down by mobile carrier, Apple is still the top choice. Its Mobile Phone Index rating—the final score that determines a winner here—ranges from 7.88 on AT&T to a stellar 9.01 on T-Mobile. Knowing that not everyone embraces the Apple ecosystem, we've also calculated the top Android phone brands. Samsung is the winner here across all the networks. Its Galaxy brand phones also take the prize for Android on both T-Mobile and Verizon. On AT&T, Google's Pixel line wins. The Best Phone for AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon When the focus is narrowed to specific phones, Apple loses its advantage. The top phone across all carriers is the Samsung Galaxy S25+. Best Phone Across All Carriers The fastest by far, the Galaxy S25+ is the only phone to earn a Speed Index higher than 9.0. Our reviewer awarded that phone a 4-star "excellent" rating, just slightly behind the 4.5-star rating ("outstanding") earned by other phones on the list, such as the Google Pixel 9a and the iPhone 17. The S25+ is also the top phone for T-Mobile users, even ahead of the newer S26 Ultra. However, for AT&T, the top phone by index score (8.60) is the Samsung Galaxy A36 5G, the company’s midrange phone. (Note: We did not take phone price into consideration for this story.) The A36 5G on AT&T’s Mobile Phone Index is boosted by its superior Speed Index as well. For Verizon, the winner is Google’s 2025 foldable, the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, which has a carrier-high Speed Index of 9.44, putting it more than a point ahead of the Galaxy Z Fold 7. Google also benefits here as the brand with the highest customer satisfaction rating in our survey results from earlier this year. The Top Phones on Each Carrier, Ranked Whichever mobile network you use, we can tell you which phone, by brand, performs best on it. (This also works for MVNO users; just pick the network that owns or partners with your MVNO of choice.) Beginning with AT&T, the top-performing phones for each major brand are: the Apple iPhone Air, the Google Pixel 9 Pro, the Motorola Edge 2025, and the Samsung Galaxy A36 5G. On T-Mobile, the top phones by the numbers are the iPhone 17 Pro Max, the Pixel 9a, the Edge 2025, and the Galaxy S25+. On Verizon, the top performers are the iPhone 16, the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Edge 2025, and the Galaxy Z Fold 7. T-Mobile boasts the most phones with a Mobile Phone Index over 9.0. (Those are the Galaxy S25+ and S26 Ultra; the iPhone 17 Pro Max, 17 Pro, and 17; and the Google Pixel 9a.) Only one other carrier, Verizon, has a phone with a Mobile Phone Index above 9.0, and that's for the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold. Our Methodology: How We Determine the Best Phones for Every Wireless Carrier We begin the same way we do with our Best Mobile Networks reporting, with speed, this time based on tests tied to specific phones. Our speed test data comes from BestPhonePlans and sister site CoverageMap.com. We limit the results to 5G phones that the manufacturers themselves have available for sale as of mid-August 2026. To be included, each phone in our results had to receive a minimum of 1,000 tests. Our data covers 2,185,418 tests made between Jan. 1 and June 30, 2026. We convert the average download and upload speeds (both in Mbps; higher is better) and latency measures (in milliseconds; lower is better) into a number on a 1-10 scale. To ensure speeds are consistent, we set a floor and ceiling for each rating: - Download speed: 30 (worst) to 350 (best) - Upload speed: 3 (worst) to 25 (best) - Latency: 100 (worst) to 15 (best) Our formula combines download speed (70%), upload speed (20%), and latency (10%) to generate the PCMag Mobile Phone Speed Index. Then we analyze the editors' rating for each phone based on its PCMag review. (We've lab-tested and rated all of the phones included.) Our review ratings are based on a 1- to 5-star scale. To get the Review Rating Index to a 1-10 scale, we set a floor of 5 and a ceiling of 10. Most of the products covered here score above 8.5 on the index. The Satisfaction Index is based on the scores from our Readers’ Choice 2026 Phones and Carriers survey; we use the existing ratings, which are on a 1-10 scale. (Google rates highest, at 8.9.) Finally, using those numbers, we calculate a final score to determine winners. The formula: 50% Speed Index + 25% Review Rating Index + 25% Satisfaction Index = Mobile Phone Index. About Our Expert I've been writing about computers, the internet, and technology professionally since 1992, more than half of that time with PCMag. I arrived at the end of the print era of PC Magazine as a senior writer. I served for a time as managing editor of business coverage before settling back into the features team for the last decade and a half. I write features on all tech topics, plus I handle several special projects, including the Readers' Choice and Business Choice surveys and yearly coverage of the Best ISPs and Best Gaming ISPs, Best Products of the Year, and Best Brands (plus the Best Brands for Tech Support, Longevity, and Reliability). I started in tech publishing right out of college, writing and editing stories about hardware and development tools. I migrated to software and hardware coverage for families, and I spent several years exclusively writing about the then-burgeoning technology called Wi-Fi. I was on the founding staff of several magazines, including Windows Sources, FamilyPC, and Access Internet Magazine. All of which are now defunct, and it's not my fault. I have freelanced for publications as diverse as Sony Style, Playboy.com, and Flux. I got my degree at Ithaca College in, of all things, television/radio. But I minored in writing so I'd have a future. In my long-lost free time, I wrote some novels, a couple of which are not just on my hard drive: BETA TEST ("an unusually lighthearted apocalyptic tale," according to Publishers' Weekly) and a YA book called KALI: THE GHOSTING OF SEPULCHER BAY. Go get them on Kindle. I work from my home in Ithaca, NY, and did it long before pandemics made it cool.

item.title: Researchers Mapped a Fruit Fly Brain. Software Engineers Got It to Play Doom
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.84
Researchers recently used AI to create a brain map of a male fruit fly, and what better way to take advantage of that breakthrough than to use it to play Doom? The team from HHMI Janelia, Google Research, and other collaborators say their "years-long project," which includes more than 166,000 neurons, "promises to be a foundational resource for neuroscience for years to come." But as PC Gamer reports, it also inspired people like Coinbase software engineer Alex Wormuth to train the fly brain to play Doom and other games. “Each Doom frame stimulates sensory neurons [in the fly brain],” Wormuth tweeted. “Neural activity is mapped to game controls. Damage triggers a stimulus to two PPL101 dopamine cells as reinforcement.” Wormuth’s website shows both the fly’s POV and a third-person fly cam, but as PC Gamers notes, the fruit fly is not very good at Doom. I could probably whoop its ass. Hacker and developer Domi got the fly playing shooters, too. “The visuals are rendered into the fly eyes and brain decides where to turn. The courtship song is responsible for shooting,” Domi explains. “The more aroused the fly is the harder it tries to shoot.” You can try out Domi's project, called Aimbug, here. Others have chimed in on X with their own projects, from a Fly Escape Room and a driving fly to a NeuroCraft Fly project inside Minecraft. Shout out to all the researchers, scientists, and engineers who made it possible for the male fruit fly to get a comprehensive education in video game history with these essential texts. About Our Expert I’m a New York-based writer currently serving as PCMag’s Editorial Intern. I cover the impact of technology and internet culture on our daily lives, with a specialization in video games and cultural criticism. I have written for Kotaku, The A.V. Club, Unwinnable, Aftermath, and more. In addition, I have a formal background in video game development and visual design. You can find all of my work on my website.

item.title: Google Launches a Gemini App for Windows With a Quick-Access Shortcut
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.65
Google has added a Gemini app for Windows, months after debuting the app on macOS. The app is designed to work seamlessly with other Windows apps and provides instant assistance wherever possible, Google said in a blog post. Like on macOS, summoning Gemini on Windows is easy with an Alt + Space keyboard shortcut. You can use the tool for regular querying or request it to fact-check documents, suggest ideas for presentations, or create images and videos using Nano Banana and Gemini Omni, respectively. You can also use Gemini Spark as a 24/7 personal AI agent. With your permission, it can connect to compatible Google services, such as Gmail and Google Drive, and pull the information you need to draft an email or presentation. It will be interesting to see how many Windows users prefer Gemini over Microsoft’s own Copilot. Google says its tool can run in the background without slowing down your PC, and that “more native desktop capabilities” will roll out over time. You can download the new Gemini app from Google’s website, and it is compatible with both Windows 10 and Windows 11. To use Gemini Spark, though, you should be 18 or above and have a Google AI subscription, which starts with the Google AI Plus plan at $4.99 per month. Network carriers sometimes offer Google AI subscriptions as a perk, and students can currently grab a limited-time offer for the annual Google AI Pro Plan for free. In addition to higher Gemini usage limits, the AI Pro plan (usually $20 per month) unlocks 5TB of additional cloud storage, while the lower-priced AI Plus plan offers 400GB. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Apple May Be Prepping Ads for Visual Intelligence on the iPhone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.54
You may soon get ads when using Visual Intelligence on your iPhone. Code spotted in the latest iOS 27 build suggests Apple is preparing an option for sponsored results within its AI-powered camera recognition tools. Visual Intelligence uses Apple Intelligence to let you learn about your surroundings, analyze items, find information about locations, or ask what’s happening on your phone’s screen. MacRumors' Aaron Perris noticed iOS 27 code that “indicates that Apple may be working on supporting ads from search providers" within the tool. “This would not be Apple selling the ads, but more so allowing sponsored images like you see in Amazon or Google listings," he says. Perris didn’t clarify which element of the code he found that suggests ads are coming, or how far through development it appears to be. If Apple is developing this, however, you may get a sponsored link to buy through an online retailer when you point your camera at an item you find in a rival brick-and-mortar store. Perris also notes how it’s unclear whether Apple would take a revenue cut from ads shown within Visual Intelligence. Apple takes a percentage of all digital sales made through its App Store, so it may choose to do something similar here. Apple hasn't made any announcements, but it has increased advertising features on its products in recent years, including a rollout of ads in Apple Maps in August. The ads appear in the Suggested Places feature when you use the search bar, labeled with a blue box icon. item.title: Asus Receives Exemption to US's Foreign-Made Wi-Fi Router Ban
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.40
Taiwanese PC maker Asus has received a temporary exemption to the US ban on foreign-made Wi-Fi routers after the Defense Department determined that its products do not pose a national security risk, the Federal Communications Commission announced on Wednesday. An FCC exemption is good for 18 months, so Asus's "conditional approval" lasts until March 6, 2028. It applies to various Wi-Fi product lines, including the RT Router Series, ROG GT Series, ROG Strix GS Series, TUF Gaming Series, ExpertWiFi Series, ZenWiFi Mesh Series, 5G MiFi Series, repeaters, and wireless access points. The exemption is good news for Asus, as the Taiwanese vendor has begun preparing Wi-Fi 8 products ahead of the wireless technology’s official standardization. Last week, Asus announced the latest ROG Rapture GT-BN98 series had launched in Canada, with a global rollout slated for October. So far, Asus hasn’t responded to a request for comment. But when applying for an exemption, the company had to answer a long list of questions, including a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States for the router.” Currently, many routers imported to the US come from Vietnam, Mexico, Taiwan, the Philippines, and Thailand. Other router vendors that have received an exemption include Netgear, Amazon’s Eero, SpaceX’s Starlink, and Taiwanese brands Zyxel, Arcadyan Technology, and Asus subsidiary Askey Computer. But so far, the US has yet to grant an exemption to the major Wi-Fi router maker TP-Link, which has long been fighting accusations over its ties to China. The US enacted the ban—which only applies to new products—over concerns that foreign-made routers introduce "supply chain vulnerabilities" that hackers and cyberspies can exploit. However, TP-Link has been stressing that it’s a US company after relocating its headquarters to Irvine, California, and splitting off from the Chinese business. In April, TP-Link told the FCC it plans to invest “hundreds of millions of dollars” to bring its manufacturing from Vietnam to the US while previewing its plan to apply for an exemption from the ban. “Conditional Approval will enable TP-Link to complete those investments,” it wrote. item.title: Want a New iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo? Here's How Much They Cost With Apple Upgrade
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.38
Apple announced during its 'Surprise and Shine' event that the iPhone 18 Pro will launch on September 18, with preorders opening on Saturday, September 12. Its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, will launch one month later on October 23, with preorder starting on October 16. If you can't wait to get your hands on either of Apple's latest premium flagships but can't afford to buy them outright, you have options. You can trade in your old device to shave some money off of your bill, finance with your carrier, or lease a device through Apple's newly launched Upgrade program. Here's how much the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo will cost through Apple Upgrade, and whether or not this leasing option makes sense for you. How Much Is the iPhone 18 Pro With Apple Upgrade? The iPhone 18 Pro will start at a retail price of $1,199 in the US. If you want to lease the iPhone 18 Pro through Apple Upgrade, prices will start at $34.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $49.99 per month for a 24-month lease. The iPhone Duo will retail for between $1,999 and $3,199. Apple Upgrade plans for the iPhone Duo will start at $57.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $82.99 for a 12-month lease. How Does Apple Upgrade Work? In partnership with "buy now, pay later" (BNPL) platform Klarna, Apple Upgrade is a new leasing program that launched on July 28, which lets you pay a monthly fee for select iPhones and Apple Watches for 24 months and MacBooks and iPads for 36 months. You'll then have the option to return the device, pay off the balance and keep it, or upgrade to a new device. Eligibility will be based on a credit check. For an iPhone, it'll need to be connected to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon when you enroll. This new service replaces Apple's iPhone Upgrade program. If you're currently a member of the iPhone Upgrade Program, your loan agreement with Citizens One remains active, and you’ll continue making your monthly payments until your 24-month term is complete, when "the iPhone will be yours to keep." Does Apple Upgrade Charge Interest or Fees? Neither Apple nor Klarna mentions any interest payments. Apple's current iPhone Upgrade Program is a zero-interest installment loan, and so was Apple Pay Later, which the company ditched in 2024. Apple says there are no fees on a monthly lease payment, but notes that you could incur a damage fee at the end of your lease term if you don't take care of the device. There are also fees if you upgrade or terminate a lease early. Plus, if you don't decide what to do at the end of your lease, Klarna will start an "automatic extension period" for up to 6 months. "During this extension, your monthly payment may increase because promotional credits (such as trade-in credits) only apply to the original lease term. If you still make no decision by the end of the extension, Klarna will charge a one-time payment, otherwise known as the Purchase Option Fee, to pay off the device. You will be notified 1 month in advance if your next payment will be the final payment." There were reports that Apple would restrict access to certain apps if payments were late, but sources tell PCMag that's not the case. "If a payment cannot be collected, Klarna will retry," Klarna says. "If that also fails, Klarna will attempt to charge a backup payment method on file. There are no late fees for this program. However, missed payments can eventually be sent to debt collection after multiple failed attempts, and missed payments may be reflected in your credit report." Should You Use Apple Upgrade to Lease a New iPhone or Mac? There are some scenarios where leasing an Apple product makes sense. Maybe you need a MacBook for grad school, but don't plan to keep it after you graduate. Or, perhaps you're already upgrading to the newest iPhone every year, and leasing will save you money. But even if the math works in your favor, make sure you understand all of the risks before you sign up. Which Products Can You Lease Through Apple Upgrade? While Apple Upgrade is available for most newer Apple devices, some older and budget versions are not available. You cannot use Apple Upgrade for the iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, Apple Watch SE, MacBook Neo, Mac mini, iPad (A16), or Studio Display. You can currently lease the following phones, MacBooks, iPads, and Apple Watches with Apple Upgrade: iPhones: - iPhone Duo - iPhone 18 Pro - iPhone Air - iPhone 17 - iPhone 17 e Macs: - MacBook Air - MacBook Pro - iMac - Mac Studio iPads: - iPad Pro - iPad Air - iPad Mini Apple Watches: - Apple Watch Series 12 - Apple Watch Ultra 4 - Apple Watch Hermès Series 12 - Apple Watch Hermès Ultra 4 How Much Does It Cost to Lease Other Apple Products? The main draw of Apple Upgrade is its low prices. Here are the starting prices by Apple device: - iPad - $11.99 per month - iPhone - $17.99 per month - Apple Watch - $11.99 per month - MacBook - $24.99 per month These are just starting prices and will vary by product (and possibly your credit score). Leasing an iPhone 17, which costs $899 to buy, starts at $25.99 per month to lease for 24 months and $36.99 to lease for 12 months. However, Apple says you can trade in your old device to lower your lease payments. For comparison, Apple's now-defunct iPhone Upgrade plan charges $42.41 per month for an iPhone 17 with 256GB of storage over a 24-month term. What's the Catch? We're glad you asked. There are a few big risks you should understand before you sign up for Apple Upgrade. Apple Upgrade Does Not Include AppleCare+ Apple Upgrade will not include AppleCare+, which protects your device against certain accidental damage. You'll have to add and pay for AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage yourself within 60 days of your lease starting. Without that protection included, you're on the hook for any damage. "You may incur damage fees if the device is...not returned in the condition required by the lease," Apple notes. If you don't have AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage, and the device is lost or stolen, you'll have to pay an early termination fee or the purchase option fee. If you do nothing, you'll continue to be charged the monthly lease fee. You May Get Trapped in a Cycle of Monthly Payments Much like streaming services require you to pay every month to continue to access your favorite movies, TV shows, and music, Apple Upgrade could keep you hooked on monthly payments for decades. Unlike financing an iPhone or MacBook, Apple Upgrade leases don't cover the full cost of the device, so when the end of your lease term arrives, you'll be on the hook for a large balloon payment, the Purchase Option Fee, if you want to buy your device outright. As an example, let's look at the cost of leasing the iPhone 18 Pro (which starts at $1,199). Lease prices start at $34.99, so if you leased this phone for 24 months, you'd have paid $839.76 after 24 months. So, you'd need to pay at least another $359.24 at one time in order to purchase and keep the phone. If you can't afford to make this large lump-sum payment on time, the easiest solution is to lease another device, essentially locking you into another couple of years of monthly payments. Suddenly, you're trapped in an endless cycle of monthly fees for a device you don't even own. About Our Experts As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well. As PCMag's managing editor of operations and evergreen content, I lead the operations, How To, and updates teams. I have 15+ years of experience writing and editing personal finance, small business, and financial software content. Prior to PCMag, I led the personal finance team at CNET. My work has also been published in the Chicago Tribune, NerdWallet, Investopedia, and BestReviews. Personal finance Project management software Tax software Accounting software Identity theft services Antivirus software A PC enthusiast for most of my life, I now work on a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3) or 13-inch MacBook Air. You won't pry my Android from my hands, though! I have a Samsung S25 that has miraculously survived hundreds of accidental tumbles down my wood staircase. My first desktop was a hand-me-down Power Macintosh in the early '90s, where I spent hours trying not to get eaten by a grue in the game Zork. I'm an avid reader, and though I prefer physical books, I travel with my old Nook GlowLight 3 (yes, they still exist).

item.title: FBI: US Customs Worker Stole Intel CPUs From Work PCs for Newegg Trade-Ins
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.17
In a bizarre case, a US Customs and Border Protection supervisor allegedly swapped out Intel CPUs, RAM, and storage from agency computers to get in-store credit from Newegg’s trade-in program. Terry Liu, 39, was arrested on Wednesday after surveillance cameras caught him removing the components at a CBP office, according to The Maine Wire. Liu worked as a supervisor at the port of entry in Calais, Maine. According to court documents, IT staffers at the site in December realized that “multiple computers” had been modified outside the regular scheduled maintenance, and “not at the direction of CBP management or IT personnel.” “Since late 2025, forty-six (46) computers had been modified without authorization of CBP IT System Managers,” the FBI’s affidavit says. “Of those computers, thirty-nine (39) had CPUs replaced, six (6) had RAM changed, and eight (8) had hard drives changed.” To find the offender, staff at the CBP site installed a camera in a training room in January. A few days later, the footage showed Liu allegedly bringing the desktop PCs into the room and then swapping out the PC parts at midnight. Liu allegedly replaced the components with older parts purchased on Newegg and Amazon, but the new parts resulted in degraded performance, which likely tipped off IT staff. “A review of the computer hardware inventory identified that many of the altered computers had their CPUs changed to 12th Generation Intel Core CPUs, 13th Generation Intel Core CPUs, or Intel Pentium CPUs,” the FBI found. Liu appears to have gone after 38 desktop computers containing Intel Core i7-14700 CPUs, which can fetch $200 from Newegg’s trade-in program. It's unclear what Liu bought via the trade-in system. But the affidavit adds that the FBI interviewed Liu on Wednesday, and he “admitted to using CBP computer parts for the Newegg trade-in program, in which he received credit.” “In initially defending his actions, Liu stated that he made these changes in order for the computers to operate more efficiently. Later during the interview, when further questioned, Liu admitted that he knew that the changes made degraded the CBP computer system efficiency and claimed he did so because he was angry with how long it took for CBP IT systems to be repaired,” the document adds. Liu is currently in detention awaiting trial. A court document says Liu is not a foreign national, though Maine Wire notes "he has described himself as a native of Guangzhou, China." CBP officers must be US citizens. Liu’s been charged with the theft and destruction of government property, each of which carries a penalty of “not more than 10 years in prison, a fine of not more than $250,000, or prison and a fine.” Replacing the stolen parts "would cost an estimated $20,460,” the FBI’s affidavit adds. “To replace all forty-six (46) modified computers with new computers, an estimated cost would be $105,800.00 based on a per computer cost from the Dell website.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Polaris Freedom LT Cordless Robotic Cleaner Review: Basic But Effective Pool Maintenace
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.17
When I reviewed the Polaris Freedom Plus back in 2024, I gave it high marks for its cordless operation, underwater controls, and superb cleaning performance, but I thought its $1,649 price was a bit steep. The Polaris Freedom LT cleaner is a more affordable version of its sibling, and it too offers excellent cordless cleaning performance. However, you don’t get underwater control or dirty canister alerts, and it doesn’t expel water when you remove it from the pool. At $799, it’s still a solid value, but you’ll get more features, including an underwater remote and AI mapping, with our top pick for smart robotic pool cleaners, the $1,499 Dreame Z1 Pro, which can usually be found for less than the price of the Freedom LT. Designed for inground pools up to 50 feet long, the Freedom LT maintains the same two-tone blue-and-black color scheme as the Freedom Plus. It measures 9 by 15 by 17 inches (HWD) and weighs 16.5 pounds. It’s powered by a lithium-ion battery and uses two drive motors and a pair of bulldozer-style treads to navigate the floor, walls, and waterline of your pool. The battery is rated to last up to 3 hours per work cycle and requires around 4 hours to fully recharge. There's a gasketed power port on the back of the robot, and front and rear scrubbing brushes on the undercarriage. An optical sensor that aids with navigation sits on the front, along with a handle for removing the robot from the water. The top of the cleaner holds a water outlet, a control panel, and a transparent cover for the 4-liter filter basket. The main filter comes with a fine-mesh inner basket for capturing particles such as sand, pollen, and other grit. The main basket lifts out and can be easily emptied and cleaned with a hose without touching any debris. As with the Aiper Scuba V3 ($1,099.99), cleaning the fine filter can get messy, especially if you remove the mesh material from the basket for a thorough rinse. The control panel consists of a power button, an LED indicator, and four mode indicators. The power button turns the robot on and off, and cycles through the four cleaning modes: floor/walls, floor, walls, and waterline. Additionally, a multi-day mode is available in the app, allowing you to program the robot for up to four days of floor cleaning with a specific start time. Just leave the robot in the pool, and it will begin a 45-minute cleaning cycle at the specified time. Unlike the Dreame Z1 Pro, the Freedom LT does not offer AI mapping; instead, it lets you choose a cleaning path best suited to your pool’s shape. The S-Pattern is recommended for most pools, while the Standard pattern is best for pools with complex shapes. The Freedom LT uses a Bluetooth radio to pair with your phone and a Wi-Fi radio to connect to your network. As with every other pool robot, wireless connectivity is lost when the machine is underwater, so the only way to stop a cleaning cycle is to let it run its course or pull it out of the water with the hook. An underwater controller, something you get with the Freedom Plus and Dreame Z1 Pro, would be helpful here. When a work cycle is complete, or the battery is low, the cleaner will climb the wall and park itself along the side of the pool. It’ll stay there for 10 minutes before sinking to the bottom, where you can retrieve it using an included hook. Unlike the Freedom Plus, the Freedom LT doesn't expel water when removed from the pool, so it’s heavy to lift out of the water. The Freedom LT is the first Polaris cleaner to use the new Fluidra Pool mobile app for iOS and Android devices, whereas previous models work with the iAqualink app. The Fluidra app adds multi-day cleaning, lets you select cleaning patterns, and makes it easy to share access with service providers without revealing your personal credentials. To use the app, you must create a Site (home location) and assign each connected device to a Space (pool or spa). Individual logins for each Space let you manage multiple homes and devices from a single app. When you open the app, you’ll see a panel for the cleaner showing its name and current status (charging or offline). Tap the panel to open a screen showing the charging progress. Once the robot is unplugged, you can select a cleaning mode and a cleaning pattern in the Cleaning Mode panel. Here you can also create a multi-day schedule. Once the cleaner is programmed, simply drop it in the pool to begin the work cycle. As with the iAqualink app, Flurida does not offer work logs or dirty-canister alerts, but it will notify you when the cleaner completes a work cycle. The Freedom LT robot comes with a retrieval hook, a user guide, buoyancy foam to help it float to the surface, and an AC charger. Preparing the Freedom LT for first use is easy. I downloaded the app, created an account and a Site (home), and charged the robot for several hours until the LED glowed solid green. I tapped Add Equipment on the home screen and followed the instructions to scan the QR code located in the filter compartment. Once the app identified the cleaner, I entered my Wi-Fi credentials, created a Space (pool), and gave the robot a name to complete the installation. The Freedom LT performed well in testing. I have a ton of small berries from a neighbor’s tree that fall into my 16-by-32-foot gunite pool, and the LT had no trouble sucking them up along with a fair amount of filter sand. It averaged nearly 3 hours of battery life between charges and needed all of that to complete a full work cycle (floor, walls, waterline). In comparison, the Polaris Freedom Plus needed 2.5 hours, and the Dreame Z1 Pro finished the job in 2 hours. I had some trouble getting the multi-day cleaning feature to work at first, but after a firmware upgrade, it worked as intended. I used the app to set the cleaner to multi-day/floor-only cleaning with an S-pattern and programmed it for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday at 5 p.m. The cleaner scrubbed the floor for 45 minutes, stopped, and started right back up at 5 p.m. the next day. It had just enough power to handle the four-day schedule before needing a recharge. As previously mentioned, cleaning the main filter basket with a hose was easy, but flushing out the fine filter took a bit more work. I had to remove the fine filter from its basket to clear all the sediment, which meant getting my hands dirty. On the plus side, I was happy to have the fine sediment out of the pool. Final Thoughts Polaris Freedom LT Cordless Robotic Cleaner - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Polaris Freedom LT lets you spend less time cleaning your pool and more time enjoying it. At $799, it won’t break the bank, and it offers great cleaning performance, good battery life, and multi-day cleaning schedules. That said, you don’t get many extra features with this model. If you’re looking for a feature-rich pool robot that offers underwater control, work logs, and even better suction, our Editors’ Choice winner, the Dreame Z1 Pro, is your best bet, and you can find it for well under its list price via several online retailers. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: Apple Satellite Features Will Be Free on iPhones for Another Year
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.12
The satellite features on supported iPhones will remain free for at least another year. "Apple is extending free access to satellite features for an additional year for existing iPhone 14, iPhone 15, and iPhone 16 users," the company wrote in the fine print of its iPhone 18 Pro announcement. That’s good news since the satellite features, including the Emergency SOS, were slated to expire in the coming weeks for affected iPhones. Satellite service keeps people connected in cellular dead zones, allowing them to send text messages via satellite. Emergency SOS has also helped emergency responders locate people stranded in remote areas. Apple describes the access as a “free trial,” so it could eventually charge for the satellite connectivity. But so far, it has instead extended free access, even though the satellite connectivity was initially advertised as a two-year free trial. Apple’s third-party partner, Globalstar, a satellite communications company, has powered the feature since late 2022, when it first arrived for the iPhone 14. Amazon is now in the process of acquiring Globalstar, including taking over Apple’s 20% stake in the company. Still, Amazon says it’ll continue supplying satellite services for iPhones and improving them through Globalstar. The iPhone satellite features have been limited to text messaging, location pinging, and emergency assistance. You also usually need to point your phone toward the right part of the sky to access it. Still, Amazon’s goal is to expand Globalstar’s technology with two next-generation satellite constellations and eventually offer voice and mobile data. But this also means the upgraded satellite tech might come at an extra cost for iPhone owners. In the coming years, consumers can also expect to see more satellite-to-phone service offerings. The two other major players, SpaceX and AST SpaceMobile, have ambitious plans to deliver cellular-focused broadband via orbiting satellites. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years.
