The Series 11 has the same claimed 24-hour battery life, but in our real-world testing, it lasted 43 hours with the always-on display enabled. However, the new heart rate tracker's continuous activity could shorten real-world battery life, bringing it closer to Apple's estimate. We won't know until we actually test the Series 12. Winner: To Be Determined Durability: A New Ceramic Display Coating The Series 12 has the same IP6X dustproof rating and is water-resistant to up to 164 feet, just like the Series 11. The aluminum version is a bit tougher, though, thanks to its new Ceramic Shield 2 glass (different from the ceramic case option), which Apple claims is 60% more durable than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11. The titanium models can probably take equal beatings, and it's safe to say the ceramic version of the watch is also pretty sturdy. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Connectivity: Dual-Band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and Optional 5G No changes here between Apple Watch generations. Both the Series 11 and Series 12 have dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, and L1 GPS standard, along with Apple's Ultra Wideband chip for precisely tracking the watch's nearby location with your phone. The cellular versions also have the same 5G and LTE radios. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Series 12 The Apple Watch Series 12 delivers some fitness and AI improvements that could make it a significant upgrade over the Series 11, which, while excellent, didn't change much compared with its predecessor, the Apple Watch Series 10. Better heart rate tracking and new holistic health information are big pluses, and Audio Intelligence could potentially be a powerful new feature. It's a lot of new tech packed into a watch that sticks to the same base price as the model it replaces. Keep an eye here in the coming weeks for our full review of the Apple Watch Series 12.

item.title: Worried About Snooping Smart Glasses? This Startup's Tech Detects Nearby Specs
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.04
If you hadn’t already, add the military-industrial complex to the growing list of parties concerned by the potential for people wearing smart glasses to engage in clandestine recording. Bastille Networks, a startup specializing in wireless intrusion detection, announced Thursday what it called “first-of-its-kind software” to spot smart glasses at customer sites. The San Diego-based firm pitches this new solution, available to companies that already subscribe to its monitoring services, as going well beyond indie apps like Nearby Glasses and the cleverly named Zuckoff that scan for Bluetooth Low Energy signals from smart glasses. “Those other ones will tell you whether there are glasses within Bluetooth range of your phone,” Bastille CEO Chris Risley said in an interview on Thursday. “What we do is tell you within two to three meters where it is.” Risley said Bastille has neither received nor sought help from such smart-glass developers as Meta in developing its glasses-tracking tools. He added that Bastille’s systems, designed to look for rogue devices by sniffing across Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and cellular frequencies, also provide an audit trail. “We tell you the history of that device–when did it show up?” Risley said. “Has it ever been here before?” Bastille charges “hundreds of thousands” of dollars and up for its installations for national-security, military, and private-sector clients to spot Flipper Zero-like hacking tools as well as misplaced personal devices. “We’ve been in those facilities for years, and people know we’re in there,” Risley said. “And we detect new devices every day being brought in.” He added, “Everybody’s going to tell you they brought it in by accident.” A video on the company’s site depicts a more menacing scenario: someone masquerading as a job candidate hands over a phone at a security checkpoint but keeps his connected glasses on during a lengthy tour of the premises, allowing him to walk away with a trove of confidential footage. That raises a question: Do sensitive installations not already check for smart glasses? Shouldn’t they? “There’s just not sufficient awareness,” Risley said. But as sales of smart glasses from firms like Meta continue to climb—even as critics mock that eyewear as “pervert glasses”—stories of creepy behavior seem likely to keep coming. Venues from bars and theaters to courtrooms have banned smart glasses, and now Apple’s new Siri Recap feature for Apple Watches brings a whole new set of surveillance fears. Places that aren’t thinking about this problem will probably have to soon enough. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Nintendo Isn't Getting Rid of Physical Games (Yet), But You Have to Watch Out for Game-Key Cards
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.02
Physical media's dying. Sony is dropping disk support in 2027. The physical version of Grand Theft Auto 6 will be a code-in-a-box. And it sounds like Xbox won't be supporting physical games for much longer. But what about Nintendo? While physical releases for the Switch 2 don't seem to be ending anytime soon, the company has its own controversial half measure: Game-key cards. If you're shopping for a new Switch 2 game, you need to be aware of game-key cards. You may already know that Nintendo's console supports regular game cards, where the game files are stored on the physical cartridge, but game-key cards are different, since they don't actually contain the full game data. It's confusing, for sure, but here's what you need to know before buying Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Resident Evil Requiem, or another big name game. What Is a Game-Key Card? As Nintendo explains, game-key cards are "your 'key' to downloading the full game to your system via the internet." They come in a case and include cartridges that slide into the Switch 2, just like any other physical release. However, you'll be shocked to learn that you need an internet connection to download the game's files before playing for the first time. It's worth noting that game-key cards don't need a continuous connection to play after the initial download, but the card does need to be inserted into the Switch 2. Additionally, these game cards aren't tied to a Nintendo account, so you can use them on other Switch 2 consoles or lend and resell your games. But the question remains: Are these truly physical games? Many have criticized Nintendo for devaluing physical media, leading the company to poll players about their feelings on the game-key card. I'm sure you're wondering why this even exists, right? Switch 2 cartridges top out at 64GB, but they're expensive for the publisher to use, so game-key cards will help get games into physical stores for a lot less money, Nintendo tells The Verge. However, this also means games like Puyo Puyo Tetris 2S—which is all of 4GB on Steam—are game-key cards because no one wants to pay more for storage they don't need. How to Tell If You're Buying a Game-Key Card Nintendo provides a helpful indicator on the box, but I needed to squint to read it. As illustrated in the image below, the case shows the game's rating in the bottom-left corner. Next to that is a key logo and the words GAME-KEY CARD. In very, very small print, it also says how many gigabytes of free space you need and a note: "Full game download via internet required." Crucially, there's a small key icon on the cartridge itself, which might not help you now but would be useful if you're looking to buy a used game without a case one day. While I think we've moved beyond the days when confused parents couldn't tell the difference between the Wii and Wii U, Nintendo notes the Switch 2 "supports both regular game cards and game-key cards," which I think still leaves some room for consumer confusion. If a publisher opts to use the game-key card format, there won't be a separate "true" physical release (at least not yet), but I fear folks might still grab a game off the shelf in Target only to get home and realize it's a game-key card. But does it matter? In the end, the game will still "be there," but if physical media matters to you, I can see this being a deal-breaker. Can you imagine buying a title before a long plane ride, only to realize the game won't load because you're not connected to Wi-Fi? If a game is on the cart, it can be theoretically played forever. If you need an internet connection to download the game, I worry what will happen when those servers go offline one day. Which Games Are Game-Key Cards? Many publishers have decided to use the game-key card format. This is allegedly because Nintendo only offered third-party developers the 64GB cartridge or the game-key card at launch—there was no smaller, standard physical cart. This would explain why nearly every major AAA release (and even some smaller games) is on a game-key card, since publishers don't want to pay extra for the more expensive storage space. Here's a list of games that are on a game-key card if you're trying to buy physical: Each of these games will require an internet connection to download before playing. It's also worth noting that titles like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Stage Tour, Civilization VII, Split Fiction, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3+4, and WWE 2K25 are actually only a code in a box. Even Nintendo is getting in on the act with Pokémon Legends: Z-A – Mega Dimension DLC. Bethesda's Fallout 4: Anniversary Edition and Skyrim Anniversary Edition were game-key cards, but Oblivion Remastered and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle received proper physical releases. Just be careful before buying online—I've seen at least one game show no Game-Key Card on one site, but feature it on another. Others are noticing as well, since "temporary" box art for pre-orders can lack the game-key card labels. I recommend checking multiple sites and reading through the product description to be sure. If you're truly dedicated to physical releases, one workaround I've seen discussed is buying the physical Switch 1 version and upgrading it to the "Switch 2 Edition" version after the fact. Nintendo seems to be banking on a lot of AAA releases heading to the Switch 2, including Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth and Elden Ring, both of which feature pretty hefty file sizes. That said, Cyberpunk 2077's devs managed to fit the game on a 64GB cart, and Bethesda switched to a true physical release for Oblivion after announcing it as a code in a box, so I think more physical releases can have the full game on the cart. It's also worth noting that smaller games are still vital to filling out Nintendo's catalog. To that end, 16GB and 32GB game cartridges have been rumored to exist since at least December, and Stellar Blade's Switch 2 release may be the first to explicitly mention a 32GB game card. If Nintendo has given publishers additional storage options, it might not mean that game-key cards are going away, but more options are a good thing, both for publishers and consumers. Given that PlayStation is dropping physical media, and Xbox isn't likely far behind, Nintendo's half-measure might soon be all we have. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Forget the Overlay: 5 Game-Changing Siri Features Coming to Your iPhone Next Week
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.93
Apple’s hardware keynotes tend to focus on camera evolution and sleek titanium curves, but the reveal of the upcoming standalone Siri application stole the show for me. As someone who frequently uses Google’s advanced AI search models for daily research, I have spent years frustrated by how restrictive iPhone software is by comparison. That paradigm is finally shifting. When this massive overhaul drops alongside iOS 27 next Monday, it promises to bridge the gap between static web retrieval and an assistant that actually thinks ahead. As we prepare for the update to officially go live next week, here is an in-depth look at the five Siri AI features I'm most excited to incorporate into my daily routine, and how Apple is finally developing Siri into a truly agentic AI powerhouse. 1. Ditching the Overlay for a Dedicated Chatbot Application Whenever I activate Siri right now, the interface does what it has always done: It temporarily takes over the device. The screen triggers that familiar, glowing rainbow outline along the edges of the display, waiting for a single prompt. If you ask it a question, it drops a small answer window over whatever you are doing, provides a one-and-done response, and then vanishes. If you forget what it said, or want to follow up on a previous thought, you’re out of luck. You have to start the conversation over. The upcoming update fixes this by introducing a dedicated Siri app icon on the Home Screen—without sacrificing its system-wide integration. Instead of a temporary screen animation, Siri will finally have its own permanent workspace, functioning exactly like ChatGPT or Gemini. It means Siri will maintain a rolling, continuous conversation history. I’ll be able to look back at research threads from three days ago, type out a long-form prompt when I'm in a quiet public space, or pick up an active brainstorming session right where I left off. The new application interface also adds an attachment paperclip toggle. This will let you drag and drop PDFs, documents, or screenshots directly into a Siri thread to instantly generate summaries or isolate data. It moves the assistant out of the voice remote control era and into a true desktop-grade workspace. 2. True Screen Context: Pixels-Aware Intelligence Right now, if a friend texts you a photo of an ambiguous landmark and you want information on it, you have to leave the conversation, save the image, upload it to a third-party search app, or manually copy and paste text between split windows. Apple’s world-class silicon can read that data instantly, but the software is a bottleneck. The iOS 27 upgrade introduces Screen Context, enabling Siri to actively read and interpret the live pixels on your display. When this goes live, you’ll be able to pull up a text message, activate Siri, and simply say, "Where was this photo taken?" or "Summarize the key points of this article." Siri will read the active application canvas, parse the information dynamically, and give you a relevant breakdown without forcing me to switch apps or copy an ounce of text. It brings a native equivalent of Google's on-screen visual search tools directly into the core of iOS, which is a win for mobile efficiency. 3. Visual Intelligence via the Camera Viewfinder We have had tools like Live Text for a few generations now, which are great for pausing a video frame or opening a captured photo to copy text. But it is still a reactive system: You have to take the photo or freeze the screen first to extract the utility. The new Siri Mode inside the Camera app gives the assistant direct access to your lens. By swiping to Siri mode in the viewfinder and tapping the shutter, Siri freezes the frame and parses it. You can snap a photo of a dinner plate to get an instant, approximate nutritional breakdown, or a historical plaque to pull up a full background biography. It turns the iPhone camera into an active data scanner rather than just a memory catcher. 4. The Agentic Pivot: True Cross-App Workflow Execution Siri’s current app integration is essentially a system of simple triggers. You can tell it to "open Spotify" or "send a text to my wife," but you can't tell it to execute a multi-step workflow. If you want to move a file from your downloads, organize it into a folder, and email it, you have to click through each app manually. Apple is finally granting Siri the system permissions to execute deep, agentic workflows natively. This is the productivity leap I am most anxious to test. You will be able to give Siri a single complex command like: "Find the Nintendo Voice Memo I created yesterday afternoon, copy the transcript, paste it into an email, and mail it to my work email address." Instead of watching your phone open and close three different apps, Siri will handle the backend asset management silently, saving you dozens of manual taps throughout the workday. 5. Personal Context and Private Cloud Compute An AI assistant is only as useful as the data it has access to. If you ask Google's AI Mode, "What time does my mom’s flight land next week?" it will naturally fail because that data is locked away inside my private text threads, emails, and calendar entries. However, opening up my entire digital life to an AI model naturally triggers a wave of privacy anxiety. Apple’s solution is a Personal Context Index tied directly to a new architecture called Private Cloud Compute. Siri will securely scan your local data to build a personal timeline, allowing you to ask hyper-specific questions about my life, such as tracking down a confirmation code buried deep in your emails or cross-referencing text messages to remember your dinner reservation time. To protect your privacy, lighter tasks stay strictly on the iPhone's local chip. For heavier processing, data is routed to Apple's new end-to-end encrypted private cloud servers. The software ensures that your personal information is processed on custom silicon, where data is never stored and remains completely unreadable by anyone—including Apple. It provides the utility of a deeply integrated personal assistant without the paranoia about tracking. Will Your Phone Get Siri AI? The Device Divide Due to the intense computational demand, Apple is dividing the Siri upgrade into two distinct tiers: - On-Device (iPhone 18 Pro/Max, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 17 Pro/Max): With 12GB of RAM or more, these iPhones will run most complex AI models entirely locally. This means instantaneous response times and maximum local privacy. - Cloud-Assisted (iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, and the full iPhone 16 lineup): These older compatible models will still get access to the same feature list and Siri app layout. However, because they lack the raw on-board memory, they will offload heavier, complex computations to Apple’s secure Private Cloud Compute servers. If you're using a standard iPhone 15 or anything older, you'll get the iOS 27 system update on Monday, Sept. 14, but you'll be locked out of the new Siri capabilities entirely. I plan on testing all of Siri's new capabilities, so be sure to check back soon. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% Review: Small Keyboard, Small Price, Big Value
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.61
You can't pigeon-hole Razer. Its gaming laptops are powerful, and esports athletes love its gaming keyboards and gaming mice for their performance-boosting features. I suppose if you were really trying, you could say Razer gear tends to be expensive. But even that's not necessarily true anymore, if you look at hardware like Razer's new Reclusa X Mini 65% keyboard, which is just $49.99. The Reclusa is not the fastest nor the most sensitive keyboard Razer has released—it’s firmly an enthusiast board, not a hardcore-gaming one. But it's also a mighty board for the money, with finger-pleasing key switches and customization features. To me, the best thing about the Reclusa is how many premium features it packs into its design while keeping the price low for any mechanical model. For that, it earns an Editors' Choice award as the best budget tenkeyless board you can buy. The Reclusa X Mini 65% is the first of a brand-new line of keyboards from Razer, denoted by “X” in the name, but it’s not the first time Razer’s used the Reclusa name. All the way back in 2007, Razer and Microsoft collaborated on the Microsoft Razer Reclusa, a distinctive oval full-size keyboard. But aside from the name, this new keyboard has no relation to the older board. It reminded me of the situation with the Karna Razer Boomslang, which was released in 1999 and then re-released as the Razer Boomslang in 2005 and again as an Anniversary Edition some months ago. (Karna, the company, was a predecessor to Razer itself, and Razer was a sub-brand of it.) The Reclusa, Razer claims, aims to deliver a rewarding experience right out of the box while also remaining open to future modifications. To that end, it uses the Razer Orange switch. Tactile and quiet, the Oranges are some of my favorite key switches, giving the Reclusa a luxurious typing feel with the stock switches. If these switches don't work for you, though, the Reclusa supports hot-swap compatibility for both three- and five-pin switches. The 65% keyboard's design is simple and clean. A small, black rectangle frame houses the five rows of keys. The body measures 1.5 by 12.4 by 4 inches and weighs 1.5 pounds. It's roughly the same size as the company's Huntsman V3 Pro Mini. It’s a sturdy device in hand, and thanks to its size, it takes up very little desk space, making it an ideal choice for cramped workspaces. I normally prefer a full-size keyboard, but the adjustment period wasn't as bad as I imagined. With only five rows of keys in the layout, additional functions such as volume control are subsumed into other keys as key combinations. Like its bigger, more expensive cousins, the Reclusa X Mini 65% incorporates silicone dampening within its frame. This reduces resonance and minimizes the hollow noise often associated with mechanical keyboards. By absorbing the excess vibration from key presses, the dampening layers produce a more consistent sound with every stroke, regardless of which switches are installed. In use, that sound translates to a clean, satisfying click. It’s not the quietest mechanical keyboard I've used (see the Be Quiet Light Mount for a recent example), but it’s quiet enough for shared office spaces and busy cafes. The keys have a travel distance of 3.5mm and an actuation force of 50 grams. (The actuation force is the minimum pressure required to register an input.) It's enough that those who spend most of their days typing will ease right into using the Reclusa, and casual gamers will find the resistance satisfying as well. Esports gamers may prefer lighter key actuation, but Razer has plenty of keyboards that cater to them. As far as its aesthetics are concerned, the Reclusa takes steps to differentiate itself from the typical black-and-white keyboards Razer usually traffics in. The keyboard features three-tone keycaps in white, black, and a light shade of green Razer calls Kelley Green. Textured double-shot ABS keycaps keep the letters and symbols on the keyboard legible over time, though I wish the keycap lettering were transparent, as it does suppress the RGB glow underneath. One subtle innovation Razer made that might excite the custom keyboard community is the change to so-called "south-facing" LEDs. With these, the LED is positioned below the switch mechanism, shining downward, as opposed to above ("north-facing") and shining straight up through the keycap. South-facing keys tend to emit more diffuse, even light, and sometimes, enable quieter operation since the LED isn't up in the keycap's movement zone. This aligns with the enthusiast-keycap standard used across the custom keyboard community, making the Reclusa compatible with a wider range of aftermarket keycaps. It's easy to see that the Reclusa is an impressive keyboard, but the more time I spent with it, the more I started to see what Razer trimmed to achieve that attractive $50 price. For one, the board has no feet to give it extra tilt. It doesn’t come with a wrist rest or a keycap puller, either. You won't find an OLED screen or a volume roller, and there are no 2.4GHz or Bluetooth wireless options; the small USB-C port at the top is the only way to connect it to your PC. These omissions don't bother me too much, though additional ergonomic options, like adjustable feet, are something Razer should consider as the line matures. Despite not being marketed as a gaming keyboard, the Reclusa X Mini 65% comes with a few gamer-focused features you might recognize from the Razer Huntsman V3. One returning favorite is Snap Tap mode, which is designed to help prevent instances where two opposing keys are pressed simultaneously. With the mode on, it’ll register the last input as the priority and keep you moving, a useful tactic in shooters and other action titles. You can also set what the keyboard prioritizes, too. If you’re keen to get granular in your keyboard’s settings, you can, for example, prioritize the depth of actuation between the two selected keys, so whichever key has a deeper depth of actuation will register first. In a similar vein, the Reclusa offers Dual Keypress Priority. During intense game sessions, you may occasionally press multiple directional keys, accidentally disrupting your own movement flow and control. Dual Keypress Priority manages that. For example, when holding A and W to move diagonally, pressing D will not override the current input. Only when A is released will the new directional input be registered. In addition to Snap Tap, Razer Snap Flex appears here. Snap Flex binds two keys to a single press, which allows both inputs to be executed together in a consistent, predictable manner. For example, if I wanted to prime a grenade in Call of Duty before I jumped and tossed it, I’d typically have to hold one button down, then the jump button, and then release the button. But with Snap Flex on, I can map the keyboard to both jump and release the grenade with a single button press. It might seem like a small adjustment, but it allows me to pull off that move every time. All these features and more are tweakable in Razer Synapse, Razer's downloadable utility. Here's where you can assign button functions, change RGB lighting effects, and more. My favorite feature is the key-switch-optimization option, which tweaks the switch sensitivity to better support you whether you're gaming or just typing. However, the Reclusa is not compatible with Razer's web app version of Synapse, so you'll have to download the software onto a Windows 11 computer to make use of the additional keyboard functions. While the Reclusa does have some features I wasn’t expecting, it’s not exactly the gaming keyboard for hardened esports players. It has a maximum polling rate of just 1,000Hz, for example. If you’re looking for a premium gaming keyboard, models such as the Corsair Vanguard Air 99 Wireless will be better suited for you. But I think enthusiasts or those new to keyboard customization and looking for a solid base to build on will find that the Reclusa is exactly what they’re after. For $50, the Reclusa is a great deal, and its out-of-the-box configuration is enough to impress even the pickiest of keyboard geeks. It’s a big improvement over the Razer BlackWidow V4 75% Barebones. And even if you don’t want to swap out any of Razer’s keycaps or switches, the gaming-forward features and strong RGB lighting will pair well with just about any casual gaming need. Final Thoughts Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% is an impressive addition to Razer’s keyboard portfolio. With the rising prices of computer goods, I was convinced that many would be priced out of keyboard customization as a hobby. But at $50, this is one of the best budget keyboards I've come across. If you’re looking to dabble in keyboard customization and don’t mind omissions like wireless connectivity, I wholeheartedly recommend the Reclusa X Mini 65% to start your experiments on. About Our Expert I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: LG Denies Claims That Its TVs Eavesdrop on Users Even When the Screen Is Off
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.38
UPDATE (09/10): LG has denied allegations made by a gaming site that its smart TVs eavesdrop on users even after the screen is turned off. “The claims made in the recently published video are not true," LG tells CNET. “LG TVs process voice data only when the voice button on the remote control is pressed and held, or when a wake word such as 'Hi LG' is recognized after the user has activated the Far-Field voice recognition feature.” The video in question was published by Gamers Nexus on Monday. The team claimed they extracted transcripts of conversations captured by the TV’s microphone and added that the device logged information about other devices connected to the same network. LG says its “TVs do not collect or record ambient conversations." On the second point, LG says the "ability to scan for and connect to nearby devices on the same network...is a standard function commonly provided by smart TVs and smart home devices." In any case, if you’re uncomfortable with LG using your activity data for its Automatic Content Recognition program, which helps advertisers serve targeted ads, you may turn off a setting called Live Plus. Head to Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus. Original Story 9/8: TV brands tracking user activity to serve targeted ads isn’t a new phenomenon, but the extent of private information they allegedly collect may worry some TV owners. In an investigative video published on Monday, Gamers Nexus claims that TVs from one of the world’s most popular brands, LG, can eavesdrop on users' conversations even with the screens turned off. The investigation was carried out with Level1Techs and other independent researchers, and the resulting video is nearly 135 minutes. In the video, Gamers Nexus says that while most TV brands collect your viewing data for their Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) systems, LG goes beyond the basics to collect valuable pieces of information, such as your location, IP address, names of nearby Wi-Fi networks, and the names of all devices connected to the same network as your TV. ACR comes enabled by default on most new TVs. The program logs your viewing habits and sells that data to any third-party company that would like to know them. On LG’s Ad Solutions website, the company says its ACR technology can help advertisers reach 49 million LG smart TVs in the US and nearly 216 million smart TVs globally. According to the video, what’s more concerning is that LG also knows about 363 million secondary devices, which may include smartphones connected to the same network as the TV. As part of the investigation, those at Gamers Nexus were able to extract the names of the secondary devices as well as transcripts of private conversations people were having around the LG TV. The video stitches a clip of an LG executive explaining the benefits of the company’s ACR system. “We know who’s in the LG household. We know which devices are there and how to extend that reach into mobile,” the executive says. Notably, the data can also be used for political campaigns. We have reached out to LG for comment on Gamers Nexus’s claims, and we’ll update the story if we hear back. In the meantime, if you’d like to turn off ACR on your LG TV, head to Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus. LG calls its ACR function Live Plus. Our detailed guide also shares steps to turn off the setting on TVs from multiple other manufacturers. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: September's Best Monitor Deals Bring You the Screen of Your Dreams on the Cheap
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.23
Updated September 11: Having a tough time making out the details on your PC's display? There's no better time to shop for a new computer monitor, and we've been combing through online retailers to find incredible discounts on screens for every purpose. We've got price drops on massive widescreens for immersive gaming, ultra-budget productivity screens, and more. Our testing and review procedure is second to nine in the industry. When a new monitor arrives at the office, we run it through extensive tests, including scientific measurements of color accuracy and quality, brightness, input lag, port placement, and more. We evaluate them using clear, replicable metrics for gaming, content creation, extended use, and numerous other situations. Here are the eight best monitor deals for September. Home and Office Monitor Deals These are your mainstream displays, which keep prices relatively low by opting for VA or IPS screens with medium refresh rates, decent if unspectacular color, and moderate brightness. Use them for productivity, Web surfing and media streaming. This category also includes a few budget monitor options. We gave an Editors' Choice award to this BenQ display in our review and rated it the best budget monitor on the market. Being able to take an additional thirty bucks off the already rock-bottom retail price makes it a steal. Senior writer Tony Hoffman said that the screen "packs in a feature set we would expect to find in a monitor selling for considerably more," including a height-adjustable stand with tilt, swivel, and pivot adjustment, a generous port selection, and good contrast for an IPS screen. While it's not the brightest or the biggest monitor on the market, it's more than capable for most home and office setups. For an ultra-affordable productivity monitor, Dell is the company to talk to. It produces a wide range of displays, and the 24 Plus on sale here for $120 is an excellent value for the price. While FHD resolution won't push a graphics card to the max, image quality is surprisingly sharp and clear, with a 1500:1 contrast ratio making it great for eyestrain-free text editing, with TÜV-certified blue light reduction. item.title: Windows 11 may finally auto-switch dark mode without PowerToys soon
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.20
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Windows 11 may soon natively support automatic light and dark mode switching, a feature previously only possible through Microsoft PowerToys. - Microsoft appears to be testing this in experimental builds, with settings allowing transitions based on fixed times or location-based sunrise and sunset cycles. - A potential release could arrive with the Windows 11 26H2 update in October, helping reduce eye strain and save power across devices. It appears Microsoft has finally decided to give Windows 11 a true, full-fledged dark mode. That’s according to Windows Latest, which discovered this by taking a closer look at the new experimental builds of Windows 11. Windows Latest says it’ll soon be possible for Windows 11 to switch automatically between light and dark modes, depending on requirements and the selected application. Until now, this has only been possible using Microsoft PowerToys or certain third-party programs. The absence of a true auto-switching light/dark mode in Windows 11 has been one of its biggest criticisms for years. Although Microsoft hasn’t yet officially announced anything, the signs are promising. Why the new Dark Mode matters With the new Dark Mode, it’ll apparently be possible to schedule when Windows 11 switches between dark and light modes. The actual trigger can be based on the day-night cycle outside (relative to your current location), fixed times of day, or your planned usage times. There are several advantages. It’s more convenient since Dark Mode will toggle automatically, without the user having to do anything. When Dark Mode is active, the system uses less power as it doesn’t need to increase the screen brightness as high. Dark Mode is also easier on the eyes and may help to prevent eye strain, migraines, and/or headaches. The plan to now customize and expand Windows 11’s Dark Mode also fits perfectly with Microsoft’s recent endeavor to give the operating system a more modern look. Learn more about how Microsoft is modernizing Windows 11’s aging user interface. However, it’s still unclear exactly when the new feature will be officially rolled out. A release later this year is possible, maybe as early as October to coincide with the launch of Windows 11 26H2.

item.title: ANTHBOT N8: A robotic lawn mower that mows, mulches, collects grass clippings, and clears leaves
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.19
Robotic lawn mowers take the hard work out of mowing, but they rarely handle the cleanup. Most models rely exclusively on mulching, cutting the grass and leaving the clippings on the lawn. During the growing season, this can result in patches of damp grass, while fallen leaves add to the mess in the fall. Under a thick layer of clippings and leaves, the lawn receives less light, creating conditions in which moss and fungal diseases can develop. Anyone who wants to keep the lawn tidy may still need to reach for a rake or pay a lawn care service to do the job. ANTHBOT With the ANTHBOT N8, the job doesn’t end when the mowing is finished. The robot can also collect the clippings left behind. Four tasks, one robot The N8 is designed as a 4-in-1 system that can mow, mulch, collect grass clippings, and remove leaves. This is made possible by a modular cutting deck with a 20-centimeter cutting width. You simply swap the module depending on the season and the condition of the lawn; the rest of the mower remains unchanged. Cyclone System: Grass clippings go into the collection bag Specially shaped blades generate powerful airflow as they rotate, lifting grass clippings and leaves and carrying them into the 23-liter collection bag, much like a vacuum cleaner. The system is powered by a brushless motor running at 4,000 rpm. ANTHBOT says it can collect up to 99 percent of clippings. That means fewer grass clippings sticking to the soles of your shoes or your dog’s paws, and a lawn that looks much tidier after mowing. ANTHBOT You don’t have to empty the full collection bag yourself. An integrated radar sensor monitors how full it is. When the bag is full, the N8 drives to a dumping point you have previously designated in the app, empties its contents, and then resumes mowing. In the fall, it can collect leaves in the same way. ANTHBOT calls this feature “Hands-Free Auto Dumping.” ANTHBOT Particle System: Fine mulch for fertilizing the lawn If you prefer to leave grass clippings on the lawn as natural fertilizer, you can switch to the Particle System. Six blades chop the clippings finely so they fall between the blades of grass and decompose. This helps minimize clumps on the lawn while returning nutrients to the soil. The blade module is bolted in place and can be replaced in a matter of minutes. Since you’ll typically need to switch modules only once or twice per season, it shouldn’t be something you have to do frequently. In practice, this gives you a choice: Leave finely chopped grass clippings on the lawn as fertilizer, or collect them in the grass bag. ANTHBOT Navigation without a boundary wire You don’t need to install a boundary wire in the ground. The ANTHBOT N8 combines full-band RTK positioning with two HDR cameras, a system ANTHBOT calls Dual Vision, to navigate with centimeter-level accuracy. According to ANTHBOT, the RTK module in the robot and its base station can receive signals from 155 satellites. The company also claims the system connects five times faster and offers 150 percent greater signal stability than narrowband RTK systems. Satellite positioning provides location data, while the cameras monitor the mower’s surroundings. If one of the two systems becomes less reliable — for example, beneath trees, alongside a hedge, or under a play structure — the other can help maintain navigation. The cameras are also used for obstacle detection. ANTHBOT says the N8 can recognize more than 1,000 types of objects, including garden hoses and children’s toys. ANTHBOT If cellular coverage on your property is good, the N8 can also use NetRTK over 4G. In that case, you may not need to install your own RTK reference station in the yard. For particularly large or complex properties, ANTHBOT also offers a second RTK station. Designed for large lawns ANTHBOT recommends the N8 for lawns of up to 1,500 square meters, or approximately 16,150 square feet. The manufacturer states a maximum mowing capacity of 135 square meters, or about 1,450 square feet, per hour. Power comes from a 9.2Ah, 198Wh lithium-ion battery, which ANTHBOT says takes around 80 minutes to fully recharge. The robot can handle slopes of up to 45 percent, or about 24 degrees. Without the grass collection bag, the N8 weighs 16.5 kilograms, or about 36 pounds. Its weight helps provide traction when mowing on slopes. Control zones, cutting height, and schedules in the app Once mapping is complete, you can create up to 30 mowing zones and connect them using virtual pathways. You can also set the cutting height between 3 and 7 centimeters, or approximately 1.2 to 2.8 inches, directly in the app, with a motor automatically adjusting the cutting deck. The N8 mows in systematic U-shaped patterns and can mow separately along the edges of flower beds and paths. Once a map has been created, you can make adjustments to it in the app. The robot also includes a rain sensor and can automatically adjust its mowing schedule when it rains. An LED light helps the cameras operate in low-light conditions. Even so, it’s best to schedule mowing during daylight hours, since hedgehogs and other small animals may be active around dusk and dawn. ANTHBOT The housing is IPX6 rated and can be rinsed with a garden hose. When mowing or mulching, the N8 operates at a claimed maximum noise level of 58 decibels. When collecting grass clippings or leaves, the maximum rises to 68 decibels. The robot can connect via 2.4GHz or 5GHz Wi-Fi, 4G, or Bluetooth. This robot handles the cleanup, too Many robotic lawn mower manufacturers focus primarily on automating the mowing itself. The N8 goes a step further by also tackling some of the cleanup that would otherwise need to be done afterward. Its Cyclone System can collect grass clippings and leaves from the lawn, while the Particle System finely chops grass clippings so they can remain on the lawn as mulch. For homeowners with lawns of up to 1,500 square meters, the N8 is the most capable model in ANTHBOT’s current lineup. The ANTHBOT N8 costs $1,699 (RRP), with sales beginning September 10, 2026. Further information on the N8 and other ANTHBOT models is available at anthbot.com.

item.title: AI agents don’t need better prompts. They need better goals
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.12
AI chatbots? So 2025. Right now, it’s all about AI agents, and we just got another one, this time from Facebook parent Meta. Meta Muse is the name of Meta’s new, cloud-based AI agent, and like Gemini Spark, ChatGPT Work, and Claude Cowork, Meta Muse doesn’t just sit in a chatbox. Instead, it’s designed to go out in the world and do things on your behalf. So … do what, exactly? Check out the “Ideas” section in Muse (you can sign in using your Meta account, and you’ll get free access within certain usage limits) and you’ll find dozens of possibilities, ranging from the usual (make a restaurant reservation, book airline tickets) to the esoteric (contact the proper authorities about a pothole, handle the details of any document you snap a picture of). These types of goal-seeking abilities aren’t exclusive to Meta Muse; Gemini Spark can do them as well, along with ChatGPT Work, Claude Cowork, and similar agentic AI tools. Another thing this new class of AI agents share is what they don’t need: prompts, or at least not the kinds of meticulously crafted, behavior-shaping prompts we regularly feed to garden-variety AI chatbots. Defining outcomes, not behavior Rather than working in a context-free environment with precious little to go on beside what you tell them, AI agents can browse web sites, absorb documents, and spawn sub-agents to gather data, giving them hard information that “grounds” them in reality. So what AI agents need from you isn’t so much the “how,” but the “what.” What exactly do you want them to do, and/or not do? Or more specifically, what’s the outcome you’re looking for? Defining outcomes is new prompt engineering when it comes to AI agents, and you’ll also need to give your agent guidelines to keep it from doing more than you asked for (which, as we know, is a bit of an issue these days). One of the most important guidelines is defining what “done” means — that is, giving your agent a finish line they can verify, so it doesn’t go overboard and burn tokens pursuing goals you didn’t ask for. If “defining done” sounds familiar, perhaps you’re remembering a prompt I’ve covered that does that very thing. AI agents also need boundaries, particularly when it comes to buying stuff or accessing local files and directories on your system. Which files can the agent open and/or edit, and which ones are off limits? How much time (and how many tokens) should it spend on a particular task? Finally, at what point (or points) should the agent stop and check in with you? This element is crucial for tasks where (again) the agent does have purchasing power, or to keep it from making decisions on its own when it runs into an unexpected roadblock. If that sounds like a lot of elements to juggle within an agentic AI prompt, it is. That’s why I asked Astra, the new ChatGPT supermodel, for a prompt that lets a regular AI chatbot create an “outcome”-oriented prompt for an AI agent. This prompt (which I’ve pasted below) will kick off a wizard that guides you through the process, asking you what you want the agent to do, what an ideal outcome would be, what constraints the agent should have, and when it should stop to ask you questions. I tried the prompt on ChatGPT Instant, with a simple, low-stakes goal: Find affordable round-trip airline tickets for the holidays. When asked, I gave a specific boundary: Don’t do anything beyond research. I then plugged the resulting “outcome” prompt into both Meta Muse and Gemini Spark, and the agents dutifully plowed through reams of airline rates and pinpointed some surprisingly cheap options. Most importantly, neither of the agents went rogue with my credit card. Here’s the prompt, and remember: Plug it into a standard AI chatbot (like ChatGPT Instant or a “flash” Gemini model) and then hand the result to Meta Muse, Gemini Spark, or another personal AI agent: Help me turn a rough task idea into an outcome prompt I can give to an AI agent. Guide me through a short wizard; don’t execute the task. Start by asking: “What would you like an AI agent to accomplish for you? A rough idea is enough.” Cover four steps, one at a time: 1. OUTCOME What should be different when the agent finishes, and why does it matter? Turn activities like “research flights” into outcomes like “find three flights that fit my schedule and budget, so I can choose.” 2. DONE What should the agent deliver, what requirements must it meet, and how should it verify success? Establish a practical stopping point. Separate what it can verify from what it cannot guarantee. 3. BOUNDARIES What information and tools may it use? What may it change or commit to? Establish time, spending, and privacy limits. Distinguish research from purchasing, booking, messaging, or changing files; don’t assume permission for those actions. 4. WHEN TO ASK Which decisions can it make independently? When should it ask—for example, missing essential information, conflicting requirements, no suitable results, or actions requiring approval? Specify what it should do while awaiting my reply. HOW TO GUIDE ME – Ask one focused question per message, with a few relevant example answers and room for my own response. – Aim for 4–6 questions total. Reuse information I’ve already provided. – If I’m unsure, suggest a practical default for me to confirm. – Distinguish requirements from preferences and suggestions. – Request only necessary information. Use placeholders for sensitive details; never ask for passwords, payment details, or identification documents. – Resolve gaps that materially affect success or permissions; label other assumptions. FINAL OUTPUT Write one self-contained, ready-to-copy prompt addressed to the agent, including: – The outcome, context, deliverables, completion checks, and stopping point. – Hard requirements and softer preferences. – Access, action, resource, and privacy boundaries. – Decisions it may make independently, triggers for asking me, and behavior while waiting. – Instructions to check its capabilities, disclose blocking limitations, and report partial results if completion is impossible within the boundaries. Keep the prompt proportional to the task and grounded in my answers. Briefly list any assumptions or placeholders I should review afterward. Don’t execute the task.

item.title: Why does Windows 11 have a keyboard shortcut just for LinkedIn?
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.07
Windows 11 has tons of useful keyboard shortcuts worth using every day, whether for boosting productivity, doing repetitive tasks faster, accessing hidden panels, or keeping your laptop secure. But did you know there are still secret shortcuts that hardly anyone knows about? Windows Latest recently uncovered one of them—and it’s truly absurd. Instead of a useful function that’d improve daily workflows, this keyboard shortcut takes you straight to LinkedIn. You know, the professional networking platform that’s now owned by Microsoft. Here, try it out for yourself: simply press Ctrl + Alt + Shift + Windows key + L on your keyboard. A new tab will open in your default web browser and immediately load LinkedIn. (There will also be a parameter appended to the URL, which tells LinkedIn you arrived via this shortcut.) Why does this LinkedIn shortcut exist? It’s unusual but not surprising that Microsoft has built this keyboard shortcut directly into Windows. According to Windows Latest, it’s not just integrated into Windows 11 Home but also into Windows 11 Pro and Windows Server. So, it seems to be very important to Microsoft. The LinkedIn shortcut may be a relic from the past, back when Microsoft had still planned to integrate LinkedIn more closely with Windows. This is pure speculation, but it’s conceivable given how Microsoft is currently handling Copilot (i.e., shoving it into every corner of Windows). Previously, this shortcut was actually linked to the Office key, which no longer exists. The relevant support page indicates that this not only allowed you to access the LinkedIn keyboard shortcut, but also a few other really useful shortcuts: - Office key + W → Word - Office key + P → PowerPoint - Office key + X → Excel - Office key + O → Outlook - Office key + T → Teams - Office key + D → OneDrive - Office key + N → OneNote To use these shortcuts now, you simply need to replace the Office key with Ctrl + Alt + Shift + Windows key—which, admittedly, is a bit tricky in how you have to contort your fingers. But it works!

item.title: Tapo’s 4K solar security camera kit hits a new low price at Amazon
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.84
If you’ve always wanted an outdoor security camera for your home but dreaded the wiring, the battery upkeep, or the paid subscriptions for storing footage, then here’s a deal for you. The Tapo C660 Kit addresses all of those concerns, and right now it’s on sale for $115.99 at Amazon. That’s a brand-new low price and a big discount off its original $169.99. My favorite thing about the C660 is how easy it is to set up. Get up on a ladder, drill a couple of screws into where you want it mounted, actually mount the thing, and you’re done. The included solar panel keeps it powered around the clock and only needs about 45 minutes of sunlight every day to stay topped off. The camera is fully wireless too, so you won’t need to worry about wiring during installation—just hook it up to your Wi-Fi network and you’re good to go. The camera itself is pretty darn good too. It records in high-res 4K and it can see everywhere. With full 360-degree pan and 98-degree tilt, there’s no spot in your yard that this camera can’t cover. You can steer it via the Tapo app, set it to auto-patrol, or let smart motion tracking follow people, cars, and/or pets as they move across the view. And yes, you don’t need a paid subscription for local storage. It can save to an inserted microSD card (sold separately) or a hard drive using the Tapo H500 CentralHub (also sold separately). The Tapo C660 Kit is a great entry point for homeowners who want easy-to-install 4K surveillance that’s solar-powered. However, it has a few caveats. If you want true 24/7 continuous recording, the C660 drops down to 1 FPS to conserve battery. The tracking system drains battery fast if it’s overlooking a high-traffic area. And while it’s compatible with Amazon Alexa and Google Home, it doesn’t support Apple HomeKit.

item.title: Microsoft is finally tackling Windows 11’s annoying Bluetooth problem
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.73
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft is finally addressing long-standing Bluetooth issues in Windows 11, with fixes rolling out through Insider builds. - The updates target audio streaming crashes, microphone compatibility problems, and unreliable Bluetooth toggle errors that have frustrated users. - Improvements also include more stable connection status displays, better Settings page reliability, and clearer volume change notifications during voice control use. Many users regard the Bluetooth function as a notorious weak point in Windows 11, and even Microsoft clearly sees Bluetooth as a problem. With the latest Windows update, the Redmond-based company is now looking to tackle this Achilles’ heel of its operating system. The changelog for the Windows 11 Insider Release Preview Build 26100.9539/26200.9539 for Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2 highlights, alongside various other improvements, places a particular focus on Windows 11’s Bluetooth functionality. According to the changelog, Windows 11 is receiving these Bluetooth-related updates to improve its reliability and usability: - During voice calls, the Windows Shell pop-up window for volume control is now displayed when the volume of a Bluetooth Classic Audio accessory is adjusted using the volume controls on the device itself. This provides visual feedback on the new volume level. - This update improves the accuracy of the connection status displayed by Windows for accessories whose connection to the PC has been interrupted. - This update improves the stability of the ‘Bluetooth & devices’ page in Settings when managing Bluetooth and audio devices. - This update resolves an issue where the Bluetooth wireless connection might have been disabled, but the toggle on the ‘Bluetooth & devices’ page in Settings was shown as enabled. - This update improves the stability and compatibility of Bluetooth audio. - This update improves microphone compatibility with certain Bluetooth Classic audio accessories. - This update resolves an issue that could cause a crash (error code 0x139) when streaming Bluetooth audio. - This update improves reliability and performance when using LE Audio accessories. - This update improves the reliability of shared audio content. It remains to be seen whether this will, in future, eliminate all the causes of Bluetooth connections becoming unstable or dropping out completely. For the time being, only Insider testers can try out the improvements anyway. It is currently unknown when Microsoft will incorporate the above-mentioned improvements into the final version of Windows 11.

item.title: Will Siri Recap make the Apple Watch creepy? Privacy experts weigh in
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.63
I’ve always thought of the Apple Watch as one of the friendliest and most helpful Apple devices, sitting on your wrist with a colorful watch face, telling the time, nudging you to get off your tush, gently tapping you (or not) with text alerts, and even sounding the alarm if it detects anything amiss with your heartbeat. But a new Siri AI feature, announced earlier this week during Apple’s fall hardware event, could land unsuspecting Apple Watch users who enable the option into the middle of a heated AI privacy debate, according to several experts I spoke with. Welcome to another edition of Prompt Mode, your weekly AI newsletter. I’m your host, Ben Patterson. Each week on Prompt Mode, I’ll be serving up analysis of the AI trends that matter to everyday users like you and me. Stay tuned for practical AI tips, hands-on experiences with the latest AI tools, and–you guessed it–prompts to help you get the most out of your AI assistants. Thanks for reading, and if you like what you see, just sign up right here. The feature, called Siri Recap, lets the new Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 keep an ear out for nearby conversations and deliver “high-level summaries” of what was said. Siri Recap will arrive later this year as a beta product, Apple says. Alongside Siri Recap, the latest Apple Watches will offer Live Rewind, an on-demand feature that gives you a “text snippet” of the prior 15 seconds of a conversation. You activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the digital crown of your Apple Watch, an action that also triggers an audible chime as well as a telltale animation on the screen. But unlike Live Rewind, Siri Recap can work passively in the background, intercepting nearby conversations whenever it’s on — which, potentially, could be all the time. Apple says Siri Recap users can choose “exactly where and when Siri Recap takes notes” via a schedule (such as “only at work” or “never at night”) and that the feature can be manually turned on or off from the pop-up Control Center. Crucially, Apple says that Siri Recap doesn’t store recordings or verbatim transcripts of conversations, but instead “creates high-level Apple Intelligence-generated summaries” intended to “jog your memory” rather than capture everything that was said. In another key caveat, Siri Recap doesn’t track who said what, thus avoiding the use of voice fingerprinting technology. Apple Apple has taken other Siri Recap privacy measures, including insuring that financial data and “certain personal identifiers” are “omitted” from the summaries, as well as detailing a “Secure Enclave” in the Apple Watch’s new S11 chip that privately processes audio on the watch itself, while Privacy Cloud Compute handles cloud processing duties in an end-to-end encrypted pipe. Those measures seem at least partially designed to avoid running afoul of state and federal privacy laws, which offer a confusing and often conflicting patchwork of regulations about what constitutes illegal eavesdropping and what doesn’t. But even if Siri Recap isn’t actually storing full recordings or transcripts of overheard conversations, the mere act of “intercepting” them without notifying the involved parties could land a user in legal hot water. “As I understand this Siri Recap feature, they don’t have any kind of notice or audible thing that’s happening, and so the individual who’s being recorded in this case is really provided no notice,” said Brian J. McGuiness, a partner at Indianapolis law firm Barnes & Thornburg and an expert in privacy and AI issues. (Apple has since clarified that an audible chime occurs when Recap is actively used to recall a conversation, and that the AI feature only provides general summaries, not pure transcription.) “So on the one hand, [Apple is] putting in some pretty serious privacy-by-design things in that they don’t necessarily have to and others aren’t doing,” McGuinnis continued. “On the other hand, they haven’t really gone the full way to say, we really want people to know when this device is being used or this feature is being used. [Apple] kind of left it up to the user … whether or not you want to tell people this is happening.” In a support document, Apple says you should “be mindful of those around you” when using its new Audio Intelligence features, including Siri Recap. “While audio is not recorded and stored, and no speakers are attributed, consider those around you where conversations might be private or sensitive.” I’ve reached out to Apple for furthen comment. Aside from the legal issues surrounding Siri Recap, there’s also the ethics and overall “ick” factor of microphone-equipped AI wearables in general, which may be listening at any given moment. “Our right to conversational privacy must include freedom from other people, without our clear opt-in consent, using technology to document what we are saying,” Electronic Frontier Foundation Privacy Litigation Director Adam Schwartz said in a statement to PCWorld, adding that the organization is EFF is “disappointed” Apple is planning to ship the Siri Recap feature. “We suggest people should think twice before using this technology, out of respect to the conversational privacy of others.” Of course, the Apple Watch isn’t the first AI-enabled device that can listen in on conversations. From Otter, the popular AI transcription app that can attend Zoom meetings (and is now embroiled in a privacy lawsuit) to Meta Glasses, AI gadgets and wearables with built-in microphones are becoming increasingly commonplace. Siri Recap on the Apple Watch appears poised to accelerate the trend. “Thinking back, you know, you go back to the old … ‘is this creepy’ meter, and everybody would think that carrying around an always-on microphone, hidden in a bag or a hidden camera in a buttonhole, is creepy,” Barnes & Thornberg’s Brian McGuiness told me. “But as we normalize this and make it so prevalent and accessible to the average consumer, you’re only going to see more and more people getting more and more comfortable with the idea of recording these things.” More in AI this week - I let ChatGPT copy my writing style with help from one of its latest tools. The result? It made me sound like AI. (PCWorld) - A growing chorus of researchers is sounding the alarm about how self-improving AI could wipe out humanity within the next decade. One proposed solution? Building more AI. (New York Times, OpenAI) - Just as solar panels can help you save on power bills, so can local AI models cut down on your cloud AI costs. (PCWorld) - Word that AI helped solve one of math’s greatest unsolved problems devolved into fingerpointing, with an NYU mathematics professor accusing OpenAI researchers of cheating in their solution. OpenAI has denied the allegations. (TechCrunch) - A new version of ChatGPT’s image-generating tool includes a feature that can make pictures based on your hand-drawn sketches. (OpenAI) Prompt of the week: The “give outcomes to your agents” prompt Unlike typical AI chatbots, AI agents like Gemini Spark, Claude Cowork, ChatGPT Work, and (now) Meta Muse don’t need prompts so much as they need outcomes. Instead of telling them how to behave, you want to tell your agents what you want at the end, whether it’s the lowest prices for holiday airline tickets or getting that pothole in front of your driveway fixed. Using OpenAI’s new GPT-6 “Astra” model, I’ve crafted a prompt that can help you create a fleshed-out agentic outcome, complete with guidelines for keeping your AI agents on track, a clear finish line for the task, and instructions on when it should reach out to you for help. That’s all for now! Thanks for reading the latest issue of Prompt Mode. Want more next week? Don’t forget to sign up to start receiving this newsletter in your inbox.

item.title: AI subscriptions are the electric bill. Your PC is the solar panel
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.59
The AI pendulum has swung back and forth throughout the last few years, from ChatGPT and Copilot in the cloud, then back to local AI and the PC’s newfound NPU, then back to independent agents like Claude. Now it’s headed the way of the PC once again, abandoning privacy arguments (which still stand strong!) for a more straightforward argument: It’s better for your wallet. A few announcements at IFA underscored what is now the prevailing argument in AI circles: AI’s selling point is that it essentially multiplies your productivity, assigning independent agents to tasks you’d otherwise perform yourself. The trouble is that it all comes at a cost. You’ll pay for a cloud AI subscription, with a limited number of tokens which typically expire at the most inopportune time. But no matter what, cloud AI will always keep charging you. It’s the exact reason so many people invest in solar panels for their home. If my local utility company is going to keep charging me money (and raising their rates) why not invest in my own power generation and get it it for “free?” We’re entering an era where your local PCs can become a personal AI “solar panel” of sorts, driven by AI goliaths like Nvidia and Microsoft — but not only by those titans. Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently. I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here. It’s a cost thing Nvidia, naturally, has always been in favor of powerful, local GPUs. Nvidia’s Personal AI Router (PAIR) is an intriguing concept, combining every GPU-equipped device (AMD or Nvidia) on your network into a shared pool of AI computing power. Nvidia said it has tested RTX PAIR on up to 18 devices on a local network, though there is a catch: PAIR assumes a hardwired network is in place, not the mesh routers throughput homes. That means that you’d have to build in a hardwired switch of some kind. Nvidia I actually think a smarter implementation is Exo, a project that’s been on my to-do list. Exo basically (supposedly) just finds and assimilates both CPU and GPU resources and storage into an AI cluster, daisy-chaining them together via Thunderbolt connections. For me, with lots of Thunderbolt cables, this seems like a no-brainer. It’s also much more forgiving for homes with existing hardware of all stripes… though hardwiring a Thunderbolt cluster likely requires much tighter quarters than an Ethernet cluster built around your house, which RTX PAIR offers. The problem with both solutions, of course, is power: you’re going to be pulling a lot of juice and generating a lot of heat to make either solution work. Wouldn’t it be nice to take advantage of the cloud and local AI? That’s where Microsoft is now, with what it’s calling “unmetered intelligence.” In a presentation at IFA in Berlin last week, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of Windows + Devices, Mark Linton, argued that PC makers and owners should just “offload to the PC” their AI workloads. “We mean that these powerful PCs can complement what you do in the cloud, but you shouldn’t have to go to the cloud for models that you can use every day,” Linton said. “What if your PC were powerful enough, and essentially you can change your token economics by running it locally on your PC?” It’s certainly a far cry from when Microsoft and hardware makers were pitching the NPU as the engine of AI, while we (and others) were discovering that the GPU was actually a better choice for generative AI, and that the CPU was more appropriate for managing AI agents. NPUs still have a role to play, it seems, but as efficient engines of small, smart tasks like the filtering algorithms in Windows Studio Effects. Chris Hoffman / Foundry We know that most of the time our laptops and desktops sit mostly idle why we, as humans, write, read and think. Background features like Windows Studio Effects and Voice Focus use AI to improve the PC experience without overwhelming your PC’s resources. Windows Foundry offered an alternative, prioritizing CPUs and GPUs. But it still feels like Microsoft is still stuck in the talking stage, rather than the doing stage. Two other companies changed that at IFA, offering intriguing visions of what local AI could be. Local AI is heading toward your desk…but will it be a PC? The first is Anker, the Chinese peripheral powerhouse that debuted the MindBase, a central smart hub that connects over 100 Anker devices via its OmniLink protocol. Apple, Google, and Amazon also have these sort of smart hubs, connected wirelessly, allowing something like a Google Home to connect your lights and thermostat. Anker Anker’s MindBase goes beyond that. At its heart is an AI layer capable of 26 TOPS, nearing the 40 TOPS of a Copilot PC. What I found especially interesting, though, was its so-called EverSafe Memory, an API layer which allowed it to connect up to 48TB (!) of local storage. That goes, way, WAY beyond what a convention “smart home” device can offer. The other candidate is Violoop, an AI product that has been knocking at my door for a week or so. Violoop is an AI appliance: connect an HDMI cable from your PC to the small box, and it can “see” what’s on your screen, intuit what needs to be done, and act — but only when you tap the big confirmation button on top of it. The company promises that the Violoop will queue up multiple independent actions, from checking your calendar to writing an email in your tone and voice. How useful is it? That remains to be seen. Violoop That’s a similar approach to what my colleague Adam Patrick Murray attempted with his mini AI PC project from two weeks ago, when he used both an MSI mini PC as a command-and-control hub as well as a Framework Desktop with an AMD Ryzen “Strix Halo” chip inside. (Why two PCs? The argument, Adam told me, was that if one crashed or ran out of resources it would be easier to reconstruct.) I have to believe that we’re going to see this trend continue. And why wouldn’t it? Take a Thunderbolt docking station. Some Thunderbolt 5 docks now include local storage in the form of an SSD slot, while docks like the Humbird 3 blur the line between docking stations and external GPUs. At CES 2026, Plugable showed off the TBT5-AI, a small local AI server connected by Thunderbolt. You know, hardware makers would kill to sell us two devices for our desk, rather than just one. And if consumers, office workers, and creatives buy into into this idea that AI can offload some of the day-to-day drudgery of their work life, they might just do it. What’s the difference between a mini PC, a single-board computer, and an AI appliance? Not a hell of a lot. And it’s a brand new world for hardware makers to play in. Productivity in the news: - Microsoft’s September security update is out, and many of the usability features Microsoft promised earlier are here, including the moveable taskbar. It might not be an enormous change, but hey, Microsoft responded to complaints. It’s only been, what, five years? - Via Macworld, Apple is talking about Siri Recap, which makes AI voice transcription really mainstream. (But kinda icky, privacy-wise?) - Speaking of the IFA show that took place in Berlin…meet the winners of our IFA Best of Show! - Microsoft’s Project Zenith isn’t aimed at you or me, but developers. Still, it’s a tailored computing experience based around AMD’s Ryzen Strix Halo chip and some specific applications. We’ve seen developer devices before, so this is nothing new. But my original premise for Smart Mode this week was the amazing niches that computing now fits into, and this is an example of that. - Buying a laptop? Here’s what matters. - I’m not a huge fan of Windows Voice Typing (transcription is just as good, really) but my colleague Sam Singleton walks you through what Windows has to offer here. - Looks like there’s a one-day-only sale on Windows 11 Pro for $10! - I could never really get into standing desks, though I tried. I like standing! I just don’t like typing while standing. What about you? Productivity on camera: I love laptop utility software. Here’s why! Productivity tip of the week: I’m really torn on the concept of task stacking. On one hand, it’s certainly useful for certain work; if I’m headed to the garage where the washer lives, I’ll check and see if any laundry needs to be taken downstairs, or removed from the dryer. Likewise, my wife or I will fold clothes while watching TV — gotta keep that laundry train moving in a house with teenagers living in it. So task stacking — performing multiple tasks at once — certainly makes sense for thoughtless tasks. In some ways, that’s the premise of local AI, right? You’re offloading drudge work. But if you need to sit down and think through something, I have an issue with optimizing my time to perform those tasks efficiently. I mean, if I have to plan out my time to maximize task stacking, could I be earning some of that back by simply performing them serially and somewhat inefficiently? If you have any thoughts, drop me a line! Thanks for reading! Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

item.title: A cheap adapter can add USB-C to your old PC
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.35
Over the past few years, USB-C has become the go-to connection for IT devices. Smartphones, external SSDs, cameras, and docking stations now rely almost exclusively on this standard. However, many older Windows PCs still have no USB-C ports, or just one. That doesn’t mean you have to do without modern devices, though. With a few simple steps, USB-C can be easily retrofitted to older systems. The quickest way is to use an existing USB-A port. All you need is a small USB-A-to-USB-C adapter. Simply plug this into a free USB-A port, and you can then connect a USB-C cable directly. For individual devices such as smartphones, webcams, external drives, or chargers, this is an affordable and straightforward solution. Such adapters usually cost just a few dollars and work surprisingly reliably in practice. They are particularly suitable if you only connect a device occasionally and do not need any additional ports. Ugreen However, you shouldn’t expect any speed boosts from this solution, as it merely changes the type of connection. The transfer speed is still determined by the USB-A port standard. If you regularly use several USB-C devices, a USB hub or a docking station is much more practical. These devices are also connected to the computer via an existing USB port and provide additional interfaces. Once connected, Windows automatically recognizes the hub as a new USB device. This gives you access to several USB-C ports as well as additional USB-A ports. Numerous models also offer further connection options such as Ethernet ports, SD card slots, or even video outputs for monitors. Please note, however, that you should connect the hub or docking station to at least a USB 3.0 port to ensure sufficient bandwidth and power. YEELIYA A docking station is particularly useful when you need to connect multiple devices at the same time. Instead of plugging several cables directly into the computer, all connections run via a central station on your desk. This not only makes things more convenient but also simplifies cable management considerably. Such a docking solution can be particularly practical for laptops, as several devices can be connected via a single port. Consequently, they are also more expensive, with prices starting at around $50, while hubs are available for well under $20. If you own a desktop PC, there’s another particularly neat and powerful solution: Many computer cases have free PCIe slots on the motherboard. Expansion cards that provide additional USB-C ports can be installed here. Installation is relatively straightforward and requires just a few steps: First, switch off the computer completely and disconnect it from the mains. Then open the case and locate a free PCIe slot on the motherboard. Benq We recommend using at least a PCIe 3.0 x4 slot to benefit from the high speeds. Remove the relevant slot cover at the rear of the case and carefully insert the expansion card into the slot. The card is then secured with a screw and the case is closed again.
